01. Introduction / This is SEB
This is SEB
SEB is a leading northern European financial services group, with a history 
dating back to 1856. Innovation, entrepreneurship and an international 
perspec­tive are part of our identity. We have a strong ambition to accelerate 
the pace towards a sustainable future for people, businesses and society.  
We want to be a leading catalyst in the sustainability transition.
Our business is divided into four divisions: Corporate & Investment  
Banking, Business & Retail Banking, Wealth & Asset Management and Baltic. 
We serve customers with a wide range of products and services in  
Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Germany and 
the United Kingdom. Switzerland, Austria and the Netherlands are defined as 
home markets with a selective approach. Furthermore, we support our home 
market customers around the world from Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, 
­Singapore, New Delhi, São Paulo, New York, to Luxembourg, Nice, Kyiv 
and Warsaw.

Customer driven growth in
a changing environment 
2025 was marked by geopolitical uncertainty, 
shifting trade patterns and declining interest 
rates, while customers and financial markets 
demonstrated strong resilience. SEB enters 
2026 from a position of strength, with a 
continued focus on developing customer 
relationships, investing to future-proof the 
bank, and enhancing its competitiveness. 
Chair of the Board Marcus Wallenberg and President and CEO Johan 
Torgeby share their reflections in a conversation about the past year 
and SEB’s path ahead. 
Which factors in the global environment had the 
greatest impact during 2025? 
Marcus Wallenberg: Trade tensions have been a dominant factor. 
Any form of protectionism leads to shifting trade patterns and higher 
cross-border transaction costs. As a result, corporate customers have 
needed to restructure supply chains and redistribute investments 
across several regions. Geopolitical uncertainty, particularly in 
­Northern Europe, has dampened investments and economic growth.
It is essential that Europe – our most important market – develops 
a new strategic direction to strengthen its competitiveness. 
Johan Torgeby, President and CEO, to the left and 
Marcus Wallenberg, Chair of the Board of Directors, to the right

Johan Torgeby: 2025 was characterised by strong equity markets, 
a significant decline in interest rates, lower inflation, and a stronger 
Swedish krona. Despite global turmoil, financial markets proved resil­
ient, meaning that uncertainty did not translate into financial risk. Both 
corporates and households demonstrated healthy cash flows, result­
ing in continued subdued lending demand. In Europe, political uncer­
tainty weighed on the economic development, although we also noted 
gradual stabilisation in several major economies.
How has SEB met customer needs and expectations 
during a year of rapid change?
Marcus Wallenberg: SEB plays an important role as a stable, interna­
tional bank. Our strong balance sheet and diversified business model 
enable us to support customers under different market conditions 
and meet their evolving needs, also when the external environment 
shifts quickly.
Johan Torgeby: SEB has a key role in supporting customers with 
responsible advice and capital. Over the year, we saw increased activ­
ity, particularly in investment banking, where advisory needs grew in 
line with healthy investor risk appetite. We also saw higher activity in 
cash management and risk management services. We are pleased to 
have maintained a leading position among large corporate customers 
in the Nordics, according to external customer satisfaction surveys. 
We also play a key advisory role for private customers during times 
of uncertainty.
How is SEB working to strengthen customer 
relationships and competitiveness?
Marcus Wallenberg: We work hard to meet customers’ high expecta­
tions. In the corporate segment, we see intensifying competition, both 
from major international banks and from the growing private credit 
market. In the Nordics, the Euro is gaining in importance and euro capa­
bility in financial services such as cash management and payments is 
essential to meet customer needs in an increasingly internationalised 
market. Stablecoins, which may become a 
key part of the future financial system and 
are traded in both Euro and US dollars, are 
also likely to be an important competitive 
­factor.
Johan Torgeby: We see increased 
­competition across the entire financial 
­sector. ­Sweden has high customer mobility, 
which means low barriers to switching banks 
and therefore strong competitive pressure. 
We therefore need to stay ahead, and 
strengthening customer relationships is a 
central focus area in our business plan. In 
the retail segment, the guiding principles are 
simplicity, speed, and customer centricity, 
delivered through digital services and per­
sonal advice. For large corporates, crucial 
factors are service, customer satisfaction 
and our international network, that knows 
our export-oriented customers well. I would 
also highlight S&P’s upgrade of SEB’s long 
term issuer credit rating to AA–. Having 
access to cost-efficient funding further 
strengthens our ability to support our 
­customers and enhances our competitive position in all markets 
where we are present. 
How would you describe this year’s results? 
Johan Torgeby: Our 2025 result was robust, considering that the 
wheels of the economy were only slowly beginning to turn. The lower 
interest rates had a negative impact on net interest income, as 
expected, corresponding to a decline of 10 per cent. At the same 
time, net fee and commission income also increased by 10 per cent.
This clearly demonstrates the strength of our diversified business 
mix. We also enter 2026 with an improved cost position. Costs are 
slowing as planned, and we are entering a 
phase in which we can make targeted invest­
ments in prioritised areas to continuously 
future proof the bank. Combined with reve­
nue driving business plan initiatives, our 
ambition is to have a trajectory where 
income grows faster than costs in the 
medium to the long term. We have a strong 
focus on profitability and on our long-term 
financial target where SEB aspires to reach 
a sustainable return on equity of 15 per cent.
Marcus Wallenberg: The result for 2025 was 
stable given the economic conditions and the
significant uncertainty that has character-
ised the global markets during the year.
The bank has a solid liquidity position and 
a strong capital base, which enables us to
support our customers – and the broader 
economy – over the long term, in different 
economic cycles.
What are the key components 
of SEB’s 2030 Strategy and 
the 2025–2027 Business plan?
Johan Torgeby: We continue to focus on two strategic priorities: 
­Business growth, and Technology and efficiency. In 2025, we continued 
to selectively expand our large corporate business – a strategy that 
over time has proven both profitable and cost efficient while main­
taining our risk profile. For example, we opened a new branch in 
Amsterdam and made targeted efforts within private capital. Within 
our wealth and asset management business, we are driving initiatives 
to strengthen digital capabilities, accelerating growth in products and 
services, and further strengthening our position in the pensions mar­
ket. Growing and future-proofing the retail banking business is also

Rapid technological development, 
especially AI, is transforming the 
financial sector. How is SEB 
approaching this shift? 
Marcus Wallenberg: Technology is a critical 
factor for competitiveness, and the pace of 
development will shape the bank over the 
long term. We have high ambitions within AI, 
and our work spans multiple dimensions – 
not only efficiency and internal processes 
but also product development and improved 
customer offerings. To meet regulatory 
demands and develop scalable solutions, we 
continue to invest in AI, automation and data, 
with a focus on accelerating implementation.
Johan Torgeby: We work with AI from three 
perspectives: strengthening productivity and 
efficiency in our operations, developing products and services that 
create customer value, and being a partner to the rapidly growing AI 
community. We also need to consider how AI will reshape the entire 
financial ecosystem. To accelerate our efforts, we have established a 
COO function focused on new technology and faster time to market. 
We are also following developments in tokenisation and digital assets 
and, in 2025, joined a consortium with the intention of issuing a 
euro-denominated stablecoin. We are also developing advanced 
AI infrastructure in Sweden together with a consortium of industry-­
leading companies, using Nvidia’s technology and through the 
co-founded company Sferical AI. 
Global sustainability initiatives 
have been marked by uncertainty. 
What role does SEB play in the 
climate transition?
Marcus Wallenberg: We remain committed 
to our high ambitions and sustainability goals 
for 2030, with continued focus on increasing 
our sustainability activities, such as green 
financing and reducing the fossil credit expo­
sure in our energy portfolio. This is a long-
term effort. At the same time, the external 
environment is changing rapidly. The political 
and regulatory developments require us to 
adapt, navigate increasing complexity, and 
continue supporting our customers’ transi­
tion with flexibility and proactivity.
Johan Torgeby: The ambitions of the 
­business sector remain, despite increased 
uncertainty. The war in Ukraine has high­
lighted the risks associated with dependency 
on non-democratic energy sources. Energy 
security is now a central factor alongside cli­
mate benefits. Solutions need to strengthen 
both climate targets and societal stability. 
SEB advocates an orderly, demand driven transition in which the use 
of fossil fuels in society decreases. Our most important contribution 
is to support customers in their transition to reduce the demand for 
oil and gas.
How do you view the dividend proposed by the Board 
of Directors for the 2026 Annual General Meeting?
Marcus Wallenberg: The proposed dividend reflects the bank’s 
strong financial results and strong financial position. The Board of 
Directors has proposed an ordinary dividend of SEK 8.50 per share 
and a special dividend of SEK 2.50 per share. In 2025, SEB communi­
cated an intention to move to semi-annual dividends from 2026. After
receiving feedback from market participants and evaluating alterna­
tive options for processing such a transition, SEB has for now decided 
to maintain its current dividend payout structure.
Johan Torgeby: We enter 2026 with a capital position that remains 
very strong, supported by solid capital generation throughout the 
year. The proposed dividend is aligned with our long-term financial 
target of distributing around half of annual profit as an ordinary divi­
dend. It is important to remember that the dividend benefits the 
broader economy – through households, foundations, and pension 
funds. We also use share buybacks as a form of capital repatriation.
What are your expectations for 2026?
Marcus Wallenberg: We entered 2026 with cautious optimism. 
At the same time, the year began with renewed threats of tariffs, 
which once again created global uncertainty. The outlook is difficult 
to assess. As a bank, we prepare for all eventualities to maintain 
our flexibility.
Johan Torgeby: For some time, we have hoped for a clear pickup in 
economic activity, which has not yet materialised. Ahead of 2026, 
however, we noted more positive signals, such as signs of higher 
­consumption and increasing investment in Sweden. At the same time, 
uncertainty remains significant, requiring optimism to be balanced 
with a degree of caution. In this environment, SEB is well positioned 
to support customers, both through challenging times, and when 
growth eventually gains momentum.
	
Uncertainty did 
not translate into 
financial risk.

President and CEO

Our contribution to societal development 
The financial services described earlier are at the core of a bank’s operations. But beyond creating value for the 
customers who demand and use these services, they also create value for the economy and society as a whole.
For entrepreneurship, innovation and 
development 
Ever since we were founded, we have helped 
pave the way for the major shifts in society and 
supported entrepreneurs and innovations that have had a major 
impact on our societies – from railways and electrification to 
industrialisation and automation. In the same way, we are today 
an important part of the big shifts of our time: the ongoing 
­sustainability transition and digitalisation.
For the sustainability transition 
Banks have a crucial role to play in helping to 
­enable the sustainability transition by channelling 
capital flows to low-carbon operations and sustain­
able business models. 
At SEB, our goal is to be a part of building a more sustainable 
and resilient future and we are convinced we can achieve the 
greatest impact by actively collaborating with and supporting our 
customers. We do this by integrating sustainability criteria into 
our lending and investment practices and supporting industries 
in their transition. 
Through comprehensive advisory services – including guid­
ance for sustainable financing, energy sector transformation, 
and investor engagement – as well as financing and investments, 
we support businesses in identifying new opportunities, manag­
ing emerging risks, and delivering positive environmental and 
social outcomes. 
By supporting our customers and society to transition to a sus­
tainable future, we shift our own credit portfolio to sustainable 
activities while reducing our fossil exposure.
For digitalisation
The development of digital technology has brought 
about an accessibility revolution for many banking 
customers. Banks, together with their customers, 
have been driving this development and been early in developing 
and applying new technology. 
In 1996, SEB became one of the first banks in the world to 
offer all its private customers services on the internet. In 2010, 
we launched a mobile app, and in collaboration with other banks, 
we have created the user-friendly solutions BankID and Swish. 
Right now, we are witnessing rapid technological develop­
ment, particularly within AI, where SEB is contributing by invest­
ing in new technologies that enhance the customer experience, 
foster innovation and help shape future financial systems. 
For financial stability 
A well-functioning banking system is a fundamen­
tal pillar of economic security in society. For the 
financial system to remain stable, it is essential 
that both the market and the public have confidence in it. This 
requires banks to be well-managed and sufficiently capitalised 
to fulfil their critical role in society. To be resilient, a bank must 
in turn be profitable, enabling it to build reserves and invest in 
its operations. 
Our contribution to the broader economy
Every year, banks return billions to society’s economic cycle, 
for example through interest payments to our customers and 
bondholders. In addition, dividends to our shareholders bene­
fit millions of Swedes, among others, through pension funds 
and fund savings.
Through SEB’s largest shareholder Investor AB and the 
Wallenberg Foundations, a part of our dividend goes to basic 
research and education. 
As a bank, SEB is a large taxpayer and employer.

02. Our strategy / Driving forces
A world in 
constant 
change 
Our operating environment is changing rapidly. As a 
bank, we must navigate this environment and adapt our 
operations, strategy, and business plan to remain rele­
vant and be able to continue supporting our customers 
and the communities in which we operate. 
We are currently experiencing strong transforma­
tional pressure across both business and society, in sev­
eral interconnected areas. This includes the geopolitical 
developments and their impact on Sweden and our 
home markets, particularly in relation to European 
­security, resilience, strategic autonomy, growth, and 
competitive­ness. It also includes the rapid pace of 
­technological development and innovation, as well as 
the ongoing transition towards net zero emissions.
A new ­geo­political ­
landscape
2025 was marked by continued geopolitical uncertainty including 
tensions in global trade and growing concerns about the world 
order and the transatlantic relationship. Ongoing armed conflicts, 
such as Russia’s war in Ukraine, have also influenced develop­
ments. This has led to new priorities in Europe with substantial 
investments in defence, security, and resilience, including energy 
supply, critical infrastructure, and emerging technologies.
As a leading financial institution in northern Europe, SEB strives 
to actively contribute to strengthening Europe’s defence, security, 
and resilience. By providing financial services and investments, we 
support initiatives that safeguard democracy, freedom, stability, 
and human rights.
In 2025:
•	 SEB established a dedicated Security and Defence unit and 
updated its Sector Policy on Arms and Defence to adapt to the 
evolving security landscape, contribute to enhancing Europe’s 
security, defence and resilience, and strengthen the bank’s 
work, offering and commitment within these areas.
•	 SEB Asset Management launched the new thematic fund 
SEB European Defence & Security Fund. The fund company 
also enabled additional funds to invest in the conventional 
defence industry.
•	 SEB engaged in dialogues with a range of stakeholders on 
­Swedish and European security and defence.
The importance of the ongoing 
climate transition
Geopolitical developments have, in several regions, affected global 
commitment to the climate transition. In some countries, political 
decisions have created uncertainty around the long-term sustain­
ability investments in the business sector. For example, the United 
States’ withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and the dissolution of 
the Net-Zero Banking Alliance, following the departure of several 
global banks, have raised questions about the pace of the global 
transition. 
Nevertheless, climate change and the related climate transition 
continue to be regarded as a defining issue for the future in many 
parts of the world, not least in Europe. Within the European Union, 
the transition and phase-out of fossil fuels constitute one of three 
key pillars in efforts to strengthen the region’s competitiveness. 
This is closely linked to geopolitical developments and the growing 
focus on Europe’s resilience, security, energy supply and strategic 
auto­nomy. The climate transition also remains a priority for SEB’s 
customers and fund investors. 
In 2025:
•	 SEB reiterated the commitment to achieving a net zero credit 
portfolio by 2050 as well as its commitment to the ambitions 
and goals it has adopted to reach that target.
•	 Climate-related ambitions and goals are the Carbon Exposure 
Index, ­Sustainability Activity Index, and SEB’s 2030 sector 
­targets. See p. 112.
•	 SEB Asset Management continued to engage with investee 
companies to encourage them to set ambitious emissions targets 
aligned with the Paris Agreement. The share of investee 
companies with science-based targets increased to 63 percent 
by the end of 2025 from 58 per cent a year earlier.

Technological development 
shaping finance
Technological advancement is accelerating rapidly. We are at a turning point, 
­particularly within the field of AI. 
As an example, the pace of development – from research and development, 
through the innovation phase, and to the creation of products, services, and offerings 
– is intensifying. Technology has become a key driver of competitiveness. This rapid 
development is affecting the financial industry, the business ­sector and society 
at large. 
SEB has long been a driving force in technological advancement, together with 
­customers and other banks. The bank has been an early adopter and developer of 
new technologies that benefit both customers and society. 
Two areas are expected to have a particularly significant impact on the financial 
industry going forward: AI and blockchain technology. AI is central to SEB’s ambition 
to strengthen the customer offering, increase productivity and future-proof the bank. 
Blockchain technology, which is evolving ­rapidly, is expected to play a key role in the 
financial systems of the future.
In 2025:
•	 SEB joined a consortium of industry-leading companies to build advanced AI infra­
structure in Sweden using Nvidia’s latest technology. Together, the companies have 
founded the joint venture Sferical AI and established an Nvidia AI Technology Center 
in Sweden.
•	 SEB joined a consortium with major European banks to launch a euro-denominated 
­stablecoin, compliant with the EU regulation on markets in crypto-assets. This digital 
payment instrument, leveraging blockchain technology, aims to become a trusted 
European ­payment standard within the digital ecosystem.
•	 The work to future-proof the bank continued, by developing AI solutions across 
­several new areas, including HR, risk management, transaction monitoring, financial 
crime ­prevention and Know Your Customer (KYC) analyses. These domains represent 
strategic opportunities where AI can contribute to significantly enhanced ­efficiency.

Sustainability targets
SEB has established strategic metrics to track the progress 
on the most important sustainability work.
Our sustainability strategy 
SEB’s sustainability strategy is built on our purpose: We exist 
to positively shape the future with responsible advice and 
­capital. Today and for generations to come. 
We are committed to partnering with our customers in their 
transition to more sustainable business models and helping 
society achieve net zero emissions by 2050.
The sustainability strategy is an important part of SEB’s 
larger strategy for 2030. It outlines our role in the transition 
towards a sustainable society and provides important con­
texts for understanding which sustainability matters are 
material for SEB. The strategy’s purpose is to integrate sus­
tainability considerations in all relevant business decisions 
and by doing so, support our customers and society at large 
to transition to a more sustainable economy. 
The sustainability strategy is built on four pillars that guide 
our ways of working:
•	 Providing transition advice, financing and investments 
•	 Innovating and setting standards 
•	 Transforming our business 
•	 Acting as a responsible corporate citizen for a resilient 
and ­inclusive society
Climate change related ambitions 
Since 2021, SEB has been tracking its progress towards net zero 
through a set of targeted metrics. These metrics guide the alignment 
of our business with our sustainability strategy and allow us to ­monitor 
the reduction of fossil exposure in our credit portfolio, the increase of 
our positive sustainability contributions, and the alignment of our 
credit portfolio with 2050 net zero pathways. The metrics are:
•	 Carbon Exposure Index 
•	 Sustainability Activity Index 
•	 2030 sector targets
  See p. 113 for information on targets and outcomes.
Responsibility beyond emissions
We cannot achieve a sustainable future by focusing solely on the 
­climate. The sustainability transition should be carried out in a way 
that promotes consideration for nature and environment, as well as 
human rights, equality, inclusion and corporate culture. 
Similarly, we take responsibility for our employees. Board estab­
lished employee-related metrics are:

SEB supports SSAB’s 
decarbonisation agenda 
SSAB, a global Sweden-based steel company, is investing 
EUR 4.5bn in a new steel mill in Luleå, aiming to signif­
icantly reduce carbon emissions and strengthen its com­
petitive position. SEB is one of the core banks supporting 
the project, which includes one of the largest green 
financing arrangements in the Nordic region to date.
SSAB’s transformation journey is centred on installing 
more capacity for advanced premium steels, as well as 
decarbonising steel production. The new mill in Luleå, 
due to start operations at the end 
of 2029, is a key step in that direc­
tion. SSAB will be able to close 
the current blast furnace and the 
coking plant, eliminating the main 
source of the company’s CO2 
emissions. The new mill will be 
based on Electric Arc Furnaces 
(EAF) technology, and can use a flexible mix of recycled 
scrap and sponge iron. 
“Our ambition is to become the first steel company to 
offer fossil-free steel on the market and to largely elimi­
nate CO2 emissions from our own operations. We will 
also improve the product mix with more premium prod­
ucts and high-strength steels. This project is essential to 
achieving those goals,” said Kati Vellinki, Vice President, 
Head of Group Treasury at SSAB.
The Luleå investment is backed by EUR 2.7bn in green 
financing, supported by export credit agencies in Europe,

the Nordic Investment Bank, the Swedish National 
Debt Office and a group of eleven financial institutions. 
SEB played a key role in the financing.
“SEB has been a long-term partner for us,” said Kati 
Vellinki. “They have shown commitment throughout the 
process, supported us with advisory services, and 
helped ensure the financing was completed smoothly.”
The financing is structured as corporate debt, not pro­
ject finance, and includes guarantees from the export 
credit agencies and the Swedish National 
Debt Office. This approach allows SSAB 
to maintain flexibility and manage finan­
cial risks in a way that other financing 
solutions would not have provided.
SSAB’s green transition is not only 
a strategic business move that will 
strengthen its cost position and increase 
flexibility, but also a major environmental effort. The 
company’s investments in Luleå and Oxelösund are 
expected to reduce Sweden’s total CO2 emissions 
by up to 10 per cent.
“Decarbonisation is a core part of our DNA 
now,” said Kati Vellinki. “We are reshaping the 
company, and we need banking partners such as 
SEB who understand our journey and can support 
us both today and in the future.”

Our people make the difference
SEB has always been committed to creating 
long-term relationships and trust with its
employees, customers and shareholders. 
Our employees are essential to supporting 
­customers and enabling them to achieve their 
ambitions. They are, therefore, our most 
important asset and the foundation of the 
bank’s success.
New talent strategy
In 2025, we introduced a new talent strategy, focused on attracting and 
supporting individuals and teams with different experiences and per­
spectives who can drive progress and change. A key focus area of this 
strategy is to develop our leaders in transformative leadership. We are 
also continuing our efforts to encourage employees to explore new tech­
nologies to enhance innovation and efficiency across the organisation.
Building skills for the future
In a rapidly evolving world, future-proofing employee skills is essential. 
At SEB, continuous learning is a core part of our culture. The bank’s 
­digital university, SEB Campus, offers a wide range of courses and 
­webinars to all employees. These learning activities feature knowl­
edge-sharing from international business schools and universities, 
as well as internal experts.
At SEB, we regard AI as a learning area of top priority. To strengthen 
AI literacy across the bank, we have introduced an initiative called 
Get going with AI. The initiative consists of a team-based dialogue that 
encourages employees to build shared knowledge of AI and explore 
potential applications.
Another key learning area is leadership development. To support and 
prepare our leaders of tomorrow, we offer a wide range of development 
opportunities, from self-leadership courses available to all employees to 
the Wallenberg Institute programme, which aims to prepare executives 
for future key positions. In addition, we provide mentorship, coaching, 
volunteering, and internal gigs – temporary assignments to explore 
other parts of the bank. The goal is to foster a culture that encourages 
curiosity and development. 
A highly engaged workforce
92 per cent of SEB’s employees participated in the 2025 Insight 
employee survey. The employee engagement score, which indicates 
how satisfied employees are and whether they would recommend SEB 
as an employer, was 82 on a 100-point scale, remaining high and above 
our target level. The survey results reflect that employees have a great 
deal of trust in their managers and feel supported in their personal and 
professional development at SEB. 
Top-rated employer by students and professionals 
For the fifth consecutive year, SEB was ranked the most attractive 
employer among Nordic banks by business and IT students from 
­Sweden’s nine largest universities. This ranking is based on the annual 
survey conducted by the research company Universum. In a separate 
survey from Universum in 2025, IT and business professionals in Sweden 
voted SEB as the most attractive employer in the Nordic banking sector.

Important events and trends in 2025
First quarter 
•	 The economic policy agenda was marked by geopolitics and US trade tariffs. The Swedish economy was 
subdued, with weak private consumption and rising unemployment. The European and Swedish central 
banks cut policy rates. Major investment plans in European defence and infrastructure were announced.
•	 Customer activity was higher, mostly in the Corporate Finance and Markets businesses. Lending 
demand increased marginally among corporates and for Swedish mortgages.
•	 A new division, Wealth & Asset Management, was created, merging the former divisions Private Wealth 
Management & Family Office, Asset Management and Life.
Second quarter 
•	 New US tariffs created uncertainty and dampened corporate and household confidence, reflected 
in weak Purchasing Managers’ Index and consumer confidence indicators. Financial markets 
­demonstrated notable resilience.
•	 In Sweden, the economic recovery progressed more slowly than expected. Weak growth and ­stabilised 
inflation prompted the Swedish central bank to lower the policy rate. ECB also reduced its policy rate.
•	 Corporate customer activity increased, particularly within investment banking. Lending and deposit 
­volumes grew moderately and there were net inflows of assets under management.
•	 SEB joined a consortium of industry-leading companies to build advanced AI infrastructure in Sweden.
Third quarter 
•	 Global tensions and unsettled trade policies hampered economic growth while financial markets 
were resilient. New US tariff levels were partially determined and significant uncertainty remained. 
•	 The Federal Reserve lowered policy rates, narrowing the interest rate differential between the US and 
Europe. In Europe, expectations of growth from increased investments, in defence and infra­structure, 
were counteracted by a negative impact from tariffs and weaker exports.
•	 The Swedish economy was subdued, with weak household consumption, while the industrial sector 
showed signs of strength. A strong krona and weaker demand in the euro area hampered export.
•	 Lending to households grew somewhat, driven by strong growth in the Baltics. Corporate customer 
activity was seasonally slower and low market volatility reduced demand for risk management 
­services. Net flows of assets under management were positive.
•	 SEB joined a consortium of European banks to launch a euro-denominated stablecoin with the aim 
to establish a regulated, cost efficient and effective digital payment standard in Europe. 
Fourth quarter 
•	 Despite geopolitical uncertainty, several major economies stabilised. Financial markets strengthened 
and risk appetite improved, contributing to broad-based gains across equity markets and lower 
­volatility. 
•	 In Sweden, there were signs of rising consumption and, investments and lower inflation. The Swedish 
central bank cut its policy rate again which in combination with fiscal policy measures, is expected 
to contribute to further growth. 
•	 Customer activity picked up in investment banking, while lending demand remained muted except in 
the Baltics, where both mortgage and corporate lending grew. Net flows of assets under management 
were positive.

Financial structure
Total assets at 31 December 2025 amounted to SEK 3,671bn (3,759).
Loans
Total loans to the public were stable during the year and amounted to 
SEK 2,238bn (2,237). The currency effect amounted to SEK –82bn.
Loans to the public are part of SEB’s credit portfolio, which also 
includes loans to other counterparties as well as contingent liabilities 
and derivatives. The credit portfolio decreased by SEK 154bn to 
SEK 3,006bn (3,160) mainly due to currency effects. Credit demand 
was subdued throughout the year, reflecting macroeconomic uncer­
tainty and cautious sentiment among households and corporates. 
In the ­Baltic credit portfolio, demand picked up in the second half of 
the year, supported by resilient economic conditions.
See note G17 and G37a. The development of the 
credit portfolio is commented on at p. 44–45.
Debt securities
Debt securities are held for the purpose of serving customer risk 
management and trading needs as well as SEB’s ­liquidity manage­
ment. SEB is also a market maker in certain debt securities. Debt 
securities decreased by SEK 50bn to SEK 229bn (279). The short 
position (liability) in debt securities amounted to SEK 19bn (24). SEB’s 
credit risk exposure in this portfolio, which consists of debt securities, 
certain credit derivatives and futures, amounted to SEK 191bn (242).
See note G18, G29 and G37a.
Equity instruments
Equity instruments held for the purpose of customer risk 
­management and trading needs as well as to facilitate the bank’s 
role as a market maker amounted to SEK 121bn (122). The short 
position (liability) in equity instruments amounted to SEK 26bn (23).
See note G19 and G29.
Insurance assets and liabilities
Financial assets within the insurance operations amounted to 
SEK 510bn (495). Out of this, financial assets where policyholders 
carry the risk (mostly unit-linked insurance) amounted to SEK 476bn 
(461) and other assets (mostly traditional and risk insurance) 
amounted to an additional SEK 33bn (34). 
Liabilities in the insurance operations amounted to SEK 511bn 
(495). Out of this, SEK 475bn (458) was related to financial commit­
ments for investment contracts (mostly unit-linked insurance), while 
SEK 37bn (37) was related to insurance contracts (mostly traditional 
and risk insurance). The insurance liabilities are mainly covered by 
financial assets.
See note G27, G37f and G39.
Derivatives
The fair value of the derivative contracts is presented as assets and 
liabilities on the balance sheet. They amounted to SEK 119bn (177) 
and SEK 129bn (156) respectively. The mix and volumes of deriva­
tives reflect the demand for derivatives by the bank’s customers for 
their management of financial risks. The bank is a market maker for 
derivatives and also uses derivatives for the purpose of protecting 
its own cash flows and fair value of its financial assets and liabilities 
from for instance interest rate fluctuations.
See note G20.

Deposits and borrowings
Deposits and borrowings from the public, an important source of 
financing, amounted to SEK 1,702bn (1,681). The most stable 
sources, household deposits, increased by SEK 5bn and deposits 
from non-financial corporations decreased by SEK 18bn. 
Debt securities issued 
SEB issues debt securities as part of its funding. In 2025, credit funds 
globally continued to experience steady inflows, which provided sup­
port for credit markets. Credit spreads generally moved tighter over 
the year, with the exception of the period between mid-March to mid-
April, when tariff-related volatility led to a temporary and notable 
­widening. Aside from this short episode, access to funding markets 
remained favourable across asset classes and maturities.
An equivalent of SEK 148bn (116) of long-term funding was issued 
during the year, of which SEK 76bn was in the form of covered bonds, 
SEK 29bn in senior unsecured debt, SEK 39bn senior non-preferred 
debt and SEK 4.5bn in subordinated debt. The subordinated debt 
issuance was a SEK Tier 2 capital note. SEB issued a green bond 
amounting to EUR 1.25bn, bringing the total amount of green bonds 
outstanding to EUR 5.25bn.
At year-end, total long-term funding amounted to SEK 587bn 
(598). Short-term funding in the form of commercial paper and 
­certificates of deposit amounted to SEK 293bn (349). 
See note G37e and the Capital Adequacy & Risk Management 
Report (at sebgroup.com) for liquidity risk information.

Total equity 
Total equity at the opening of 2025 amounted to SEK 231bn. Total 
dividends (for the year 2024) paid out amounted to SEK 23bn. Net 
profit amounted to SEK 31bn and other comprehensive income 
increased equity by SEK 1.3bn. The change from the equity-­based 
programmes and the holdings of own shares amounted to 
SEK –1.3bn. At year-end 2025, total equity was SEK 230bn. 
SEB’s share capital amounts to SEK 21,942m distributed on 2,000 
million shares. In line with strategic planning, SEB bought back shares 
for a total amount of SEK 10bn during 2025 (8.75) and 57 million 
Class A shares were cancelled (40 million). 
Each Class A share entitles the holder to one vote and each Class C 
share to 1/10 of a vote.
Dividend
Dividend distributed
An ordinary dividend of SEK 8.50 and a special dividend of SEK 3.00 
per Class A and Class C share were distributed to the shareholders in 
2025. The dividend corresponded to around 66 per cent of SEB’s net 
profit for the financial year 2024. 
Dividend proposed
For 2025, the Board of Directors proposes to the Annual General 
Meeting 2026 an ordinary dividend of SEK 8.50 and a special divi­
dend of SEK 2.50 per Class A and Class C share, which corresponds 
to around 70 per cent of the 2025 net profit. The proposed total divi­
dend amounts to SEK 21.6bn based on the total number of issued 
shares as per 31 December 2025, excluding own shares held. 
The proposed record date for the dividend is 26 March 2026 and 
if the Annual General Meeting resolves in accordance with the pro­
posal, the share will be traded ex-dividend on 25 March 2026 and 
dividends are expected to be paid out on 31 March 2026. 
Last year, SEB communicated an intention to move to semi-annual 
dividends from 2026. After receiving feedback from market partici­
pants and evaluating alternative options for processing such a transi­
tion, SEB has for now decided to maintain its current dividend payout 
structure.
Share value and stock exchange trading
The closing price at year-end of the SEB class A share was 
SEK 195.10 (151.45). Earnings per share amounted to SEK 15.60 
(17.51). The SEB share is listed on Nasdaq Stockholm.

Between 6 February 2025 and 27 January 2026, SEB bought back 
shares amounting to a total of SEK 10bn. The Board of Directors has 
resolved to initiate a new quarterly buyback programme, amounting 
to SEK 1.25bn to be completed by 23 March 2026.

Capital management
SEB takes various types of risks in line with the business strategy 
and the Board’s risk appetite. In order to protect against unexpected 
losses, sufficient capital strength must be maintained. SEB’s 
­capitalisation shall be risk-based, founded on an assessment of all 
risks incurred in the business, and forward-looking, aligned with 
the strategy and business plan. The Board of Directors sets SEB’s 
­capital targets, based on their view on capital need and credit rating 
ambitions, taking into consideration financial stability requirements 
by the regulators, debt investors and business counterparties. 
These requirements are balanced with the shareholders’ required 
rate of return.
 Regulatory capital requirements applied for Swedish banks are 
based on the Basel agreement as transposed into EU and Swedish 
law. SEB targets a buffer of 100–300 basis points relative the 
­regulatory requirements and supervisory guidance for the Common 
Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio. 
The capital position remains strong 
 SEB’s CET1 capital ratio at year-end was 17.7 per cent (17.6), imply­
ing a buffer of 300 basis points above the regulatory requirement 
including Pillar 2 Guidance (P2G). The risk exposure amount (REA) 
increased to SEK 986bn (948) driven by the implementation of Basel 
IV. REA relating to operational risk increased significantly due to the 
introduction of a new standardised model. Changes in the regulation 
related to credit risk models and the stronger Swedish krona reduced 
REA. SEB’s applicable CET1 capital requirement and P2G per the 
end of the year was 14.7 per cent (14.7). CET1 capital increased to 
SEK 175bn (167). 
SEB’s ongoing work to update its Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) 
models continues. Since 2023, SEB holds 100 basis points of addi­
tional capital related to the ongoing IRB work and, as communicated 
in 2025, REA is expected to increase by approximately 5 per cent 
until the models for the Baltic subsidiaries have been approved by the 
ECB. In 2025, SEB started to phase in this increase in REA. Taking the 
remaining increase into consideration, SEB’s capital buffer, pro forma, 
stands at 250 basis points.
The leverage ratio is a non risk-based regulatory capital require­
ment. At year-end, the requirement, including P2G, was 3.15 per cent 
(3.5) of the leverage exposure. SEB’s leverage ratio was 5.7 per cent 
(5.4) at the end of 2025. 
Finalisation of the Basel III framework 
The framework for revisions to the Basel III framework (also referred 
to as Basel IV), with the objective to reduce excessive variability of 
REA among banks, was implemented into EU-legislation and applica­
ble for banks as of 1 January 2025. The framework has a gradual 
phase-in of the so-called output floor, which will reach its steady 
state calibration of 72.5 per cent by 1 January 2030. Due to a benefi­
cial transitional rule for unrated investment grade corporates, the full 
impact of the output floor will take effect from 1 January 2033.
The internal model for operational risk was replaced by a standard­
ised method on 1 January 2025.

Risk development
Managing risk is an integral part of banking, and risk awareness is 
deeply embedded in SEB’s corporate culture. The bank has a compre­
hensive framework for risk, liquidity and capital management to 
ensure regulatory compliance and safeguard the bank’s financial 
position. The framework is continuously developed to reflect current 
market trends, new regulations as well as to detect emerging risks.
The Board sets out SEB’s risk strategy in the Risk Appetite Frame­
work (RAF) which states the Board’s long-term view on the types and 
levels of risk SEB is able and willing to assume in order to achieve its 
overall business objectives. Together with the Risk Policy for the SEB 
Group, the RAF is a core component of SEB’s risk management frame­
work. The CEO has the overall responsibility for the management of 
all risks within SEB and for ensuring that the risk profile remains 
within the Board’s risk appetite and capital adequacy targets. The 
Chief Risk Officer is responsible for independently ensuring that the 
RAF is adhered to. 
The RAF is based on SEB’s risk capacity and is comprised of risk 
appetite statements which articulate the Board’s risk strategy. These 
statements are further detailed and quantified in risk appetite meas­
ures that enable monitoring and control. Proactive management of 
adherence to the risk appetite is enabled through allocation of the risk 
appetite to divisions, countries, business units, etc., using limit frame­
works, key risk indicators, portfolio caps, mandates, and risk controls. 
The development of SEB’s risk profile in relation to the risk appetite 
is regularly monitored, assessed and reported to the Group Risk 
­Committee, the Board’s Risk and Capital Committee and the Board. 
Risk development in 2025 
The past year has once again highlighted how risks across the global 
economy are increasingly interconnected. Macroeconomic volatility, 
technological advancement and geopolitical tension have continued 
to blur the lines between financial and operational/non-financial risks. 
This has reinforced the importance of an integrated approach that 
links strategy and risk management which enables us to respond and 
adapt to unexpected developments. Despite these challenges, SEB’s 
risk profile remained stable in 2025 with continued low credit losses 
and a strong capital and liquidity position. The significant market vol­
atility that followed the US administration’s decision to impose tariffs 
at the beginning of the year had limited impact on SEB’s market risk 
due to proactive risk management. Average annual Value-at-Risk, 
which measures and estimates the expected maximum market risk 
loss during a period of ten trading days with 99 per cent probability, 
declined to SEK 135m (139m). 
The uncertainty around US trade and central bank policies and the 
geopolitical uncertainty impacted financial markets and economic 
growth most of the year. In response, many corporate customers 
adopted a more cautious approach to investing, and household con­
sumption remained weak despite several policy rate cuts. This led to 
subdued credit growth and SEB’s total credit portfolio decreased to 
SEK 3,006bn (3,160).
Overall asset quality remained solid and net expected credit losses 
(ECL) remained low. In total net ECL amounted to SEK 1,548m (886), 
which corresponds to a net ECL level of 5 basis points (3). In the cor­
porate portfolio, focus was on the risks and uncertainties related to 
the effects of the US tariffs and certain infrastructure projects. A 
portfolio provision was built up but partially released towards the 
end of the year. Supported by the lower interest rates, the real estate 
segment continued to demonstrate resilience in terms of asset qual­
ity, although rising office and retail vacancy rates warrant attention.
SEB is, to a large degree, an Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) bank, 
meaning we use internal models, approved by supervisory authori­
ties, to calculate credit risk and determine capital requirements 
instead of relying on standardised models. This approach is consid­
ered key to effective internal steering, capital efficiency, and robust 
risk management processes. For a number of years, regulators have 
worked to address concerns about undue variability of capital 
requirements for credit risk. The objective has been to enhance 
robustness and comparability of internal models across banks. Rec­
ognising the significance of these evolving regulatory expectations, 
aligning our IRB models has remained a strategic priority, with efforts 
accelerating further in 2025. This work is expected to continue for 
a number of years, in close dialogue with supervisory authorities.
In 2025, the total risk exposure amount (REA) increased to SEK 
986bn (948bn) primarily because of the implementation of the 
­Capital Requirements Regulation III (CRR3), Basel IV. 
SEB’s liquidity position remained strong throughout 2025. Assets 
and liabilities are managed in line with the Net Stable Funding Ratio 
(NSFR) regulatory requirement, ensuring illiquid long-term assets are 
financed by a sufficient level of stable long-term funding. In 2025, the 
ratio strengthened from increased stable funding and at year-end, the 
ratio was 113 per cent (111). The size and composition of liquid assets 
are continuously assessed against estimated needs. The Liquidity 
Coverage Ratio (LCR) measures to what extent SEB’s liquid assets 
cover short-term cash ­outflows in a short-term stressed scenario. At 
the end of 2025, SEB’s LCR was 150 per cent (160), well above the 
regulatory requirement of 100 per cent. SEB also met the minimum 
LCR requirement for individual currencies, including EUR, USD and 
other significant currencies.

Operational resilience, the ability to continue to deliver critical ser­
vices during disruptions, has been a priority in light of the geopolitical 
tensions. In Europe hybrid threats targeting corporations and institu­
tions have increased, including cyberattacks and influence operations 
carried out by both state-sponsored and criminal actors. These activi­
ties pose both direct and indirect threats, such as attacks on third-
party providers. SEB has focused its efforts on strengthening prepar­
edness, response, and recovery capabilities, with particular emphasis 
on compliance with the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) 
a key regulatory initiative aimed at enhancing the financial sector’s 
digital resilience. While SEB experienced no major incidents or disrup­
tions in 2025 and operational losses (net) remained low at SEK 95m 
(358), further enhancing the bank’s ability to mitigate potential 
impacts on customers, markets and the broader financial system, 
remains a priority. 
The rapid adoption of AI is increasing several already existing 
non-financial risks. AI is being used by criminals to perpetrate fraud 
and by other malicious actors for cyberattacks, targeting both SEB 
and our third parties. At the same time, SEB’s own use of AI for build­
ing systems and models drive risks related to data privacy, informa­
tion security, model, third-party and regulation. To mitigate these 
risks and ensuring compliance with relevant regulation, governance 
for using AI and for embedding it into our existing governance struc­
tures and risk frameworks, is being established. Enhancing our under­
standing of how AI will impact SEB and our customers in the future is 
one of our most important priorities.
Risk management in an evolving landscape 
In a rapidly changing environment, sound risk management builds 
resilience and trust. It is a strategic enabler that serves as a corner­
stone of sustainable growth and long-term value creation. This is fun­
damental not only for SEB as a bank, but also for the financial stability 
in the markets where we are present. 
SEB’s risk management framework is embedded into our strategy, 
product development, and daily operations across all markets in 
which we operate. As the external environment evolved during the 
year, we integrated new perspectives into our risk mitigation strate­
gies to remain forward-looking and adaptive. This safeguarded capi­
tal strength and upheld resilience, enabling SEB to support customers 
in both favourable and challenging times. 
The risk management framework is reinforced by a strong risk 
culture that embeds principles and policies for risk management 
across all levels of the bank. This in turn is essential to maintaining the 
trust placed in us by customers, investors, regulators and society. SEB 
fosters an environment where prudent risk-taking and accountability 
are consistently demonstrated in how we work and make decisions 
across the SEB Group, regardless of role or location. 
All employees – not only those in dedicated risk units – take part 
in identifying, managing, and mitigating risk. SEB promotes an open 
dialogue, continuous learning, and a culture where risk awareness 
is high, and accountability is clearly defined. 
Sound risk management is not about avoiding risk; it is about 
understanding risk and anticipating what may lie ahead. SEB has 
translated that understanding and leveraged that knowledge to make 
balanced and responsible risk decisions. By nurturing our strong risk 
culture that has been shaped over decades, SEB is well positioned to 
navigate uncertainty, support our customers, and deliver long-term 
value for our shareholders.

Holistic management
Creating sustainable value is a continuous process in an environment 
that is under constant change. The Board of Directors sets the condi­
tions by deciding on the bank’s long-term strategic direction, financial 
targets, business plans and overall risk appetite.
In order to maximise stakeholder value, the financial consequences 
of business decisions are evaluated and operations are managed 
­proactively based on these aspects: 
•	 growth, mix and risk level of business volumes
•	 capital and liquidity requirements driven by the business
•	 profitability
•	 environmental, social and governance aspects, and 
•	 regulatory requirements.
In 2025, macroeconomic factors such as geopolitical uncertainty, 
lower interest rates and as in the last several years, climate-related 
challenges and other sustainability related matters were increasingly 
in focus. Such challenges are reflected throughout SEB’s risk manage­
ment. SEB strives to continuously identify and manage potential risks, 
for instance by using stress tests and scenario analysis. The capital 
buffer and liquidity reserves are held to cover the risk in case of 
unforeseen events. 
All activities are carried out responsibly and in accordance with 
­regulations and expectations – all in order to maintain the trust of 
the stakeholders.

Long-term financial targets
The long-term financial targets are unchanged in the business plan for 
2026–2028. With the overall purpose of having capital management 
flexibility, the Board of Directors’ long-term financial targets are:
•	 to pay a yearly dividend that is around 50 per cent of the earnings 
per share, excluding items affecting comparability, and to distrib­
ute potential capital in excess of the targeted capital position, 
mainly through share buybacks,
•	 to maintain a Common Equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 100–300 basis 
points above the requirement from the Swedish Financial Super­
visory Authority, and
•	 to generate a return on equity that is competitive with peers. 
Financial aspirations for the divisions 
The long-term divisional aspirations for profitability (RoBE) are set 
mainly based on two factors. Firstly, each division will have the ambi­
tion to achieve best in class profitability compared with similar busi­
nesses among relevant peers. Secondly, each division’s aspirations 
are set so that they enable SEB to achieve its long-term aspiration of 
15 per cent return on equity on group level. The following table pro­

Regulatory supervision of SEB 
Regulatory supervision is an integral part of day-to-day banking 
operations. The Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority (the 
Swedish FSA) is the competent authority with primary responsi­
bility for the supervision of SEB AB. As SEB operates across 
­several jurisdictions, the Group is also subject to supervision by 
authorities in the countries in which it conducts business.
In 2025, more than 90 new supervisory matters (80 in 2024) 
were initiated concerning SEB AB and its Swedish subsidiaries. 
In addition, approximately 80 new supervisory matters (110 in 
2024) related to the Group’s international operations, of which 
around 30 concerned the home markets. Supervisory matters 
relating to the Baltic banking subsidiaries, initiated by the ECB 
within the framework of the Single Supervisory Mechanism as 
well as by local authorities, amounted to approximately 40 during 
the year (50 in 2024).
As in previous years, not all supervisory matters were formally 
classified as inspections. Many instead took the form of question­
naires, information requests or ad hoc reporting requirements. 
These nonetheless required significant resources to ensure 
timely, complete and high-quality responses.

Profit and business volumes, explanation
Customers’ financial needs are the source of SEB’s business volumes 
and result. Here, some general relationships between customer-­
driven business volumes reported on- and ­off-balance sheet, and 
the income statement as well as external factors are outlined.
The macroeconomic situation, and the interest rate levels, are of 
great importance for customer behaviour and, together with the 
bank’s own actions, it is a major factor impacting the business and 
result.
In times of positive economic development, both businesses and 
private individuals are more likely to invest and consume. This may 
lead to increased lending, more payments, a higher number of corpo­
rate transactions, among other things, all of which affect net interest 
and net commission income positively. All else equal, the bank’s net 
interest income will increase with higher interest rates.
In an unfavourable part of the business cycle, customers may be 
more restrictive and growth in business and transaction volumes 
may level out while credit losses may increase. On the other hand, 
customers hedge their risks in uncertain and volatile times, which 
may increase net financial income.

Uncertainties
SEB assumes credit, market, liquidity, non-financial as well as life 
insurance risks. The risk composition of the group, as well as the 
related risk, liquidity and capital management, are described in note 
G37 and G38, in the Capital Adequacy and Risk Management Report 
for 2025 as well as the quarterly additional Pillar 3 disclosures. 
­Further information is available in the Fact Book that is published 
quarterly.
Re-assessment of credited withholding 
tax in Germany
SEB and its subsidiaries are continuously subject to tax field audits 
where local tax authorities review previous years’ tax returns. As 
­initially reported in the interim report in the third quarter 2017, and 
thereafter elaborated on, the German tax authority has in relation to 
SEB’s wholly owned German subsidiary, DSK Deutsch-Skandinavische 
Verwaltungs GmbH (“DSK”, formerly DSK Hyp AG) re-assessed DSK’s 
crediting of withholding tax in its securities finance business for the 
years 2008–2014 and claimed the repayment by DSK of EUR 936m 
and EUR 290m in interest. Further reclaims cannot be ruled out as 
DSK, over the years 2008–2015, has claimed and credited approxi­
mately a total of EUR 1,500m in withholding tax against its corporate 
income tax. 
DSK has objected to the tax reclaims. DSK and SEB are of the opin­
ion that the securities finance business of DSK under review by the 
German tax authorities was conducted in accordance with market 
practice, law and administrative guidance applicable at the time. SEB 
and DSK, as supported by its external legal advisor, are of the view 
that it is more likely than not that it will be ultimately confirmed in a 
fiscal court proceeding that the withholding tax has been claimed 
and credited correctly by DSK. Hence, to date and in accordance with 
­current accounting rules, no provisions have been made on a group 
level. The legal proceedings are estimated to take several years as 
it is expected that the matter will be appealed to the highest fiscal 
court. It cannot be ruled out that the final outcome of the legal pro­
ceedings may lead to negative financial effects for the SEB group.
Investigation of alleged tax evasion 
of a severe nature
The public prosecutor in Cologne, Germany, is investigating whether 
former and current employees of DSK and SEB, as part of DSK’s secu­
rities finance business, have been involved in alleged tax evasion of 
a severe nature. DSK and SEB are cooperating with the prosecutor 
in the investigation. As far as SEB and DSK are aware, no indictments 
have been filed against any of the aforementioned employees. It is 
unclear what impact the criminal investigation may have on the re-­
assessment by the German tax authorities of DSK’s crediting of with­
holding tax referred to above. It cannot be ruled out that the criminal 
investigation or potential indictments may delay the re-assessment of 
the credited withholding tax and lead to negative financial effects for 
the SEB group.
Supervisory matters
SEB is subject to various legal regimes, laws and requirements in all 
jurisdictions where the bank operates. Over the past years, the laws 
and regulations of the financial industry have expanded and further 
sharpened, and the regulators have increased their supervision. 
This is a development which is expected to continue to evolve. 
­Competent authorities regularly conduct reviews of SEB’s regulatory 
compliance, including areas such as financial stability, transaction 
reporting, anti-money laundering, investor protection and data 
­privacy. SEB has policies and procedures in place with the purpose 
to comply with applicable laws and regulations and has continuous 
dialogues and cooperates with authorities. SEB has received requests 
from authorities in jurisdictions where it operates, including US 
authorities, to provide information concerning measures against 
money laundering, which SEB is responding to in dialogue with these 
authorities. It cannot be ruled out that current and future supervisory 
activities and requests from authorities could lead to criticism or 
sanctions.

Corporate governance
A robust corporate governance framework based on internal and 
external rules forms the basis for the trust that underpins SEB’s 
­operations.
 
Rules and regulations 
As a Swedish public limited financial institution with securities 
listed on Nasdaq Stockholm, SEB is subject to numerous rules 
and regulations. The external framework for corporate governance 
includes among other things the following rules and regulations: 
•	 Companies Act 
•	 Annual Accounts Act 
•	 Nasdaq Stockholm Issuer Rules 
•	 Swedish Corporate Governance Code 
•	 Banking and Financing Business Act 
•	 Securities Market Act
•	 Rules and guidelines issued by the Swedish Financial Supervisory 
Authority and other authorities within the European Union.
SEB also adheres to an internal framework that includes, among 
other things, the Articles of Association, which are adopted by the 
general meeting of shareholders. Policies and instructions that define 
the division of duties within SEB are tools for the Board of Directors 
(the Board) and the President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) in 
their governing and controlling roles. Such policies and instructions 
include, among others: 
•	 Rules of Procedure for the Board and the Instructions for the 
Board committees 
•	 Instructions for the CEO and the Group Executive Committee (GEC) 
•	 General Credit Policy and Risk Policy 
•	 Instruction for Handling of Conflicts of Interest 
•	 Policy on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating Financing of 
­Terrorism, and Sanctions Policy1)
•	 Code of Conduct and Anti-Corruption Policy1)
•	 Remuneration Policy
•	 Security Policy1)
•	 Corporate Sustainability Policy1)
•	 Inclusion & Diversity Policy1) 
•	 Policies on Suitability, Diversity and Composition of the Board, 
the Group Executive Committee and other key ­function holders. 
SEB’s ethical and sustainability endeavours are an integral part of 
the business and are regularly included on the Board’s agenda. SEB’s 
Code of Conduct describes the bank’s values, ethics and standards 
of business conduct and provides guidance on how employees are to 
abide by these values. Policies and instructions for sustainability and 
group-wide thematic and sector policies addressing environmental, 
social and governance (ESG) issues are also of vital importance.2)
This corporate governance report has been prepared in accord­
ance with the Annual Accounts Act and the Swedish Corporate 
­Governance Code (the Code). SEB strives to ­follow the Code where 
appropriate and has no deviations to report for 2025. Some of the 
disclosures that are required in the ­Sustainability Statement accord­
ing to the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), incor­
porated into the Swedish Annual Accounts Act, and the European 
Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) have been incorporated 
by reference in this Corporate Governance Report. Such incorpora­
tions have been identified by a reference to the relevant ESRS 
­Disclosure Requirement.

Shareholders and annual general meetings
The shareholders exercise their influence at general meetings of 
­shareholders by, among other things, electing directors of the Board 
and the external auditor. 
SEB has approximately 290,000 shareholders. SEB’s share capital 
­consists of two classes of shares – A shares and C shares. Each Class A 
share carries one vote and each Class C share carries one tenth of a vote.
The Annual General Meeting (AGM) of shareholders is held in 
Stockholm, in Swedish. All shareholders listed in the shareholder 
­register who have duly notified their attendance have the right to 
­participate at the AGM and to vote for the full number of their shares. 
Shareholders who cannot attend may appoint a representative.

re-election of the Chair of the Board

•	 approval of Remuneration Report and long-term share 
­programmes for 2025 
•	 approval to acquire and sell SEB shares, issue convertibles, and 
reduce the share capital with redemption of shares and bonus 
issue of new shares 
The 2026 AGM will be held on 24 March 2026 at Stockholm ­Concert 
Hall, Hötorget, Stockholm.

of the Board and the adjunct member. 
The Board’s composition shall adhere to applicable laws and regu­
lations and to the Policy on Suitability, Diversity and Composition of 
the Board of Directors, adopted by the Board. An important principle 
is that the Board’s size and composition shall be such as to serve the 
bank in the best possible way and to safeguard that the Board can 
exercise independent judgement, free from any external influence or 
conflicts of interest. Therefore, as the starting point for its work, the 
Nomination Committee is tasked with assessing the degree to which 
the Board meets the demands that will be placed on the Board in 
view of the bank’s operations, organisation and future direction. 
The Board’s size and composition is discussed and reviewed in 
terms of suitable competence, diverse backgrounds, and experience 
in the financial sector and in the geographies where SEB operates. 
In addition, the directors of the Board should have sufficient time to 
perform their duties and understand SEB’s business and its main 
risks: credit, market, liquidity and non-financial risk, such as informa­
tion, communication and technology risks (including cyber risks), 
financial crime risks (including money laundering, terrorist financing, 
and sanctions risks), compliance risks, and environmental, social and 
governance risks.1) 
The Nomination Committee also reviews the evaluations of 
the Chair of the Board and the directors of the Board. See p. 59.

The Board has overarching responsibility for the organisation, 
administration and operations of SEB and SEB Group. 
The Board has adopted Rules of Procedure that regulate the 
Board’s role and ways of working as well as specific instructions 
for the Board’s committees.1)
The Board has the following duties, among others: 
•	 deciding on the objectives, strategy and framework of the 
­business activities as well as the business plan, including 
the ­sustainability strategy1)
•	 following up and evaluating operations in relation to the objectives 
and guidelines established by the Board 
•	 ensuring that the business is organised in such a way that the 
accounting risks inherent in the business as well as financial 
and sustainability reporting are accurate and controlled in 
a ­satisfactory manner1) 
•	 adopting policies and instructions for the business operations
•	 deciding on major acquisitions and divestments as well as other 
major investments 
•	 appointing or dismissing of the CEO, members of GEC, the Chief 
Risk Officer (CRO), and the Head of Group Internal Audit, as well as 
setting the remuneration for these individuals 
•	 deciding on a framework for granting loans and other transactions 
with the directors of the Board and other persons in a managerial 
position in SEB and their related parties as well as deciding on 
such transactions.
The Chair of the Board organises and leads the work of the Board 
and ensures among other things that the directors on a regular basis 
receive information and education on regulatory changes concerning 
the bank’s operations and on the responsibilities of directors of 
a listed financial company. Other educational and specialisation 
­seminars are held each year. New directors are offered educational 
seminars with information on, and discussions about, SEB’s various 
operations including the internal control framework. 
The directors are elected by the shareholders at the AGM for a 
one-year term. Since the 2025 AGM, the Board consists of eleven 
AGM-elected directors, without deputies, and of two directors along 
with two deputies appointed by the trade unions who serve as 
employee representatives. There was no change in the gender distri­
bution of the directors of the Board at the 2025 AGM, as retiring 
members were replaced with new members of the same gender. 
However, one male deputy director appointed by the trade unions, 
was replaced by a female deputy director.
In order for a quorum to exist at a board meeting, more than half of 
the directors must be present. The CEO is the only AGM-elected 
director employed by the bank. The Nomination Committee has made 
an individual and a collective assessment of the directors’ independ­
ence in relation to the bank and the bank’s management as well as in 
relation to shareholders controlling 10 per cent or more of the shares 
or votes and has found that the composition of the Board meets the 
requirements of the Swedish Corporate Governance Code.

Evaluation of the Board of Directors, the CEO and the Group Executive Committee (GEC) 
The Board uses an annual self-assessment method including a question­
naire which is followed by discussions within the Board. Through this pro­
cess the activities and work methods of the Board, the Chair of the Board 
and the respective Board committees are evaluated. Among the issues 
examined are: 
•	 the extent to which the individual directors take an active part in board 
and committee discussions
•	 whether directors contribute independent opinions
•	 whether the meeting atmosphere is conducive to open discussions.
The outcome of the evaluation is presented to and discussed by the Board 
and the Nomination Committee. The evaluation process and its outcome 
contribute to further improvement of the Board’s work and help the Nomi­
nation Committee determine the appropriate size and composition of the 
Board. Marcus Wallenberg does not participate in the evaluation of the 
Chair’s work, which was instead led by Vice Chair Jacob Aarup-Andersen. 
The Board evaluates the work of the CEO and the Group Executive Commit­
tee on a regular basis without participation of the CEO or any other 
­member of the Group Executive Committee.

The directors of the Board shall be of good repute and possess sufficient 
knowledge, skills and expertise to perform their duties. To make sure that the 
Board has the necessary skills and expertise, the Board annually conducts an 
individual assessment of the directors and a collective suitability assessment 
of the Board2). The result of the assessments conducted in 2025 showed that

business conduct in the following areas: (i) SEB Group’s business plan and 
strategy, including the business operations in divisions and geographies, (ii) 
SEB Group’s governance model, including legal structure, organisation, inter­
nal controls and internal rules, (iii) SEB Group’s remuneration policy and 
incentives to influence behaviours, succession planning and inclusion and 
diversity, and (iv) SEB Group’s risk management framework, including its 
risk appetite. The result also showed high competence in relation to SEB 
Group’s sustainability impacts, risks and opportunities, and financial and 
­sustainability reporting.1) 
The outcome of the assessment is presented to the Board and the Nomina­
tion Committee, and contributes to the planning of training programmes for 
the Board, and helps the Nomination Committee determine the appropriate 
size and composition of the Board. In addition to the comprehensive introduc­

and development of the directors of the Board. The directors receive annual 
and mandatory training to continue their development and maintain their 
know­ledge in key areas for the Group, where the topics are determined by

Directors’ fees1)
The AGM sets the total fees for the directors of the Board and decides 
how the fees are to be distributed among the directors and committees.
Directors’ fees are paid on a running basis during the mandate period. 
Following a recommendation by the Nomination Committee, the 
directors are expected to own shares in SEB with a market value 
­corresponding to at least one year’s director’s fee, excluding tax and 
committee fees. The shareholding may be built up over a five-year 
period from appointment. 
Neither the CEO nor the directors appointed by the trade unions 
receive any directors’ fee.
Board committees2)
The Board’s responsibility cannot be delegated. However, the Board has 
established committees to handle certain defined issues and to prepare 
such issues for decision by the Board.
In order to increase the efficiency of its work and enable a more 
detailed analysis of certain issues, the Board has formed committees. 
At present there are three Board committees: The Remuneration and 
Human Resources Committee (RemCo), the Audit and Compliance 
Committee (ACC), and the Risk and Capital Committee (RCC). 
The committees’ duties and decision-making authorities are regu­
lated in annually adopted committee instructions. The issues consid­
ered at committee meetings are recorded in minutes and reported at 
the ­following Board meeting. 
The members of the committees are appointed for one year at 
the statutory Board meeting. An important principle is that as many 
in­dependent directors as possible shall actively participate in the 
committee work. No committees are composed of the same group 
of directors, and the bank occasionally rotates chairs and directors 
of the committees, taking into account the specific experience, 
knowledge and skills that are individually or collectively required 
for the committees.

The three lines of defence model is a risk management framework. The first 
line involves operational management of business activities. The second line 
consists of the CRO function and Group Compliance and the third line includes 
Group Internal Audit to provide independent assurance. 
The first line of defence 
Business divisions as well as Group Staff and Support functions represent 
first line of defence and are responsible for all risks relating to their activities 
which shall be identified, assessed, measured, monitored, managed and 
­mitigated.    See p. 65.
The second line of defence 
The CRO function and Group Compliance are group-wide control functions 
independent from the first line of defence and represent the second line 
of defence. The second line of defence controls and evaluates the first line 
of defence and provides independent reporting on risks to the CEO and 
the Board. 
 See p. 65 and 66.
Third line of defence
Group Internal Audit, an assurance function, is the third line of defence, 
responsible for evaluating the first and second lines of defence. Group 
­Internal Audit evaluates and gives assurance to the Board and the CEO that 
governance, risk management and internal control processes are adequate 
and effective. 
 See p. 66.

Internal control over financial reporting1)
Internal Control over Financial Reporting (ICFR) encompasses the 
processes and mechanisms established by SEB to ensure the accu­
racy, completeness and reliability of its financial statements. These 
controls are designed to prevent and detect errors in financial report­
ing and include a structured framework of policies, procedures and 
monitoring activities. ICFR forms an integral part of SEB’s corporate 
governance and is subject to annual review by the Group Internal 
­Control and Compliance Committee (GICC) and the Audit and 
­Compliance Committee (ACC).
The ICFR framework is well-established and aims to provide rea­
sonable assurance regarding the integrity of financial reporting and to 
mitigate the risk of material misstatements. The framework is based 
on the principles outlined by the Committee of Sponsoring Organiza­
tions of the Treadway Commission (COSO) and is implemented 
through an annual cycle comprising the following key activities:
1) Incorporated into the Sustainability Statement, ESRS 2, GOV-1, GOV-5.
Perform risk assessment and scoping
Financial results and balance sheets are analysed at both Group and 
unit levels to identify relevant and material risks. This analysis deter­
mines the selection of units, financial processes, business operations, 
and IT systems to be included in the ICFR scope for the upcoming year.
Identify risks and controls
Based on the scoping outcome and the risk assessment, Group 
Finance determines the processes to be reviewed. These processes 
are then examined in collaboration with control owners to identify and 
assess associated risks and controls.
Evaluate controls
Control owners conduct regular self-assessments throughout the year 
to evaluate the effectiveness of controls. This process facilitates the 
identification of control deficiencies, implementation of compensating 
controls, and continuous improvement. Evaluations highlight material 
financial reporting risks and comments on any significant deviations 
from previous reporting periods.
Report
Monitoring results are consolidated and analysed to assess residual 
risk within the ICFR framework. Quarterly reports are submitted to the 
Chief Financial Officer (CFO) in conjunction with external financial 
reporting. These reports enhance transparency and support prioritisa­
tion of improvement initiatives. Reporting is also conducted quarterly 
to Group Internal Audit and the Group Reporting Committee, and 
annually to GICC and ACC.
Independent review
In addition to internal monitoring, Group Internal Audit performs 
independent reviews of controls within the ICFR framework. External 
auditors also test ICFR-related controls as part of the financial audit 
process.
ICFR focus areas 2025
•	 A new system has been implemented to support the 
ICFR ­framework.
•	 ICFR controls have been established within the area 
of data quality.
•	 ICFR controls have been implemented for lending within 
the Wealth & Asset Management division.
•	 The IT General Controls catalogue was expanded 
to incorporate Transaction Flow Controls.
Risk management and internal controls over 
sustainability reporting
In addition to the focus areas outlined above, further key 
controls have been developed to enhance sustainability 
reporting, specifically within areas such as taxonomy 
reporting and financed emissions. The organisation 
remains committed to this progression and plans to 
gradually introduce additional ICFR key controls aligned 
with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards 
throughout 2026.
All identified controls are integrated into the annual 
ICFR cycle. Findings from this process are reported 
annually to the ACC.
