The President and Chief Executive Officer1)
The President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO), shall act in the 
best interest of SEB and the shareholders. The CEO is responsible 
for the ­day-to-day management of the activities of the SEB Group in 
accordance with the directives of the Board.
The CEO is overall responsible for managing all risks of SEB in accord­
ance with the policies and instructions of the Board and the intentions 
as stated in the Board’s risk appetite. The CEO shall ensure that the 
organisation and administration of SEB are appropriate. The CEO shall 
furthermore take those measures which are necessary to ensure that 
the accounting of SEB Group is undertaken in compliance with appli­
cable laws, that the Code of Conduct is duly implemented, and that 
the management of the funds is handled in a satisfactory manner.
The Board has adopted an instruction for the CEO’s duties and 
responsibilities. The CEO reports to the Board and at each board 
meeting submits a report on, among other things, the performance 
of the business, based on the decisions made by the Board. 
The CEO’s committees1)
The CEO has seven main committees at his disposal for the ­purpose 
of managing the business operations.
The Group Executive Committee (GEC)1) 
To best safeguard the interests of the SEB Group, the CEO consults 
with GEC on matters of major importance or of importance as to princi­
ples. GEC addresses, among other things, matters of common concern 
to several Business divisions, strategic issues, IT, business plans and 
financial forecasts and reports. GEC held 14 meetings in 2025. GEC has 
11 executive members other than the CEO. The CEO has also appointed 
two managers as adjunct members of GEC. The adjunct members 
­participate in GEC meetings to provide expertise and insight primarily 
in their respective areas of responsibility. 
The activities of GEC are governed by the Instruction for 
the ­President and Chief Executive Officer.
Senior Leadership Committee (SLC)1)
The CEO has established a Senior Leadership Committee (SLC). The 
purpose of SLC is to give the CEO a forum to discuss business matters 
in a broader context, and share information and knowledge among 
senior managers in the SEB Group. SLC consists of GEC members, 
adjunct GEC members and additional senior managers as decided by 
the CEO from time to time. SLC held three meetings in 2025. 
The activities of SLC are governed by the Instruction for the 
­President and Chief Executive Officer.
Asset and Liability Committee (ALCO)1) 
ALCO, chaired by the CEO and with the CFO as vice chair, is a group-wide 
decision-making and consultative body to the CEO. ALCO, which held 
eleven meetings in 2025, handles the following matters, among others:
•	 financial stability, particularly in the new regulatory framework 
•	 strategic capital and liquidity issues, including internal capital 
­allocation and principles for internal pricing.
The activities of ALCO are governed by the Instruction for the Asset 
and Liability Committee.
Group Risk Committee (GRC)1) 
GRC, chaired by the CEO and with the CRO as vice chair, is a group-
wide decision-making committee which addresses all types of risk at 
Group level, including sustainability and reputational risks, in order to 
evaluate portfolios, products and customers from a comprehensive 
risk perspective. GRC held 53 meetings in 2025. GRC is tasked with:
•	 making crucial credit decisions 
•	 ensuring that all risks inherent in the Group’s activities are 
­identified, measured, monitored and reported in accordance 
with internal and external rules 
•	 supporting the CEO in ensuring that decisions ­regarding the Group’s 
long-term risk appetite are adhered to in the business ­operations
•	 ensuring that the Board’s guidelines for risk management and risk 
control are implemented and that the necessary rules and policies 
for risk-taking in the Group are maintained and enforced.
The activities of GRC are governed by the Instruction for the Group 
Risk Committee.

Business divisions 
SEB’s business is organised in business divisions with a number of 
­business areas and business units. The business divisions are Corporate 
& Investment Banking, Business & Retail ­Banking, Wealth & Asset 
­Management and Baltic.
The Board regulates the activities of the Group through an instruction 
for internal governance which establishes how the Group’s business 
divisions, including the international activities conducted through 
branches and subsidiaries, are to be governed and organised. The 
head of a business division has overall responsibility for the activities 
in the business division. 
Country managers are appointed for home markets outside 
­Sweden in which SEB conducts business operations, and the country 
managers ­coordinate the Group’s business activities locally.
See p. 36–39 for information on divisions and 
­geographical markets.
Group Staff and Support functions 
The Group Staff and Support functions are set up to add value and 
­support the SEB Group through centralised functions. 
Staff functions perform regulated activities, such as activities related 
to financial reporting, human resources, financial crime prevention, 
brand and marketing, corporate governance and other legal services.
Support functions are established primarily to leverage economies 
of scale and expertise in various transactional, processing and IT 
­services. Typically, support functions perform operational tasks to 
support the business activities conducted in the business divisions.
Group Control functions1)
The Group Control functions are group-wide control ­functions 
­independent from the business operations. 
The three Group ­Control functions are (i) the CRO function, 
(ii) Group Compliance, and (iii) Group Internal Audit.

Remuneration report 2025
SEB’s competitive remuneration structure aims to attract and retain committed 
and competent employees who contribute to SEB’s long-term success.
Remuneration in SEB
Remuneration is an important component of SEB’s total employee 
offering where the aim is to attract and retain ambitious employees 
who are eager to continuously develop and embrace new ways of 
working. Employee remuneration shall encourage high performance, 
sound and responsible behaviour, and risk-taking that is aligned with 
SEB’s behaviours and the level of risk appetite set by the Board. 
It shall promote the employees’ long-term commitment to create 
­sustainable value for customers and shareholders. Remuneration 
is based on experience, ­responsibility and performance. Performance 
is evaluated on the basis of financial and non-financial goals, with 
SEB’s behaviours as a starting point.
SEB’s remuneration structure is solid and compared to 2024 
­relatively few changes were made. 
Remuneration policy
SEB’s remuneration principles, structure and governance are laid out 
in the Remuneration Policy, adopted by the Board. An integral part of 
the policy is the emphasis on the alignment between remuneration 
and the bank’s strategy, goals, behaviours and long-term interests, 
as well as the connection to individual performance. 
The remuneration offering and its components are structured in 
different ways for different employee categories to create the best 
balance. Remuneration shall be competitive in the markets and seg­
ments where SEB operates. SEB’s remuneration structure, processes 
and reviews shall always support equal opportunities and secure 
non-bias, fair and transparent remuneration decision-making. 
SEB believes that each employee’s position, long-term perfor­
mance and value creation shall be reflected in an appropriate total 
remuneration. An employee’s individual remuneration shall reflect 
the complexity, responsibility and leadership qualities required of 
the role, as well as the individual’s own performance. SEB regularly 
evaluates employee performance and development, based on trans­
parent, individual financial and non-financial targets derived from 
the business plan and with SEB’s behaviours as the starting point. 
The policy also sets out the governance principles for remunera­tion 
decisions, both in general and at the individual level. All decisions are 
to be approved at least at a level corresponding to the remuneration-­
setting managers’ manager (grand­parent principle).
Remuneration structure
SEB’s remuneration structure consists mainly of base salary, variable 
remuneration, pension and other benefits.
Base salary
The base salary is the foundation of an employee’s remuneration. It 
shall be market-aligned and reflect the requirements on the position 
and the employee’s long-term performance. SEB conducts annual 
equal pay reviews to identify and close potential gaps in terms of 
­gender-neutral pay. The outcome of the review is published internally.
Variable remuneration
All variable remuneration is based on SEB’s risk-adjusted performance 
and is adapted to applicable rules governing the maximum ratio of 
­variable remuneration to an employee’s base salary, the deferred 
­portion of remuneration, shares and fund units, and the right to with­
hold and reduce remuneration that has not yet been paid. 
SEB complies with the Swedish Financial ­Supervisory Authority 
(FSA) regulations on remuneration in financial companies, the 
­Swedish Corporate Governance Code and Swedish and international 
regulations and guidelines in relevant parts. ­According to the 
­regulations, SEB shall identify categories of staff whose professional 
activities have a material impact on SEB’s risk profile (Identified 
staff). See the Capital Adequacy and Risk Management Report 
(­Pillar 3) for detailed information. 
Governance model for remuneration in SEB
Group Risk and Group Compliance: Jointly provide risk analysis for 
­remuneration structure review.
Risk and Capital Committee (RCC): Reviews remuneration structure 
to take into account SEB’s risks, long-term earnings capacity and cost of 
liquidity and capital.
Remuneration and Human Resources Committee (RemCo): Continuously 
monitors and evaluates the remuneration structure and ­levels of remu­
neration of SEB and prepares the remuneration policy for decision by 
the Board.
Board of Directors: Annually reviews and adopts the remuneration policy.

All employee programme
The largest variable remuneration programme is the SEB All 
Employee Programme 2025 (AEP), which covers essentially all 
employees. The programme is linked to SEB’s business plan and 
­consists of the financial targets for return on equity and SEB’s cost 
development, which are also communicated externally, and the 
non-financial targets for customer satisfaction and sustainability. 
The 2025 outcome was determined to be 53.3 per cent (61.3) 
of the maximum amount, which in Sweden was SEK 75,000.
Individual variable remuneration
Individual variable remuneration is offered to senior managers, other 
key employees and employees in certain business units where it is 
standard market practice. The ambition is that part of the individual 
remuneration shall be deferred and paid out in SEB shares, so-called 
equity-based remuneration. Such remuneration is a means to attract 
and retain employees with key competence and provides an incentive 
for employees to be shareholders of SEB, which promotes long-term 
commitment that is aligned with shareholders’ interests. In addition, 
financial industry regulations require that a portion of variable 
­remuneration is paid out in the form of shares or fund units.
The models for individual variable remuneration are based on 
financial and non-financial key performance indicators at group, unit 
and individual level, including an evaluation of the employee’s con­
duct. Non-financial goals take into account factors such as customer 
satisfaction, compliance and sustainability related to, for example, 
the bank’s own environmental impact and integration of sustainability 
risks into the business model. SEB’s established sustainability ambi­
tions and goals are part of the criteria for potential allocation of the 
programmes, when applicable. 
At the individual level, key parameters include compliance with 
rules and policies for risk-taking in the group, including risks related 
to sustainability, SEB’s Code of Conduct and the requirements on 
internal controls in the respective business area. Performance is 
­evaluated over several years. 
SEB has two individual equity-based programmes: 
(i) the SEB Share Deferral Programme 2025 for members of the 
Group Executive Committee, certain other senior managers and 
a number of other key employees, and 
(ii) the SEB Restricted Share Programme 2025, for employees in 
­certain business units. 
For regulatory reasons, the programmes also exist in a form where 
the outcome is linked to the performance of mutual funds. Both pro­
grammes include a scope for risk adjustment for current and future 
risks. The final outcome may subsequently be reduced or cancelled 
entirely in accordance with applicable rules, such as taking into 
account SEB’s earnings and the capital and liquidity required for 
its operations. 
Approximately 11 (11) per cent of employees are offered 
­individual variable remuneration. Approximately 7 (7) per cent of 
the employees – such as those in Investment Banking – receive 
­variable remuneration with a cash component, but only in cases 
where it entails low or no residual risk for SEB. Variable remuneration 
above a certain level is always partly deferred and revocable. In 
2025, individual cash-based variable remuneration accounted for 
approximately 2.5 per cent (3) of SEB’s total staff costs.

Remuneration of the CEO, the Deputy CEO 
and members of the Group Executive Committee
The Annual General Meeting has established guidelines for salary 
and other remuneration for the CEO and members of the Group 
­Executive Committee (Guidelines). The Annual General Meeting may 
– irrespective of the Guidelines – resolve on, among other things, 
equity-based remuneration. 
Remuneration of the CEO, the Deputy CEO as well as the other 
­members of the Group Executive Committee (Executives) shall be in 
line with the Guidelines. The Guidelines cover base pay, equity-based 
remuneration, pension benefits and other benefits. No cash-based 
­variable remuneration is paid to the Executives, nor are they eligible 
for the SEB All Employee Programme. The pension plans are 
defined-contribution based, except for a defined-benefit component 
provided under collective bargaining agreements. The total remunera­
tion shall reflect the complexity, responsibility and leadership skills 
required as well as the performance of the individual Executive. 
In the case of termination of employment initiated by SEB, a 
­maximum of 12 months’ severance pay is payable, after the agreed 
notice period of maximum 12 months. SEB has the right to deduct any 
income earned from other employment from the severance pay.
SEB complies with the Swedish FSA’s regulations on remun­eration 
in financial companies, the Swedish Corporate ­Governance Code and 
Swedish and international regulations and guidelines in relevant 
parts. The Executives’ positions are among those identified as having 
a material impact on the risk profile of the SEB Group.
There has been no use of the right to reclaim variable remuneration 
in 2025 and there have been no expressed views at the Annual 
­General Meeting in relation to previous Remuneration reports.
Long-term equity-based programmes
The CEO participates in the SEB Share Deferral Program­mes 
2018–2025 (SDP) that were allotted in the current position and 
that have remaining vesting or other conditions before becoming 
fully exercisable. The deputy CEO and all other Executives, except  
the Chief Risk Officer, participate in the SEB Share Deferral 
­Programmes allotted in their current positions.
The Share Deferral Programmes are performance-based with 
pre-determined quantitative and qualitative performance criteria that 
define the allocation level. As for all employees, the model is based 
on financial and non-financial key performance indicators in relation 
to their responsibility. There are no specific percentages linked to the 
outcome of each KPI. Sustainability KPI’s are integrated in remunera­
tion for all Executives. SEB’s established sustainability ambitions and 
goals are part of the criteria for allocation. The main ambitions and 
goals linked to climate are the Carbon Exposure Index (fossil credit 
exposure in our energy port­folio) and financed emissions measured 
according to our 2030 sector targets. The application of the perfor­
mance criteria, as well as the evaluation, for Executives mirrors that 
of the CEO as set out below (see section “Performance criteria for 
the CEO’s remuneration”), taking into account SEB’s as well as the 
­relevant division’s or function’s business plan.
The participants are granted an initial number of conditional share 
rights. Each share right entitles to an SEB Class A share subject to the 
fulfilment of certain vesting, restriction and holding requirements.

Performance criteria for the 
CEO’s remuneration
The Board’s view is that the CEO’s total remuneration to a large 
extent should be based on fixed pay which is evalu­ated ­annually and 
set on a competitive level, in light of the CEO’s and the bank’s short- 
and long-term performance.
At the same time, there is a strong desire to link the ­CEO’s pay to 
the interest of the shareholders and strive towards a sustainable and 
long-term alignment. Consequently, the CEO’s total remuneration also 
contains pay in form of deferred shares on a moderate level relative 
to the total remuneration, as described in the above sections. These 
shares are restricted, linked to certain vesting and risk adjustment 
conditions, and follows the SEB A share’s development without any 
leverage structures. 
Even though the pay structure is seen as mainly fixed, the actual 
annual deferred share allocation, but not the final outcome, is linked 
to certain performance criteria as outlined in SEB’s three-year busi­
ness plan. 50 per cent of the shares are deferred for a minimum of 
four years, the remaining part for a minimum of six years.
The performance measures for the CEO’s remuneration have been 
selected to deliver on SEB’s strategy and to encourage behaviours 
which are in the long-term interest of SEB. In the selection of perfor­
mance measures, the strategic objectives and both short- and long-
term business priorities for 2025 have been taken into account. 
At present, these are clustered into four main focus areas: 
(i) Financial, which comprises SEB’s operating income, cost, profit 
and return on equity. 
(ii) Customer satisfaction, based on external ratings. 
(iii) Environment, Social and Governance (ESG), including for example 
sustainability, people and conduct. 
(iv) Strategic initiatives to future-proof customer relationships, 
profit generation and the bank’s platforms. 
The evaluation of the CEO is made in a multi-year perspective without 
a relative weighting of the different performance criteria, rather an 
aggregated and holistic evaluation of the performance relative the 
three-year business plan. This resonates well with the remuneration

Basis for preparation of 
the ­Sustainability Statement
This section outlines the basis for preparation, key principles and 
­specific circumstances underpinning the Sustainability Statement. 
SEB Group has prepared its statutory Sustainability Statement in 
accordance with the Swedish Annual Accounts Act (1995:1559), 
Chapter 6, 12-12f §, which includes the implementation of EU 
­Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the European 
Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), and the disclosure 
requirements related to Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy including 
­delegated acts. 
The Sustainability Statement has been prepared on the same 
­consolidated basis as the financial statements. SEB’s subsidiaries, 
SEB Life and Pension Holding AB (Sweden), SEB Asset Management 
Holding AB (Sweden), SEB Kort Bank AB (Sweden), AS SEB Pank 
(Estonia), AS SEB banka (Latvia), and AB SEB Bankas (Lithuania), 
fall within the scope of CSRD and apply the subsidiary exemption, 
as their CSRD reporting obligations are fulfilled through this 
­Sustainability Statement. 
Consistent with the financial statements, the Sustainability 
­Statement covers the period 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2025, 
­corresponding to SEB’s financial year. Unless otherwise stated, 
the reported information applies to the entire SEB Group.
For more information, see Note G1, p.211, G21, p. 250 as well as 
P19 and P20, p.313.
Reporting undertaking and value chain
The information disclosed in the Sustainability Statement is based on 
the impacts, risks and opportunities identified as material through 
SEB’s double materiality assessment (DMA) 2025. The assessment 
includes both SEB own operations and its upstream (suppliers) and 
downstream (customers) value chains. 
 
­
­
Classified and sensitive information
SEB has exercised the option to omit certain information relating to 
information security and financial crime prevention, where such 
­information is classified and/or sensitive in nature. Accordingly, 
­omissions have been made in S4-5 for information security (p. 143) 
and in selected metrics under MDR-M for financial crime (p. 156).

Description of SEB’s approach
Time horizon
SEB applies time horizons aligned with its risk-management framework: current (short-term): the financial 
year (1 Jan–31 Dec); medium-term: 1–5 years; long-term: 5–10 years; and a very long-term: beyond 
10 years (to reflect the long-term nature of climate-related effects).
Value-chain estimation
SEB uses customer-reported data as primary source in its reporting, but in the absence of such data, 
proxy-based estimates and industry benchmarks are applied. The most significant estimates are used in the 
calculation of financed, invested, and facilitated GHG emissions, which contain both methodological and data 
limitations, for example sector-average emission factors that may not accurately reflect individual customer 
emission profiles, and a one-year lag in the emission data, see p. 123.
The complexity of value chains and the absence of fully standardised practices for calculating Scope 3 
emissions affect the reported GHG emissions. Despite this, SEB considers the reported GHG emissions 
sufficiently reliable for assessing climate impact and progress towards decarbonisation targets. 
Taxonomy-related KPIs reported by SEB’s customers are collected with a one-year delay from external 
data providers. Data deficiencies have been observed, but processes have been implemented to improve 
data quality, see p. 165.
Sources of estimation and outcome uncertainty
Forward-looking estimates, including those based on climate scenarios, are subject to uncertainty as external 
assumptions and transition pathways evolve. See E1 SBM-3 and Figure 17, p. 102, and E1 IRO-1 p. 106.
Reporting errors in prior periods
Financed emissions for 2020 and 2023 have been restated, affecting Figures 38, 39 and 42 (p. 121, 122 and 
124). Invested emissions for 2023 have also been restated, affecting Figures 38, 39, 44 and 45 (p. 121, 122 
and 126). The reasons for the restatements are explained on p. 123 and 126, respectively.
Incorporation by reference

Board and management 
roles and ­responsibilities
SEB’s Board of Directors (the Board) and its committees have the 	
responsibility for SEB’s organisation, administration, and ­operations, 
including sustainability matters. The Chief Executive Officer (CEO), 
who is also the President, is responsible for the ­day-to-day manage­
ment of the activities of SEB in accordance with the Board’s direc­
tives. The CEO and the CEO committees are SEB’s executive manage­
ment bodies.
SEB’s corporate governance report (p. 51–69) provides an over­
view of the composition and diversity of the Board and the Group 
Executive Committee (including the CEO), their roles, responsibilities 
and skills on sustainability matters. 
SEB’s operations are managed, controlled and followed up in 
accordance with policies and instructions established by the Board 
and the CEO, including those related to sustainability. SEB’s sustaina­
bility governance model defines roles and mandates that cover SEB’s 
impacts, risks and opportunities, including environmental, social and 
governance aspects.
The Board and its committees
The Board has the responsibility of oversight of SEB’s work to iden­
tify, assess and integrate sustainability-related impacts, risks and 
opportunities in e.g., its strategy and business plan, risk management, 
and policy frameworks. The Board takes a holistic view in their 
­oversight, including decisions on trade-offs considered in the short, 
medium and long term. Trade-offs are part of the Board’s regular 
decision making. One example is restrictions on exposure, adoption 
of sector policies or sector specific sustainability targets. The Board 
receives reports on SEB’s progress on key sustainability issues on a 
periodic basis.
The Board has established committees, (Figure 2) to handle 
­certain defined issues and prepare them for decision by the Board. 
The Board committees meet at least quarterly and sustainability-­
related matters are addressed as required.
For more information, see the Corporate governance report 
p. 55–63.
Risk and Capital Committee (RCC) supports the Board in ensuring 
that the risks inherent in SEB Group’s business are identified, meas­
ured, assessed, monitored, managed, mitigated and reported in 
accordance with external and internal rules. The committee also 
­support the Board in matters related to financial stability, strategic 
capital and liquidity matters. The committee provides oversight of 
SEB’s risk management framework, the sustainability policy frame­
work and the capital and liquidity framework. 
Audit and Compliance Committee (ACC) supports the Board in 
its work with quality assurance of, and internal control over, SEB’s 
financial and sustainability reporting and reporting to the supervisory 
authorities. ACC has oversight over the internal controls and proce­
dures related to SEB’s group Sustainability Statement. 
Remuneration and Human Resources Committee (RemCo) ­supports 
the Board in its work in developing and evaluating the remuneration 
policy, incentive models and risk adjustments. RemCo also evalu­
ates SEB’s talent, learning, inclusion and diversity, and succession 
planning activities.
The CEO, CEO committees and SEB External ­Sustainability 
Advisory Board (SESAB)
The CEO is responsible for the day-to-day management of the activi­
ties of SEB, the execution of the sustainability strategy, and the 
implementation of the governance structure set by the Board. When 
implementing the sustainability strategy and throughout the decision-­
making processes, consideration is given to sustainability impacts, 
risks, opportunities, and the associated trade-offs.

During 2025, the CEO had seven CEO committees at his disposal for 
the purpose of managing the business operations, of which all but

The CEO is the chair of the CEO committees. All members of the 
CEO committees are employed by SEB, hence not independent in 
relation to SEB. The frequency of meetings varies due to the CEO 
committees’ responsibilities and requirements. Sustainability-­
related matters are handled when needed in the same manner as 
other topics. The members of the CEO committees have various 
­profiles in terms of experience and skills, relevant to the topics of 
the CEO committees. 
For more information, see the Corporate Governance report, 
p. 63–64 and 67–69.
Group Executive Committee (GEC) is a consultative forum for 
the CEO, with the purpose of managing the execution of the overall 
business strategy in the SEB Group. In 2025, the CEO adopted, after 
consultation in GEC, SEB’s Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) 
in accordance with CSRD. 
Group Executive Sustainability Committee (GESC), with the Chief 
of Staff as vice chair, manages the execution of the sustainability 
strategy in SEB. 
Group Risk Committee (GRC), with the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) as 
vice chair, addresses all types of risks in SEB, including sustainability 
risks, and evaluates portfolios, products, and ­customers from a 
risk perspective. 
Group Internal Control and Compliance Committee (GICC), with the 
Chief of Staff as vice chair, addresses and follows up on reports from 
the control functions Group Internal Audit, Group Compliance and, 
where relevant, the CRO function, as well as reporting and escala­
tions from the Financial Crime Prevention (FCP) Senior Manager and 
the Group Data Privacy Committee. GICC also follows up on whistle­
blowing matters.
Group Human Resources Committee (GHRC), with a Senior Advisor 
to the CEO as vice chair, handles matters of strategic importance 
­concerning the workforce of SEB. Areas of responsibility include, 
but are not limited to, preventive, detective and reactive measures 
against internal fraud, insider risk management, staff misconduct and 
sustainability matters, and other risks directly or indirectly associ­
ated with the workforce of SEB. GHRC shall ensure that the mitigating 
actions SEB takes against these risks are proportionate and aligned 
with SEB’s purpose, behaviours and culture using a risk-based 
approach.
Asset and Liability Committee (ALCO), with the Chief Financial 
Officer (CFO) as vice chair, handles financial stability, strategic capi­
tal and liquidity issues, including internal capital allocation and princi­
ples for internal pricing. The Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment 
Process (ICAAP) and the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment 
Process (ILAAP) include stressed scenarios due to climate change.
Senior Leadership Committee (SLC) has as its purpose to give the 
CEO a forum to discuss business matters in a broader context, share 
information and knowledge among senior managers in the SEB Group. 
Sustainability-related matters are on SLC’s agenda when relevant.
 
SEB External Sustainability Advisory Board (SESAB) provides SEB 
with strategic intelligence in matters concerning sustainability from 
outside the banking industry, based on academic research and, when 
desired, complemented with industrial experience. SESAB was estab­
lished as SEB recognised its need to understand the direction and 
speed of sustainability-related change, including future opportunities 
and challenges. SESAB is composed of external experts by invitation 
of the CEO. 
Group Control functions
The Group Control functions are independent from the business 
­operations. The three Group Control functions are (i) the CRO 
­function, (ii) Group Compliance and (iii) Group Internal Audit. 
The CRO function ensures that SEB’s risks are identified, measured, 
assessed, monitored, managed, mitigated and reported. The respon­
sibility includes sustainability-related risks. 
Group Compliance advises the business and management to ensure­
that the Group’s business is carried out in compliance with regulatory 
requirements. Sustainability-related matters within Group Compli­
ance’s areas of responsibility include, e.g. customer protection and 
prevention of money laundering, terrorism financing, and sanctions. 
Group Compliance is also responsible for SEB’s Code of Conduct. 
Group Internal Audit is a group-wide control function commissioned 
by the Board to independently evaluate SEB’s operations. The main 
task of Group Internal Audit is to evaluate and give assurance to the 
Board and the President that governance, risk management and 
­internal controls are adequate and effective.
Business Divisions, Group Staff and Support functions
To execute on the policies, instructions and decisions by the Board 
and the CEO, several decision-making bodies are established in the 
Business Divisions, Group Staff and Support functions. These are 
responsible for continuously identifying, assessing, controlling, and 
managing sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities 
relating to their daily conduct of business and that the activities 
­comply with applicable SEB group-wide policies and instructions 
and are supported by a clear decision-making hierarchy. 
For more information on SEB’s control functions, business 
­divisions, Group Staff and support functions, see the 
­Corporate Governance report p. 65–66.
Sustainable Banking
Sustainable Banking is a function responsible for driving and coordi­
nating SEB’s overall sustainability agenda. This work is carried out in 
close collaboration with Business Divisions, Group Staff and Support 
functions. Before new or revised sustainability-related policies, 
instructions, metrics or ambitions are proposed, Sustainable Banking 
conducts a review process in which draft proposals are shared with 
Business Divisions and relevant Group Staff and Support functions 
(including Group Legal, Group Finance, Group Compliance and the 
CRO function) for feedback. To ensure correct labelling of sustainable 
products, they undergo review by committees led by experts from 
Sustainable Banking.

over the sustainability reporting
SEB maintains a robust internal control framework over financial 
reporting (ICFR), which has been extended to cover the Sustainability

include: interpretation of regulatory requirements, reliance on 
­external ESG data, and integration of ESG data into existing ­internal 
processes. 
To assess risks related to sustainability reporting, SEB applies the 
same risk assessment methodology as used for financial reporting. 
This methodology distinguishes between causes, events, impacts and 
controls. In 2024 and 2025, SEB conducted dedicated workshops to 
identify potential risks and define mitigating actions. These efforts 
have informed the design and implementation of relevant controls, 
which are subject to continuous development over time. 
The effectiveness of the controls is reviewed annually and 
reported to the Audit and Compliance Committee.

This is SEB
Founded in 1856, SEB is a leading northern European financial ser­
vices group serving approximately 280,000 corporate customers and 
1.4 million private individuals. The bank supports customers both in 
its home markets and in their international business activities. SEB’s 
home markets comprise Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Norway, Estonia, 
Latvia, Lithuania, Germany and the United Kingdom. In addition, 
­Switzerland, Austria and the Netherlands are defined as home 
­markets with a selective approach. Around 95 percent of the bank’s 
19,922 employees work within these home markets. 
As a financial institution, SEB plays a vital role in society, and main­
taining the trust of its stakeholders is essential. The bank’s business 
is grounded in solid governance, ethical practices, and long-term 
­relationships.
For more information on employees by ­geography, 
see  S1-6 ­Figure 53, p. 137.
SEB offers a broad range of products and services, including:
•	 Core banking products, such as loans, leasing, card and 
­payment-related products
•	 Capital market products, including trading and issues on 
­financial markets
•	 	Asset management, including fund management, advisory 
and ­custody
•	 	Life insurance and pension solutions
•	 	Other products and services, including treasury operations 
Gross income derived from these products is shown in Figure 7. 
SEB provides products and services through four divisions to meet 
the specific needs of different customer groups and markets. The 
sustainability matters that are the most important in the different 
divisions vary due to different customer groups, products and ser­
vices. Matters such as climate change mitigation, financial crime, 
­corporate culture, and information security are important across all 
divisions. SEB’s divisions and their primary sustainability matters are: 
Corporate & Investment Banking: Serves large corporate custom­
ers and financial institutions in the Nordic region, Germany, and the 
United Kingdom, as well as through SEB’s international presence, 
with advisory-­driven commercial and investment banking services. 
A significant share of SEB’s financed and facilitated emissions origi­
nate from customers served by this division, making climate change 
mitigation a particularly important sustainability matter.
Business & Retail Banking: Provides advisory services and financial 
solutions to private customers, as well as a range of financial products 
and services for small and medium-sized businesses in Sweden. 
Social sustainability matters, such as data privacy, access to (quality) 
information, and financial inclusion, together with climate change 
­miti­gation, adaptation, and energy efficiency for mortgages, are 
­particularly relevant for this division due to its large private custom­
ers base.
Wealth & Asset Management: Offers tailored solutions in private 
wealth, asset management and life insurance. SEB’s invested 
­emissions stem from assets under management in this division. 
Baltic: Provides universal banking services to private individuals 
and businesses in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Social sustainability 
matters, such as data privacy, access to (quality) information, and 
financial inclusion are important within this division, alongside climate 
change mitigation through the reduction of financed emissions. 
For more information about SEB’s operating segments and 
­products, see note G2 in the financial statements, p. 220.

Sustainability strategy cornerstones
Providing transition advice, financing and investments 
We partner with our customers on the path to a low-carbon, 
­sustainable and resilient society. We engage with our private, 
­corporate and institutional customers to identify sustainability-­
related risks and opportunities. Through deep insights, quality 
information, responsible advice and capital, we help them to 
reach their targets. 
Innovating and setting standards 
We share our knowledge, develop innovative products and 
­services, and engage in setting standards, both at industry and 
national level, for how the financial industry can contribute to 
a more sustainable and inclusive society.
Transforming our business 
Based on solid governance, we continuously develop our policies, 
metrics and goals and enhance our employees’ competence to 
ensure our advisory, credit and investment portfolios support 
the transition towards a sustain­able future for people, businesses 
and society.
Acting as a responsible corporate citizen 
for a resilient and ­inclusive society
In line with our long tradition, we drive and encourage initiatives 
for sustainable entrepreneurship and promote financial inclusion 
and the respect of human rights. Being an important part of 
­society’s financial infrastructure, we protect the integrity of 
our ­clients’ data in an increasingly ­digital world, and we fight 
­financial crime.
Sustainability strategy – facilitating transition and 
­supporting resilience
SEB’s overarching 2030 Strategy focuses on the following key areas: 
acceleration of efforts, strategic change, strategic partnerships and 
efficiency improvements. The primary aims are to future-proof the 
business and accelerate income growth. 
Sustainability matters are addressed across all these areas to 
­varying degrees. For example, SEB is accelerating its sustainable 
financing initiatives and forming strategic partnerships to uphold 
security standards and data protection. SEB is also collaborating 
with regulators and industry peers to combat financial crime. 
SEB’s sustainability strategy underpins the overarching 2030 
Strategy by guiding the prioritisation of efforts that support the 
­transition to a more sustainable future. It provides a framework for 
integrating sustainability considerations into relevant business deci­
sions, thereby enabling better support for customers. The strategy is 
built around four cornerstones that address SEB’s key sustainability 
matters, as outlined in Figure 9. 
The skills, engagement and ethical conduct of SEB’s employees are 
fundamental to delivering the bank’s strategy. SEB is committed to 
providing a supportive working environment and continuous learning 
opportunities, enabling employees to deliver responsible advice and 
capital to customers.
Sustainability-related ambitions and goals
To implement its sustainability strategy, SEB has established a num­
ber of ambitions and targets, most of which relate to climate change 
­mitigation given the high materiality and urgency of the transition. 
SEB is part of the UN Principles for Responsible Banking, with the 
aim of aligning its business strategy with the Paris Agreement and 
the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The bank has also 
joined several other important initiatives, including the Net Zero 
Asset Managers initiative (NZAMi) and the Poseidon Principles for 
shipping finance.
SEB’s ambition is to achieve net zero emissions by 2050 at the 
­latest. To guide this work and monitor progress, the bank has devel­
oped two proprietary metrics: the Carbon Exposure Index and the 
Sustainable Activity Index. These indices track progress in reducing 
the bank’s fossil fuel exposure and increasing its positive environmen­
tal impact through sustainable lending, advice and investments.

SEB has also set net zero-aligned 2030 targets for seven sectors in its 
credit portfolio. 
In addition to the climate-related ambitions and targets, Figure 10 
highlights SEB’s social and governance-related targets for two other 
sustainability matters: its own workforce and corporate culture. 
SEB regularly reviews its ambitions and targets in relation to its strat­
egy, business, and stakeholders, making adjustments where ­necessary. 
Further details on the ambitions and targets, including their defini­
tions, the products and services covered, customer groups, and geo­
graphical scope, can be found in chapters E1, p. 101, S1, p. 132 and 
G1, p. 151 of the Sustainability Statement. 
SEB’s sustainability strategy and efforts are based on several inter­
national agreements, frameworks and business-related commitments. 
SEB supports the following international agreements and 
­international frameworks:

Figure 11: Business model and value creation
Inputs
The primary inputs needed to produce SEB’s financial products and 
­services are five types of capital: 
Financial capital: SEB’s capital base, together with diversified sources 
of deposits and funding from customers and investors, constitutes the 
bank’s key financial resources. These resources are essential, as they 
serve as the foundation for delivering the bank’s services.
Human capital: Employees, corporate culture, collective ­knowledge, 
skills, experience, ethics and innovation capacity.
Social and relationship capital: Trust and long-term ­relationships with 
stakeholders, SEB’s brand, reputation, partnerships, networks 
and community engagement.
Manufactured capital: Physical assets and technological infrastruc­
ture that enable SEB’s operations, such as office buildings, information 
and communication technology and cybersecurity systems.
Natural capital: Less central in SEB’s own operations and limited 
to e.g. energy and water use, waste and business travel, but more 
­significant indirectly through business activities, particularly through 
financing and advisory of and investments in large corporations with 
high GHG emissions.
SEB’s business model
SEB’s business model is designed to create value not only for 
shareholders, but also for a broader range of stakeholders, 
including customers, suppliers, employees and society.
SEB’s main role as a bank is to act as a financial intermediary. 
This means collecting funds from businesses and private individ­
uals who want to save and invest and directing these funds to 
organisations and people that need financing, through loans 
and equity. This process helps to ensure that capital is used 
­efficiently. By helping businesses and households achieve their 
goals, SEB promotes innovation, encourages savings and invest­
ments, and contributes to overall ­economic growth. As a financial 
intermediary, SEB takes on calculated risks. These are carefully 
managed to minimise potential losses and to support overall 
financial stability.

and ­society. 
In addition to creating financial value, SEB’s business model 
­contributes to a broader set of values: 
Human value: Generated through the training and development of 
employees, the promotion of positive working conditions and a commit­
ment to equal treatment and opportunities. SEB’s success depends on 
the skills, engagement and ethical conduct of its employees. Fostering a 
sound corporate culture and continuously investing in professional devel­
opment are key elements of our human resources strategy. Human value 
outside SEB is also created through financial literacy initiatives and advi­
sory services that help customers make informed financial decisions. 
Social and relationship value: Created by building strong, long-term 
relationships with clients, regulators, and other stakeholders and by 
­providing high-quality products and services. Earning and maintaining 
trust as a reliable, long-term financial partner is a top priority for SEB. 
The bank’s corporate governance, regulatory compliance, and risk man­
agement practices help address key challenges such as financial crime, 
cybersecurity threats, and the integration of sustainability considera­
tions in decision-making. SEB also contributes to society through social 
initiatives, such as promoting financial inclusion. 
Manufactured value: Created through the innovation and development 
of digital banking solutions, investment in advanced security systems 
to safeguard customer data and finances, and ensuring uninterrupted 
access to services. As part of the central payment infrastructure in the 
Nordic and Baltic countries, SEB plays a vital role in keeping payment 
systems operating smoothly 24/7, a service essential to customers and 
society at large. SEB’s physical premises also support a safe and positive 
working environment and enhance in-person customer interactions.
Natural value: Generated primarily through our efforts to increase sus­
tainable lending and investments and reduce financed, facilitated and 
invested greenhouse gas emissions. SEB aims to reduce its indirect nega­
tive impact on climate and nature by actively engaging with clients in 
high-emission sectors and supporting them in their transition towards 
more environmentally sustainable operations.

SEB’s value chain
SEB’s upstream value chain consists of suppliers that provide manu­
factured capital such as office buildings, data, technology and profes­
sional services. The downstream value chain includes corporate 
credit and capital market advisory customers, private customers, 
assets under management, account holders (deposits), and users of 
transaction and payment services. As deposits form part of SEB’s 
financial capital, they can be considered to belong to both the 
upstream and downstream value chains. 
Through relationships with corporate customers, SEB engages with 
a broad section of society across many industries. These clients face 
their own sustainability matters, including those within their 
­respective value chains. SEB’s efforts to address climate change 
are primarily focused on these corporate customers, where most 
of our environmental impacts occur.
Sustainability matters in the upstream value chain are more limited 
in scope, as SEB’s suppliers are concentrated mainly in information 
and communication technology sectors as well as in real estate. 
­Relevant sustainability matters in relation to our suppliers include 
information security and the protection of customer data.
SEB’s own operations also play an important role in addressing 
sustainability matters. As an employer, SEB has a direct impact on 
its workforce. Solid governance and risk management are essential 
to preventing financial crime and maintaining societal trust. SEB also 
seeks to contribute to social value through initiatives that promote 
financial inclusion and by providing high-quality financial advice and 
information to customers.

Impact, risk and opportunity management
IRO-1
The double materiality 
assessment ­process
Introduction
Under CSRD, companies are required to conduct a double materiality 
assessment (DMA) annually to determine their material sustainability 
matters, along with the related impacts, risks, and opportunities 
(IROs) to be disclosed in the sustainability statement. 
SEB conducted its first DMA, including the development of the 
methodology, in 2024. In 2025, the methodology was refined and 
the previous year’s conclusions were reviewed to assess whether 
any changes in SEB’s operating context could result in new or modi­
fied IROs or affect the relevance of certain disclosures. The review 
covered potential developments in the business environment, 
­customer needs, operations, products and services, regulatory 
­developments and market trends, and was informed by existing risk 
and sustainability frameworks, internal and externa data, as well as 
external stakeholder input. SEB’s sustainability specialists were 
involved throughout the whole DMA process.
The assessment covered the entire SEB Group, including subsidiar­
ies and geographical regions. Where relevant, analyses were con­
ducted at business-segment level to identify potential differences 
in material IROs within the Group. 
As is the case for financial institutions more generally, SEB has 
a large and diverse customer base across many sectors, which, 
together with limited access to customer value chain data, makes it 
impracticable to assess the full value chains of the customers. As a 
result, SEB’s DMA focused mainly on direct customer relationships 
rather than on customers’ full value chains. 
SEB is working to integrate the DMA into its risk management 
framework, business development, strategy, and relevant due 
­diligence processes. Sustainability-related risks are treated as 
­drivers of traditional risk types, such as credit, market, liquidity, and 
non-financial risks and the DMA both informs and is informed by 
existing practises for risk assessment, management and monitoring 
across these areas, supporting a holistic and integrated approach to 
risk management. In addition, SEB has implemented internal controls 
over the DMA process to ensure quality, see p. 86.
For further information on SEB’s risk management framework, 
see note G37 in the financial statements p. 264–279.
The DMA process
SEB’s DMA process consists of four steps:
1. Understanding the sustainability context of SEB’s business and 
value chains 
2. Identifying IROs that may be material for SEB
3. Assessing materiality, considering both impact materiality and 
financial materiality
4. Determining the material sustainability matters and their 
related IROs. 
Step 1: Understanding the sustainability context of SEB’s 
­business and value chains
The first step focused on identifying SEB’s business activities, prod­
ucts, services and value chains that are relevant from a sustainability 
perspective. The scope was defined based on an analysis of core busi­
ness activities, customer segments, policy frameworks, organisational 
structure, significant processes and relevant linkages to the financial 
statements. 
In 2025, one additional business activity and one downstream 
value chain were included in the scope: advisory services to private 
individuals (own operations) and capital markets advisory services 
to corporate clients, specifically debt capital market issuances facili­
tated through Debt Capital Markets (downstream value chain). 
Included operations and value chains are shown in Figure 12, 
p. 91.
Step 2: Identification of IROs that may be material
In the second step, SEB identified and assessed a broad set of 
­sustainability matters, including matters covered by the ESRS 
­framework as well as matters specifically relevant to SEB and the 
financial services sector. 
To identify IROs across SEB’s own operations and value chains, 
two complementary approaches were applied:
The first approach was qualitative and focused on SEB’s own oper­
ations. The identification of IROs was based on in-depth consultations 
with internal stakeholders and assessments by specialists across 
functions and business divisions, supported by sustainability experts.
The second approach was quantitative and focused on SEB’s value 
chains. Due to limited data availability, SEB could not rely on direct 
IRO information from customers or suppliers1). Instead sector-specific 
sustainability data from external sources, such as SASB, UNEP 
Encore, ISS, and MSCI2) were used. 
SEB’s credit exposures, assets under management, capital market 
issuance volumes, and procurement expenditures were mapped 
against this sector-specific data to generate a weighted heatmap of 
sustainability-related impacts and risks by sector.
To identify which of these should be considered possible material 
IROs, thresholds were applied based on SEB’s aggregated exposure 
across activities (irrespective of sector). A threshold of above zero 
per cent was applied for human rights impacts and risks, while a 
threshold of ten per cent or more was applied for all other sustain­
ability matters. The results of the quantitative analysis were 
­validated by SEB’s sustainability experts.
1) In addition, SEB has not been able to screen customer or supplier locations or activities for potential impacts 
related to pollution, water, biodiversity or resource use, as referenced in ESRS E2, E3, E4 and E5 IRO-1.
2) Information about these data sources can be found in the Sustainability glossary, p. 348.

Step 3: Assessment of the IROs’ materiality
In the third step, a structured process was applied to assess the 
materiality of all IROs identified in previous steps. Separate scoring 
methodologies were used for impact and financial materiality: 
•	 Negative impacts were evaluated by severity (scale, scope, and 
irremediability), and likelihood, with severity taking precedence for 
human rights. 
•	 	Positive impacts were evaluated by scale, scope and likelihood. 
•	 	Risks and opportunities were assessed by potential magnitude and 
likelihood of financial effect.
To ensure a consistent approach, the assessment criteria for financial 
materiality in the DMA are based on SEB’s internal risk assessment 
tools and methodology. Compared to 2024, the scoring scale was 
expanded from four to five steps to improve analysis granularity.
It was evaluated whether each IRO was positive or negative, actual 
or potential, and to what extent it was linked to other identified 
impacts, risks or opportunities. Where relevant, different time hori­
zons were also considered: current (within 1 year), medium-term 
(1–5 years), long-term (6–10 years) and very long-term (beyond 
10 years). 
Step 4: Determination of material topics 
The final step in the DMA process involved setting thresholds for 
impact and financial materiality to determine which IROs were 
­material to SEB. The materiality threshold was set at “moderate” 
(step 3) on a scale from negligible to very high (5 steps). 
To ensure the quality of the proposed DMA outcome, it was 
reviewed and verified by management from the business divisions and 
Group functions responsible for the material matters. The proposed 
outcome was also verified with employee representatives. 
SEB’s Group Executive Committee was consulted, and the final 
DMA outcome was decided by the CEO. The Board’s Audit and 
­Compliance Committee was informed of the CEO’s decision.
SEB’s material sustainability matters for 2025 and their associated 
IROs are presented in Figure 15, p. 94–97, including explanations of 
how they are connected to the business model, strategy and value 
chains across different time horizons.
IRO-2
ESRS required disclosures covered in 
the ­Sustainability ­Statement
The material impacts, risks and opportunities identified through the 
DMA determine the information to be disclosed in the Sustainability 
Statement. These IROs guide the filtering of requirements relevant to 
SEB Group, based on EFRAG’s data point list (Implementation Guide 
IG3). When appropriate, SEB has added entity-specific disclosures, 
derived from existing regulations (e.g., AML) or inspired by recog­

How impacts, risks and opportunities 
link to strategy
SEB works to support society’s transition towards a low-carbon econ­
omy, aligned with the goals of the Paris Agreement. Achieving this will 
require significant investments, and as a bank, SEB plays a key role in 
facilitating these financial flows. 
SEB’s core business includes funding corporates and households 
through financing, advisory and investment. It is therefore essential to 
understand these activities’ impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) 
associated with climate change.
The DMA identified seven material IROs related to climate change, 
summarised in Figure 16 and described below. 
Climate change mitigation IROs
Positive impacts: By providing financing, advice and investing, SEB 
actively supports customers’ transition to a low-­carbon economy. 
This includes ’green’ funding through loans and bonds, and through 
investment products aimed at reducing ­emissions.
Negative impacts: SEB’s credit portfolio, debt capital markets advi­
sory, and assets under management (AuM) include clients in sectors 
that contribute to significant greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
Risks: Climate-related transition risk refers to potential negative finan­
cial impacts on SEB arising from, for example, regulatory changes, 
technological developments and shifts in market preferences. These 
may affect the bank’s counterparties or invested assets by influencing 
asset values, profitability and refinancing capacities.
Opportunities: SEB sees opportunities to finance customers with 
clear emission reduction and energy transition targets. This includes 
expanding green financing, promoting resource-efficient innovation 
and enabling transition solutions. 
Climate change adaptation IROs
Positive impacts: SEB supports activities that enhance resilience 
to climate impact and, as part of its long-term strategy, advises 
and finances customers as they adapt to climate-related risks. 
This includes investments in infrastructure and the development 
of solutions to manage changing environmental conditions. In doing so, 
SEB helps customers and stakeholders in addressing climate-related

Risks: Physical risk refers to the risk of negative financial impacts on 
SEB arising from current or future physical effects of environmental 
factors. These factors are primarily material over the long-term, and 
include acute event, such as flooding and storms, and chronic risks, 
such as changing weather patterns. Physical risks may affect the

or disrupting supply chains.
Opportunities: SEB identifies opportunities to finance adaptation 
measures to mitigate the impacts of extreme weather, such as flood 
defences and investments in climate-resilient infrastructure. 
Strategic levers
To implement SEB’s sustainability strategy addressing ­climate 
change, SEB applies three key decarbonisation levers: 
• Financing the transition 
• Innovating and setting standards
• Transforming our business 
Each lever guides targeted initiatives and directs financial and 
human resources, advisory support, and operational tools to achieve 
measurable outcomes. These levers both set the scope for SEB’s 
actions (Figure 22, p. 111) and provide the framework through 
which climate-related IROs are addressed in SEB’s business model.
Financing the transition
Significant investment is required to support the transition to a low-­
carbon economy in line with the Paris Agreement. At the same time, 
substantial investment is needed to protect society against increased 
physical risks arising from the impacts of climate change. By financing 
the transition for private, corporate and institutional customers, SEB 
addresses both the positive impacts of climate change mitigation and 
opportunities related to adaptation to physical climate risks. Through 
products, insights, responsible advice and capital, customers are 
­supported in achieving their targets.
Innovating and setting standards
SEB has continued to advance the development of products and 
­advisory services related to climate change since we developed and 
advised on the first green bond in 2008. As a leader in sustainable 
finance, SEB contributes to the establishment of relevant market 
standards, a supportive policy environment and effective regulation 
that facilitate large-scale capital mobilisation towards sustainable 
opportunities. These initiatives form a key part of SEB’s positive 
impact on climate change mitigation.
Transforming our business
SEB addresses climate change mitigation by assessing and managing 
the impacts and risks arising primarily from customers’ activities. 
­Climate change adaptation is addressed by identifying and evaluating 
the physical climate risks that may affect customers and suppliers. 
To support this, SEB has established sustainability policies, risk 
and impact assessment tools, and systems that enable informed 
decision-making and strengthen the business model’s ability to 
­withstand climate-related challenges.
Strategy and business model resilience 
Through the capital it allocates, SEB has both the opportunity and 
responsibility to positively influence the world we live in. For several 
years, SEB has worked to future-proof its strategy and strengthen the 
climate resilience of its business plan by integrating climate change 
mitigation and adaptation into its 2030 business strategy, which is 
implemented through the bank’s sustainability framework. SEB’s 
­sustainability strategy aims to align the bank’s overall strategy and 
business model with the objectives of the Paris Agreement and the 
ambition to achieve net zero emissions by 2050 at the latest. This 
ambition is supported by Paris-aligned transition trajectories, with 
ESRS E1-4, p. 112, explaining how this ambition is translated into 
metrics and emissions reduction targets for financed emissions, 
and factors affecting delivery. 
SEB manages climate risks by incorporating them in the business 
and risk strategies, which are aligned with the overall risk appetite. 
SEB’s Risk Appetite Framework sets out the aggregated level of risk 
that is tolerated by the Board. Material climate risks are currently 
embedded within SEB’s asset quality and reputational risk state­
ments, and climate transition risk is monitored as a driver of both 
credit and reputational risks.

IRO-1
Processes to identify and assess 
­climate-­related IROs
SEB has established processes to identify and assess climate-related 
IROs. These processes provide a structured approach to understand­
ing how SEB affects the climate, and how climate change may, in turn, 
affect the bank’s business. They are embedded in the policy frame­
works, supported by dedicated assessment tools, and form an 
­integral part of the DMA (outlined in ESRS 2 IRO-1 p. 98–99). 
SEB’s most significant climate-related impacts and risks arise from 
its credit portfolio, and, to a lesser extent, from assets under manage­
ment and debt capital markets advisory. Suppliers are identified as 
material only in relation to climate change adaptation risks, while 
SEB’s own operations are not assessed as material. The processes 
described below reflect this materiality. 
Impacts on climate change 
Credit portfolio impacts
SEB’s processes to identify and assess climate-related impacts 
from its credit portfolio are the following: 
Sector categorisation: SEB classifies counterparties by carbon 
­footprint, prioritising high-emission sectors for review.
Counterparty transition pathway assessments: Using the Customer 
Sustainability Classification (CSC) tool, SEB evaluates clients’ transi­
tion plans against Paris Agreement pathways. 
Evaluation of policy compliance and transition plans: Customer 
assessment and escalation of policy deviations and status quo 
­transition plans.
Baltic ESG scorecard: A structured due diligence tool used in the 
­Baltic division to collect and assess quantitative and qualitative 
­sustainability data.
Sector categorisation according to their carbon footprint
SEB categorises credit exposures by sector based on their carbon 
footprint to identify climate-related impacts and risks, support 
financed emissions reporting and prioritise sectors requiring 
enhanced transition risk assessments. As shown in Figure 18, corpo­
rate clients accounted for 55 per cent of SEB’s credit portfolio in 
2025, and the majority of the bank’s indirect climate impact arises 
from this part of the portfolio. 
Figure 19, p. 104, illustrates the exposures across different sectors 
over the past two years. In 2025, credit demand in local currencies 
was broadly unchanged compared with 2024, reflecting subdued 
demand. However, at reported level, credit exposure decreased due 
to negative currency effects. The exposure to sectors with a material 
carbon footprint decreased, driven primarily by transportation and 
food and beverages. 
SEB has set 2030 financed emissions sector targets for several 
sectors with a material carbon footprint, aiming to reduce its indirect 
climate impact and mitigate transition risks in the credit portfolio, see 
Figure 24, p. 113. Sectors with a material carbon footprint but less 
significant financed emissions and few customers (such as textiles), 
or with high complexity and diversity (such as food and beverages), 
are included in financed emissions calculations but do not have 
­specific sector targets.

Counterparty transition path assessment 
Understanding customers’ current GHG emissions, their transition 
plans and their emission-reduction ambitions are essential for identi­
fying and assessing SEB’s impacts on climate change. SEB’s business 
divisions, supported by the Sustainable Banking function, use the pro­
prietary Customer Sustainability Classification (CSC) tool to assess 
customers’ climate transition plans and benchmark them against the 
objectives of the Paris Agreement. The CSC tool incorporates infor­
mation collected from customers together with sector transition 
pathways developed by third parties, resulting in a classification 
of transition plans across five categories: 
•	 Sustainable
•	 Paris-aligned 
•	 Transition 
•	 Gradual change
•	 Status quo 
In 2025, SEB began developing processes to assess the credibility of 
customers’ transition paths, which are expected to be implemented 
in 2026. 
Evaluation of policy compliance and transition plans
Business areas are responsible for conducting annual compliance 
screenings of their customers and escalate the following cases, in 
accordance with the escalation procedure outlined in E1-2, p. 107: 
•	 A customer in deviation of the restrictions or requirements defined 
in sector policies 
•	 A customer (or a customer within a group) classified as status quo 
in the CSC tool
Baltic ESG scorecard
The Baltic division uses a complementary due diligence tool (the ESG 
scorecard) to ensure consistency across customer assessments. 
The tool is used to collect and assess environmental, social and 
­governance-related sustainability data, including customers’ Scope 
1–3 emissions, targets, taxonomy related data and various policies. 
AuM impacts
SEB Asset Management (SEB AM) assesses the greenhouse gas 
emissions associated with its investments, covering Scopes 1, 2 
and 3, together with total emissions and emissions intensity. 
­Additionally, SEB AM assesses the following categories to identify 
and assess climate change impact from the portfolio:
•	 Transition companies and high emitters 
•	 The share of companies committed to Science Based Targets and 
with Paris-aligned transition plans
•	 The share of non-renewable energy consumption or production in 
relation to renewable energy sources among investee companies 
SEB AM uses its proprietary tool SIMS-S that screens all companies 
with available data, enabling analysis of potential and current port­
folio companies relating to climate change.
Climate-related risks
Credit portfolio risks
SEB has identified and assessed climate-related physical risks and 
transition risks as material drivers of credit risk. Both risk types are 
integrated within the risk management framework and assessed 
through SEB’s credit processes, portfolio analysis, scenario analysis 
and stress testing.
Transition risks are considered more imminent given SEB’s expo­
sure to industries currently undergoing transition, while physical risks 
and related adaptation risks are expected to increase over time, even 
as acute events are already intensifying.

transition risks over different time horizons is shown in Figure 20.

Climate transition risk assessment in the credit process 
Industry transformation and sustainability-related risks form an 
­integral part of SEB’s credit analysis and credit-granting process. 
­Customers operating in sectors exposed to medium to high climate-­
transition risks are subject to dedicated assessments. These assess­
ments consider customers’ exposure to transition risks, their strate­
gies to mitigate those risks, and the anticipated financial effects of 
implementing such strategies. The outcomes inform the customer’s 
credit risk profile in the short to medium term and provide an 
­indication of how it may evolve over the longer term. 
Portfolio analysis 
SEB regularly conducts portfolio reviews of sectors exposed to 
­significant transition risks as they move towards a low-carbon 
­economy. These analyses provide insights into risk development and 
market dynamics of the sector and are presented to the Group Risk 
Committee to support the oversight and management of ESG risks. 
Climate scenario analysis 
SEB conducts both climate transition risk and physical risk scenario 
analyses for sectors with material climate-related risks. The analyses 
consider the largest and most exposed customers in carbon-intensive 
sectors including oil and gas, power generation, steel, car manufac­
turing, heavy vehicle manufacturing, food and beverages, and real 
estate. They consider how different climate scenarios may affect 
their financial and risk profile and to what extent this could affect 
credit worthiness. Long-term climate impacts are assumed to take 
effect within the average maturity of the loan.
The scenario assumptions used are based on two scenarios within 
the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) framework, 
applying the ­narratives with some adjustments to reflect the charac­
teristics of SEB’s portfolios:
•	 NGFS Net zero 2050 scenario, assuming an orderly transition 
­consistent with a 1.5°C pathway, resulting in accelerated transition 
risks and lower physical risks
•	 NGFS Current Policies, where global efforts fall short of limiting 
significant warming, leading to global warming of about 3°C in 
2050, accelerated physical risks and lower transition risks
The NGFS scenarios are developed by an expert group to design a 
set of hypothetical long-term scenarios. They provide a common and 
up-to-date reference point for understanding how climate change 
(physical risk) and climate policy and technology trends (transition 
risk) could evolve in different futures but are not forecasts. NGFS 
scenarios assume different evolutions of climate policy, emissions, 
and temperatures, based on socio-economic assumptions. Key 
assumptions include the pace and stringency of climate policy, result­
ing in varied outcomes for transition and physical risks, and different 
impacts on global growth and employment.
Depending on the portfolio, SEB applies different assumptions in its 
climate scenarios. For corporate customers in carbon-intensive sec­
tors, changes in factors such as EU ETS carbon prices and oil and gas 
prices affect profitability, cash flow and probability of default. For real 
estate companies, the main effects relate to collateral values, driven 
by changes in Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) ratings combined 
with acute physical risk events, such as flooding. The scenario analysis 
is carried out on counterparty or collateral level and assesses to what 
extent the financial effects could lead to credit ­rating downgrades.
Climate stress testing framework and methodology 
In 2025, climate-related risks were integrated into SEB’s stress 
­testing framework. This allows the financial effects of different 
­transition and physical risk scenarios to be assessed as part of 
the regular ­evaluation of the credit portfolio. 
SEB applies a range of future scenario pathways, assuming that 
­climate-related events, covering both transition and physical risks, 
occur simultaneously and with increasing severity. These scenarios 
consider both SEB’s current exposures to climate risks and forward-­
looking assessments of potential impacts, enabling SEB to ­estimate 
risk exposure and expected credit losses.
SEB’s stress testing methodology consists of three components:
i.	 Customer and sector level assessment
The first component builds on the scenario analyses for corporate 
customers in high-emitting sectors described above. The potential 
effects on individual credit ratings are extrapolated to companies 
within the same emission-intensive sectors to estimate expected 
impacts on credit losses.
ii.	 Impact of physical and transition risk
The second component uses the results of bottom-up scenario 
analyses for real estate companies, as described above, to 
stress test the full commercial and residential real-estate port­
folio. This captures the effects of acute physical risks (such as 
flooding caused by to high precipitation) and chronic physical risks 
(such as sea-level rise) on collateral values, as well as the poten­
tial effects of changes in energy performance certificate (EPC) 
ratings.
iii.	 General macroeconomic assessment
For customers in sectors other than the high-emitting industries or 
real estate, the stress tests apply macroeconomic pathways 
developed by the Network for Greening the Financial System 
(NGFS). These pathways are used to reflect the potential adverse 
effects of transition and physical climate risks on overall economic 
activity, as reflected in GDP, extending to 2050 and beyond. The 
NGFS pathways incorporate the effects of heatwaves, floods,
