The bottom-up scenario analyses show that, for customers operating 
in carbon-intensive sectors, transition and physical risk factors 
increase the likelihood that their credit rating could deteriorate or, in 
severe cases, lead to default. At the same time, collateral values are 
stressed to reflect potential losses linked to flooding, lower EPCs, or 
assets becoming unusable due to the transition away from fossil fuels 
(so called stranded assets). SEB’s climate stress tests combine these 
effects to estimate how climate-related risks may influence expected 
credit losses across the portfolio. Results are expected to vary over 
time depending on market conditions, regulatory developments, 
­customer transition progress, and other external factors.
Overall, the expected portfolio impact is limited, with sectors 
showing negligible to low sensitivity as shown in Figure 17, p. 102.
AuM risks
SEB AM uses its proprietary tool SIMS-S to identify and assess 
­climate risks, including transition and physical risks, as part of a 
broader assessment of environmental, social, and corporate govern­
ance ­factors. The tool screens all companies for which relevant data is 
available, supporting the assessment of both current and potential 
portfolio holdings. SIMS-S incorporates indicators such as CO2 inten­
sity, the existence of Science Based Targets or equivalent emission-­
reduction plans, exposure to physical climate risks, EU Taxonomy 
alignment, links to climate-related the UN Sustainable Development 
Goals (SDGs) related to climate, and external assessments of 
­companies’ management of climate-related financial risks.
Supplier risks 
While the greatest adaptation risks for SEB are associated with its 
customers, the bank has also identified medium-term adaptation 
risks related to its suppliers, namely infrastructure such as office 
buildings, information and communication technology (ICT) and 
energy systems that may be exposed to flooding, extreme weather 
and other climate-related events. SEB manages these risks through 
ongoing assessment of supplier sustainability performance and is 
implementing a risk-based process to evaluate and monitor critical 
suppliers’ resilience. This includes assessing their capacity to with­
stand, respond to and recover from disruptions caused by climate 
change or environmental degradation. 
Climate-related opportunities
Credit portfolio opportunities
In contrast to negative impacts and risks, the identification of opportu­
nities is not managed through formalised processes. Instead, opportu­
nities are identified and developed through ongoing partnerships and 
continuous dialogue with customers and external stakeholders, includ­
ing companies, investors, governments and, where relevant, academic 
institutions. These interactions help confirm insights and identify new 
business opportunities. SEB works with product innovation and transi­
tion financing as key opportunity areas within the bank’s strategy.
AuM opportunities
SEB AM’s SIMS-S tool is also used to identify financial opportunities 
in the sustainability transition. This includes identifying companies 
that are leaders in innovation, climate solutions, and resource effi­
ciency. Furthermore, the intention is to increase exposure to compa­
nies and business models that actively contribute to the mitigation of 
and adaptation to climate change. Through the assessments of both 
impacts and risks, SEB AM identifies areas where climate change 
­mitigation or climate risks could provide opportunities for new SEB 
products to be developed.
E1-2
Policies related to climate change mitigation 
and adaptation
SEB integrates climate considerations into the overall strategy and 
applies relevant policies to guide key processes such as customer 
onboarding, credit and investment decisions. The policies define 
SEB’s positions on climate change mitigation and, where relevant, 
adaptation, and set requirements on business relationships for 
­managing climate-related financial risks, supporting the bank’s 
­commitment to align its portfolios with net-zero emissions by 2050 
in line with the Paris Agreement. 
For an overview of the sustainability policy framework governance, 
see Figure 3 in ESRS 2 p 83.
As illustrated in Figure 21, p. 108, the SEB Group sustainability policy 
framework is distinct from that of SEB AM. Described on p. 109, SEB 
AM’s sustainability policy framework is relevant to the management 
of climate change mitigation and adaptation IROs within this part of 
the SEB Group. The policies within these two frameworks are publicly 
available on the SEB Group website (sebgroup.com).
SEB Sustainability Policy Framework
SEB’s Sustainability Policy framework governs how climate change 
mitigation and adaptation is managed through two thematic policies 
and multiple sector policies, establishing restrictions, requirements, 
and expectations, and, where relevant, risk management and 
climate-­related opportunities. The full framework is illustrated below, 
with those policies that are particularly relevant to climate change 
highlighted. 
Governance integrating sustainability into SEB’s business decisions 
is outlined by the Sustainability Policy and detailed in the Environ­
mental Policy. SEB’s Credit Policy requires all lending to be in line with 
the framework, integrating climate risk and credit portfolio manage­
ment. Deviations from thematic or sector policies are managed 
through an escalation process involving divisional business and credit 
committees. All policies focus on managing impacts while mitigating 
reputational and credit risk and are reviewed annually. These policies 
are operationalised through SEB’s actions as outlined in E1-3, p. 109.

Thematic policies 
Two thematic policies form the basis for SEB’s work to protect climate 
and nature and to respect human rights, including a just transition. 
The policies set positions on specific themes, define overall 
approaches and articulate expectations regarding certain corporate 
behaviours. They apply across SEB’s whole value chain and cover 
activities and operations globally. 
Climate change mitigation and adaptation are explicitly addressed 
in SEB’s Environmental Policy, which supports customers in the tran­
sition towards a low-carbon economy. SEB aims to reduce demand 
for high-carbon-intensity products and to transition customers’ oper­
ations towards lower-carbon products and systems, moving away 
from fossil fuels and other GHG-intensive production. The policy 
requires efforts to achieve emissions reductions based on credible 
strategies. It also sets out SEB’s processes for assessing risks related 
to climate change adaptation, with the aim of supporting customers in 
adapting to physical climate risks and strengthening their resilience to 
climate change impacts.
Sector policies 
The purpose of the sector policies is to establish SEB’s position in the 
form of restrictions, requirements and expectations on relevant envi­
ronmental, social and governance topics in sectors with a potential 
material sustainability impact. Sector policies that are particularly 
­relevant regarding climate change are: 
Fossil fuel: Focus on extraction and power generation using thermal 
coal, oil & gas and thermal peat, including transition requirements 
and phase-outs. The policy has requirements on GHG disclosures 
and ­targets, as well as expectations that companies have a transi­
tion plan. Physical climate risks are also identified for this sector.
Mining and metals: Focus on restricting harmful mining practices 
and expecting best practices in existing and new mines and steel 
plants, including low-carbon technologies and renewable energy.
Transportation: Focus on the transportation of goods and people 
by air, train and road, as well as the manufacturing of equipment 
enabling such transportation, i.e. aeroplanes, trains, trucks and 
cars. For climate mitigation, the policy includes requirements on 
GHG disclosures and targets, the use of renewable fuels, and 
expectations on good practices, including just transition plans.

Forestry, pulp & paper and timber: Climate mitigation and adapta­
tion covered with focus on deforestation, management of biodiversity 
and efficient and low-carbon manufacturing practices. Physical cli­
mate risks, including fire, disease and extreme weather are identified.
Agriculture, fishing, aquaculture and animal welfare: Focus on 
deforestation, biodiversity, risk commodities, and good agriculture 
practices, including increasing carbon storage, reducing methane 
emissions and transitioning to renewable energy. Cattle added 
in 2025.
Electricity and renewable energy: Focus on new projects and emis­
sion intensity, biodiversity and human rights. Energy infrastructure 
transition risks are also addressed. In 2025, climate impacts from 
energy from waste was added. 
Shipping: Focus on climate mitigation via decarbonisation and fuel 
efficiency, ship recycling and sustainable maritime practices for 
­shipping assets. 
Real estate and construction: Focus on climate mitigation and 
­adaptation, addressing both operational and embodied carbon, 
­biodiversity, and health and safety across real estate ownership, 
development, and construction. 
Policy on Sustainability Considerations in Investments
The Policy on Sustainability Considerations in Investments has been 
developed to support business and investment decisions in alignment 
with SEB’s Sustainability Policy, risk appetite framework and long-
term strategy, including how climate impacts and, where relevant, 
transition and physical risks are integrated into investment decisions.
SEB Asset Management Sustainability Policy Framework
SEB AM, a business area within SEB Group comprising wholly owned 
subsidiaries, mirrors SEB Group policies and guidelines where appli­
cable. Its Sustainability Policy and Principles for Shareholder Engage­
ment of SEB AM guide the integration of climate and other sustaina­
bility factors into investment decisions and the management of 
negative impacts. These documents are reviewed annually by the 
Boards of SEB Asset Management entities. 
SEB AM applies a strict approach to fossil fuel holdings in the funds 
it manages, excluding companies involved in the extraction and pro­
cessing of fossil fuels, including unconventional methods such as oil 
sands and deep-sea drilling, as well as fossil fuel-based power 
­generation. Exceptions may be granted for transition companies with 
strategies to reduce emissions. To qualify, companies must demon­
strate a clear transition plan, commitment to global climate goals like 
the Paris Agreement, and alignment with frameworks such as the UN 
Global Compact and Science Based Target Initiative (SBTi). This 
approach supports SEB AM’s climate strategy, which emphasises the 
reduction of greenhouse gas emissions in its portfolios and prioritises 
companies that can contribute to climate mitigation and adaptation. 
By the end of 2025, SEB AM had 10 active transition companies in 
its portfolios.
The Sustainability Policy also ensures that material financial risks 
and opportunities related to climate mitigation and adaptation are 
integrated into investment strategies. Through active ownership, SEB 
AM can influence companies to develop more sustainable business 
practices, thereby adding value to the various investment strategies 
and contributing to the transition to a more sustainable global econ­
omy. Each company’s CEO is responsible for ensuring compliance 
with the policy. 
ESG-related risk policies
SEB’s risk framework addresses ESG-related risks, not as a separate 
risk category, but as risk drivers that may have bearing on the existing 
risk categories, such as credit risk, market risk, liquidity risk or non-­
financial risk. This means that the management of ESG-related risks is 
integrated into the existing governance and processes for identifying, 
measuring, assessing, monitoring, managing, mitigating, reporting and 
pricing risks. Applicable to the whole SEB Group, some of the key 
­policies include:
•	 The SEB Group Risk Policy defines the overall aim and framework 
of risk-taking in the SEB Group, as well as principles for risk 
­management.
•	 The SEB’s Group Risk Appetite Framework consists of risk state­
ments and corresponding measures that quantify the level of risk 
tolerated by the Board. Subject to materiality, climate-related risks 
are implicitly incorporated into several statements within existing 
risk categories. Currently, climate-related risks are considered 
within the statements relating to credit risk and reputational risk. 
Mitigating activities and restrictions are applied to ensure that 
these risks are appropriately managed. 
•	 SEB Group Customer Acceptance Policy represents what SEB 
­considers to be the critical requirements when accepting custom­
ers. Multiple principles draw on ESG aspects, such as transpar­
ency, business conduct, credible transition planning, adherence to 
the thematic environmental and social and human rights policies, 
and compliance with the relevant sector policy. 
E1-3
Climate change  
actions and resources
SEB has undertaken actions across its value chain to address its 
material ­climate-related impacts, risks and opportunities. These 
actions are structured around SEB’s three strategic levers, which 
­support the implementation of the bank’s ­climate strategy and policy 
framework across financing, investment, advisory activities and its 
own operations. Governance of these actions is described in ESRS 2, 
p. 81–85 and in the previous section (E1-2).
Financing the transition
SEB supports its customers in transitioning to low-carbon operations 
by focusing on decarbonisation, energy efficiency and reduced fossil-­
fuel dependence. 
In 2025, SEB updated its Green Bond Framework, which underpins 
the Group’s green product offering and aligns broadly with the 
­“substantial contribution” criteria of the EU Taxonomy. The frame­
work channels financing to renewable energy, green buildings and 
resource-efficiency projects.
SEB continued to implement its 2030 sector targets and credit 
portfolio transition plan using tools to assess and steer GHG emission 
impacts from the credit portfolio.
SEB provided debt capital markets (DCM) advisory services across 
all sectors and had an indirect climate impact through emissions from 
companies advised on bond issuances, referred to as facilitated emis­
sions. SEB monitored these emissions and promoted the use of green 
bonds to mitigate climate impact. The bank supported clients in issu­
ing green and transition bonds aligned with international standards, 
such as the International Capital Market Association’s (ICMA) Green 
Bond Principles and the EU Green Bond Standard (EuGBS), thereby­
helping to attract sustainability-focused investors. For example, in 
2025, SEB advised the Danish government on the first EuGBS-aligned 
sovereign factsheet. Proceeds from Denmark’s green bond are

Effects and challenges – emissions reduction and resilience
SEB’s influence on GHG emissions primarily arise through its financ­
ing, investment and advisory services, which support clients in 
­de­carbonising and adapting to the physical effects of climate change. 
While SEB tracks financed, invested , and facilitated emissions, it is 
not possible to precisely attribute emission reductions to SEB’s activi­
ties as outcomes depend on clients’ implementation of their transition 
measures. Progress on mitigation is assessed using the Carbon 
­Exposure Index, Sustainability Activity Index, and progress toward 
2030 sector targets.
Resources
Climate related actions are supported by the allocation of financial, 
human and data resources. During 2025, SEB continued to allocate 
resources to implement its climate goals and actions. These activities 
are not traditional capital expenditure, CapEx, but are better 
reflected as ongoing lending and operating expenditure, OpEx, 
encompassing efforts such as financing green projects, provision of 
ESG data, complying with regulatory requirements, and developing 
sustainable financial products. 
Key resources include:
Human resources: approximately 50 employees dedicated to 
­sustainability functions across the Group.
Financial resources: capital allocated to green financing and invest­
ment (Green Bond pool, Greentech Venture Capital Article 9 funds).
Data and systems: Oganisation-wide, externally sourced ESG data­
base, supported by upgraded data platforms. Internally developed 
tools such as the Customer Sustainability Classification tool, the ESG 
Scorecard, Carbon Exposure Index and Sustainability Activity Index.
Training and capacity building: ongoing ESG integration training for 
customer facing managers, analysts and general staff to enhance 
their capacity to engage and advise SEB’s clients and assess sustain­
ability-related impacts and risks. The effectiveness of training efforts 
is assessed through, amongst others, independent sustainability 
advisory rankings.
These resources ensure that sustainability considerations are embed­
ded in decision-making, lending, investment and risk management 
processes.
 Metrics and targets
E1-4
Climate change metrics 
and targets
As SEB’s most significant impact on climate change mitigation is indi­
rect and arises from its financing, advisory and investment activities, 
such as loans, bonds and assets under management, the bank uses 
metrics to estimate financed, facilitated and invested emissions. 
SEB’s targets, outlined in this section, address climate change mitiga­
tion, currently focusing on its credit portfolio. No targets have yet 
been established for climate change adaptation. 
Overview of targets
SEB has a long-term ambition to reach net-zero by 2050 at the latest, 
applying to the credit portfolio, assets under management, and 
­emissions from its own operations.
To support the transition of its business and track progress, SEB 
applies a set of metrics and targets for its credit portfolio, summarised 
in Figure 23. Two proprietary metrics have been developed, the 
­Carbon Exposure Index and the Sustainability Activity Index, each 
with time-bound targets. The Carbon Exposure Index is designed 
to help mitigate the indirect impact on climate change from SEB’s 
financing activities within the energy portfolio, while the Sustainability 
Activity Index aims to capture SEB’s indirect positive impact on 
­climate change mitigation through financing, advisory and investment 
activities. In addition, SEB has established seven 2030 sector targets. 
SEB’s climate-related targets are based on available data, esti­
mates and frameworks, as well as the bank’s business mix and risk 
appetite. These targets reflect forward-looking ambitions and are 
subject to uncertainty. SEB will continuously review them in light of, 
for example, regulatory developments, market conditions, technolog­
ical progress, geopolitical events and changes in business mix and 
risk appetite. Such reviews may lead to adjustments to the ambitions 
and targets. Accordingly, they should not be regarded as guarantees 
of future performance, are not legally binding, and may not form the 
basis for claims against SEB.

Methodology for target setting
SEB uses three types of metrics for its 2030 sector targets (see 
­Figure 25, p. 113):
Absolute financed emissions: This metric is applied to the oil & gas: 
E&P and refining sector. The choice of metric reflects the limited 
potential for the sector to reduce emission intensity over time and 
captures the necessary reductions in absolute demand and emissions 
consistent with the objectives of the Paris Agreement.
Emission intensity per physical unit: For power generation, steel, 
car manufacturing and household mortgage, the metric is calculated 
as the sum of the financed emissions divided by the sum of the 
financed volumes of output or physical unit. For shipping, the metric is 
calculated as the debt-weighted average portfolio annual efficiency 
ratio. Emission intensity metrics are relevant for sectors where the 
key driver of emission reduction is a transition to lower carbon-­
emitting processes and technologies. 
Technology mix: The metric is used for the heavy vehicle manufac­
turing sector due to limited reporting of Scope 3 use of sold products 
emissions by several large customers. Technology mix serves as a 
leading indicator of the reductions of Scope 3 use of sold products 
emissions, which represent the largest share of the emissions within 
the sector.
Scope and governance
The 2030 sector targets apply consistently across all SEB’s regions 
and subsidiaries. The Group Executive Sustainability Committee 
(GESC) is the decision-making body approving the 2030 sector 
­targets methodology and goals.
Performance monitoring of targets and results
Dynamics and decarbonisation levers differ between sectors influ­
enced by regulatory developments, technology adoption and con­
sumption habits. The development of our 2030 sector targets metrics 
will depend on our customers’ ability to successfully deliver on their 
emission reduction ambitions and the composition of our lending com­
mitments. Volatility arising from year-on-year fluctuations in attribu­
tion factors could further affect the development of the metrics.
For information about attribution factors  
and methodology see E1-6, p. 122.

Sector dynamics and decarbonisation levers
Electricity and heat production contributed 40 per cent of global CO2 
emissions in 2024, according to the IEA. Under the IEA NZE scenario, 
emissions from the sector need to halve by 2030 and fall by nearly 
95 per cent by 2040.
Global electricity generation is expected to increase 2.5 times by 
2050, driven by rising demand from electrification in areas such as 
electric vehicles and heating, alongside economic growth and popula­
tion expansion. Decarbonisation efforts require tripling global renew­
able energy capacity by 2030 (compared to 2022) and reducing 
­electricity generated from unabated fossil fuels by 40 per cent. 
Benchmark scenario and progress
The IEA NZE scenario suggests global electricity generation emission 
intensity needs to be reduced by 60 per cent by 2030 compared to 
2022 to reach 186 g CO2e/kWh by 2030. SEB has set a target to 
reduce the emission intensity of the sector to 70 g CO2e/kWh by 
2030, a 45 per cent reduction from the 2020 baseline. This target 
represents a 62 per cent lower emission intensity than the IEA NZE 
scenario for 2030.
As of year-end 2024, the financed emission intensity had 
decreased by 41 per cent compared to the 2020 baseline, and by 10 
per cent compared to 2023, reaching 74 g CO2e/kWh. This reduction 
was driven by increased lending to renewable energy producers 
(mainly wind power) and greater exposure to customers with emis­
sion intensities below the sector average. Between 2020 and 2024, 
the share of fossil based financed power production1) in the portfolio 
has decreased from 24 per cent to 14 per cent. Over the same period 
the share of coal based financed power production has decreased 
from 5 per cent to 2 per cent.
Steel
Overview
The sector includes customers involved in the production of carbon 
and stainless steel but excludes those involved in iron ore extraction 
or the production of processed iron ore products. As of year-end 
2024, SEB’s lending commitments to the steel sector amounted to 
SEK 11bn, representing 0.4 per cent of the total lending commitments 
(0.5 per cent in 2020). Financed emissions totalled 0.7 million tonnes 
CO2e, accounting for 3 per cent of SEB’s total financed emissions 
(2 per cent in 2020).
Sector dynamics and decarbonisation levers
Steel production accounted for 7 per cent of global CO2 emissions in 
2024, according to the IEA. The IEA NZE scenario suggests that emis­
sions from the steel sector must decrease by 19 per cent by 2030 
compared to 2022. Steel is vital for industries such as construction, 
capital goods and equipment.
Given the growing global demand for buildings and renewable 
energy infrastructure, reducing steel’s emission intensity is essential 
to achieve the Paris Agreement’s objectives. However, steel is a 
“hard-to-abate” sector, as zero-emission technologies are not yet 
widely available.
Short-term emission reductions will come from optimising existing 
production processes, while medium- and long-term solutions include 
maximising scrap steel use and deploying innovative technologies like 
Direct Reduced Iron (DRI) with Electric Arc Furnaces (EAF).
Benchmark scenario and progress
SEB used assumptions from the Sustainable Steel Principles Working 
Group and the IEA NZE scenario to create a net zero-aligned bench­
mark covering Scope 1 and 2 emissions. This benchmark anticipates a 
29 per cent reduction in sectoral emission intensity from 2020 to 2030.
SEB has set a target aligned with this benchmark, aiming for a 29 
per cent reduction in steel portfolio emissions intensity by 2030 com-
pared to 2020. As of year-end 2024, emissions intensity rose by 7 per

Decarbonisation in the short- to medium-term hinges on energy 
­efficiency improvements. These include operational measures such 
as hydrodynamic optimisation, improved propulsion systems, and 
weather/voyage routing, as well as technical upgrades like bow 
­retrofits and lubrication system enhancements. Achieving deeper 
emissions reductions requires scaling up low or zero-emission fuels 
(e.g., biofuels, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen) and adopting new 
­propulsion technologies compatible with such fuels.
Benchmark scenario and progress
SEB has set a target to reduce the debt-weighted average portfolio 
Average Efficiency Ratio (AER) for shipping asset financing by 41 per 
cent by 2030, using a 2022 baseline. This target is based on decar­
bonisation trajectories aligned with the objective of the Paris 
­Agreement developed by DNV Maritime Advisory.
As of year-end 2024, the debt-weighted average portfolio AER had 
decreased by 14 per cent to 8.4 g CO2e/tonne.nautical mile compared 
with the 2022 baseline, and by 2 per cent compared with 2023. The 
reduction reflects a mix effect and efficiency improvements across 
most vessel types.
Car manufacturing
Overview
This sector comprises customers producing passenger cars and light 
commercial vehicles. As of year-end 2024, SEB’s lending commit­
ments to the sector amounted to SEK 16bn, corresponding to 0.6 per 
cent of its total lending commitments (0.8 per cent in 2020). Financed

Sector dynamics and decarbonisation levers
In 2024, emissions from passenger cars and light commercial vehicles 
accounted for 8 per cent of global CO2 emissions, according to the 
IEA. The IEA NZE scenario suggests that emissions from this sector 
must decrease by 41 per cent by 2030, 86 per cent by 2040, and 
99 per cent by 2050, relative to 2022 levels. 
Electrification is the key lever for emissions reduction in this sector. 
The IEA NZE scenario assumes that electric vehicles (EVs) will com­
prise 65 per cent of global sales by 2030 and 95 per cent by 2035, 
compared to 18 per cent in 2023.
Benchmark scenario and progress
SEB used assumptions from the IEA NZE pathway to develop a 
benchmark scenario for the reduction of tailpipe emissions of new 
vehicle sales. This benchmark implies a 62 per cent reduction in

SEB has set a target aligned with this benchmark, aiming for a

pared to 2020. By year-end 2024, emission intensity of SEB’s port­

Carbon Exposure Index
The Carbon Exposure Index (CEI) is an internal volume-based metric 
measuring the fossil credit exposure within the energy portfolio. 
The fossil credit exposure is measured in Euro. The energy portfolio 
includes the following sectors as reported in Figure 19, p. 104: Oil & 
Gas: upstream-related (Exploration & Production, Energy services, 
Offshore), Oil & Gas: other (Transmission, Distribution & Storage 
(TD&S), Refining, Wholesale and retail), Power generation 
­(Conventional/mixed and Renewables).
At year-end 2019, the energy portfolio amounted to EUR 19.3bn 
and the fossil credit exposure to EUR 11.5bn. The goal is to reduce 
fossil credit exposure by 45 to 60 per cent by 2030 compared to the 
2019 baseline. The reduction pathway over the 2019–2030 period is 
illustrated by the green corridor in Figure 32, p.117. The lower limit of 
the CEI corridor is aligned with the fossil energy demand reduction 
assumptions of the NGFS Divergent Net Zero – EUROPE – Remind 
­scenario.

The fossil credit exposure is calculated by multiplying the credit expo­
sure with a fossil share. The credit exposure includes lending, obliga­
tions and trading products. The fossil share reflects the percentage of 
a counterparty or a project’s activity derived from fossil fuels (oil, 
natural gas, coal, peat and fossil portion of waste). The assessment 
of the fossil share differs depending on the sector:

development was driven by both reduced credit exposure and an 
increased share of dedicated financing to non-fossil activities. 
Fossil credit exposure to Power generation had decreased by 3 per 
cent at year-end 2025 compared to 2019 and accounted for 46 per 
cent of the total fossil credit exposure (19 per cent in 2019). This 
development reflects a 38 per cent increase in credit exposure over 
the period, mitigated by customers’ lower average fossil share and 
an increased portion of dedicated financing allocated to non-fossil 
activities. 
Sustainability Activity Index
The Sustainability Activity Index (SAI) is an internal, volume-based 
metric that captures four different aspects of SEB’s sustainability 
activities. SEB’s ambition is to increase activity by 6–8 times by 2030 
compared with a 2021 baseline, as illustrated in Figure 36, p. 119. At 
year-end 2025, the index had increased by 3.1 times compared with 
year-end 2021. 
Methodology
The SAI is calculated by assessing activity within several key 
­sustainability-related areas of lending and investing:
Sustainability-related financing
•	 Volume, indexed – measuring the development of 
­sustainability-­labelled loan financing products (such as green 
loans, sustainability-linked loans, leasing and ­mortgages). 
•	 SEB aims for an increase of ten times by 2030. 
•	 Outcome 2025: 2.9 times increase compared to 2021 
to SEK 328bn.
Sustainable finance advisory
•	 Volume, indexed – measuring the results of advising customers in 
the capital markets on sustainable finance, including volumes 
related to green bonds and sustainability-linked bonds. 
•	 SEB aims for a threefold increase by 2030.

The scientific basis for the Carbon Exposure Index and 2030 sector

Target baseline years and prior progress 
SEB has established multiple climate-related targets and ambitions, 
each with its own baseline year, determined depending on when the 
target was adopted and adjusted to ensure representativeness. 
External factors, such as temperature anomalies or the effects of

SEB’s direct and 
indirect GHG emissions
As outlined in the previous section, SEB’s climate-related metrics and 
targets are used to assess progress in climate mitigation across the 
credit portfolio, DCM activities and AuM. The metrics establish base­
lines for monitoring commitments to reduce GHG emissions and form 
the basis for the bank’s GHG disclosures. 
This section presents SEB’s direct and indirect GHG emissions 
across its own operations and value chains.
SEB’s emission reporting according to the GHG Protocol 
SEB’s GHG emissions are reported by Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 
in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate 
­Standard, ­using the operational control method. 
Scope 1: SEB’s direct emissions, such as company cars and ­leakage 
of refrigerants.
Scope 2: generation of electricity, heating and cooling purchased for 
own consumption.
Scope 3, categories 1 to 14: own operations and supply chain, 
such as purchased goods and services, waste and business travel.
Scope 3, category 15:
•	 Financed emissions: emissions related to lending commitments 
to customers.
•	 Facilitated emissions: emissions related to capital markets ­advisory 
business.
•	 Invested emissions: emissions related to ­managing funds and 
­discretionary mandates in the asset management business.
The GHG emissions are reported based on materiality, data availabil­
ity and relevance to SEB’s operations and business model, see Figure 
37. All emissions are disclosed at consolidated Group level.
The GHG disclosure for Scope 3 category 15 is based on emissions 
data from 2024, the most recent available data. For details on 
­calculation methods, see p. 122–128.
For Scope 3 categories 1-14, SEB is reviewing the possibility of 
expanding disclosures, where feasible.

Quantification of Scope 3 category 15 
Investments emissions
Methodology 
The emissions disclosed under Scope 3 category 15 Investments in 
Figure 38, p. 121, can be broken down into financed, facilitated and 
invested emissions, as shown in Figure 39. 
The emissions are estimated by multiplying the GHG emissions of 
customers, assets or investees by an attribution factor, which links a 
counterparty’s emissions to the size of SEB’s involvement. The 
­attribution factor is defined differently for financed, facilitated and 
invested emissions:
•	 Financed emissions: the ratio of the lending commitment (lending 
and obligations) to either the customer’s total assets (book value) 
or the market value of the financed assets. 
•	 Facilitated emissions: the ratio of the DCM issuances facilitated 
by SEB to the issuer’s total assets (book value), multiplied by a 
33 per cent weighting factor as per the PCAF Standard for 
­facilitated emissions. 
•	 Invested emissions: the ratio of the AuM (equity and debt instru­
ments) to the investee’s Enterprise Value Including Cash (EVIC).

Financed emissions 
Financed emissions are the GHG emissions attributed to SEB in 
­relation to its lending commitments. Lending commitments include 
lending only for asset-based financing (Shipping-asset financing, 
Household mortgages, Real estate management and Car leasing) 
and both lending and obligations for all other financing. For the 2024 
financed emissions, the lending commitments in scope amounted to 
SEK 2,049bn (up from SEK 1,779bn in 2020), representing 72 per 
cent of SEB’s total lending commitments (78 per cent in 2020). 
Financed emissions for the reporting years 2020 and 2023 have 
been restated to reflect a reclassification of exposures between 
­sectors and restated Scope 3 emission data for a few large corporate 
customers. Compared with the 2020 financed emissions disclosed in 
the Annual Report 2024, restated customers’ emissions resulted in a 
decrease of 1.3 million tonnes primarily related to the Heavy vehicle 
manufacturing sector. Compared with the 2023 financed emissions 
disclosed in the Annual Report 2024, the reclassification of expo­
sures reduced financed emissions by 0.4 million tonnes CO2e while 
restated customers emissions resulted in a further decrease of 0.4 
million tonnes CO2e. The restated 2020 and 2023 financed emissions 
are fully comparable in scope and methodology to the 2020 and 2024 
financed emissions. 
Financed emissions amounted to 24.1 million tonnes of CO2e in 
2024, corresponding to a decrease of 48 per cent compared to 2020 
(Figure 42, p. 124). The decrease is explained by changes in the com­
position of lending commitments (about 29 per cent), and changes in 
the size of the corporate customers’ balance sheets (about 22 per 
cent), while changes in customers’ emissions contributed to an increase 
of approximately 3 per cent. 
Financed emissions are concentrated in a limited number of cus­
tomers within carbon-intensive sectors. In 2024, the top ten sectors 
accounted for 80 per cent of total financed emissions while repre­
senting only 24 per cent of the total lending commitments in scope.2)
Facilitated emissions
Facilitated emissions are the GHG emissions attributed to SEB when 
acting as facilitator (bookrunner or manager) in DCM activities and 
bond issuances. Issuance volumes in scope include corporates and 
real estate customers. Issuances for sovereigns/public administration 
and banks are not included. The sector scope mirrors that used for 
financed emissions: all corporate sectors are included except for 
finance and insurance, services, IT and media, and other non-material 
sectors.
The issuance volumes in scope for the estimation of facilitated 
emissions amounted to SEK 154bn in 2024, representing 92 per cent 
of the total corporate and real estate management volumes. Green 
bond issuances are not treated differently in the calculation of facili­
tated emissions and are included as general corporate purpose 
bonds. This represents a conservative approach, as green bonds 
are generally expected to be associated with lower emissions than 
general corporate purpose bonds. In 2024, green bonds accounted 
for 44 per cent of total corporate and real estate bond issuance 
within SEB’s portfolio, exceeding the European market average of 
6.9 per cent of total corporate and government bond issuance 
reported across the European Union in the same year.3)
Facilitated emissions for corporate and real estate management 
customers amounted to 2.0 million tonnes CO2e in 2024, a reduction 
of  2 per cent compared to 2020 (Figure 43, p. 125). The five largest 
sectors contributed 91 per cent of the total facilitated emissions 
in 2024 with heavy vehicle manufacturing alone accounting for 
73 per cent.4)

Invested emissions
SEB’s invested emissions represent the GHG emissions associated 
with financial assets managed by SEB AM. Assets under management 
AuM) included in the calculation of invested emissions comprise 
assets managed within SEB funds and discretionary mandates where 
SEB AM has mandate responsibility. 
As shown in Figure 40, p. 122, the sectors included in the calcula­
tion of invested emissions are identical to those used for financed and 
facilitated emissions, namely corporates and real estate manage­
ment, with one exception. For invested emissions, investments in 
­covered bonds issued by banks are included, whereas bank-related 
exposures are excluded entirely from the calculations of financed and 
facilitated emissions. Figure 44 provides an overview of the scope 
used for estimating invested emissions as at year-end 2024. Excluded 
sectors are characterised by a low-carbon footprint and, in some 
cases, limited GHG emissions data availability.
Invested emissions for the 2023 reporting year have been restated 
to reflect a revision of the AuM included in the calculation scope. 
Compared with the invested emissions for 2023 disclosed in the 
­Sustainability Statement 2024, this revision resulted in an increase of 
0.6 million tonnes of CO2e, primarily attributable to the heavy vehicle 
manufacturing sector.
Invested emissions amounted to 9.9 million tonnes CO2e in 2024 
corresponding to an increase of 4 per cent or 0.4 million tonnes CO2e 
compared to 2023. The increase was primarily attributable to the 
heavy vehicle manufacturing sector (+1.1 million tonnes CO2e), 
mainly due to increased AuM. The development was partly mitigated 
by a decrease in invested emissions for the car manufacturing sector 
(–0.8 million tonnes CO2e) as the result of a change in holding alloca­
tion. The five largest sectors (heavy vehicle manufacturing, car 
­manufacturing, metals and mining, oil and gas E&P and refining and 
steel) contributed 93 per cent of the total invested emissions, 
with heavy vehicle manufacturing accounting for 82 per cent, as 
shown in Figure 45, p. 127.

Quantification of Scope 1, Scope 2 and 
Scope 3 categories 1–14 emissions
Methodology 
SEB’s methodology for reporting of GHG emissions across Scope 1, 
Scope 2, and Scope 3 (categories 1–14) calculates GHG emissions 
using activity-based data and are determined by multiplying a rele­
vant business activity data point, measured in specific units, by a 
­corresponding emission factor that expresses the amount of CO2 
equivalent emissions per unit of activity.
Where business data points include greenhouse gases other than 
carbon dioxide (CO2), these emissions have been converted to CO2 
equivalents (CO2e) using the latest Global Warming Potential (GWP) 
values.
See Figure 73, p. 164 for a complete list of emission factors.
Where activity-based data were unavailable, emissions were esti­
mated using defined estimation principles to ensure consistency and 
accuracy. For example, SEB may use November as an estimate for 
December or a rolling 12-month average to estimate the missing 
data. These principles are designed to make the reported GHG 
­emissions as precise and reliable as possible. 
The GHG emissions (reported in Figure 38, p. 121) for Scope 1, 
Scope 2, and Scope 3 categories 1–14 cover SEB Group, except for 
legal entities and branch offices where the GHG emissions are 
assessed to be immaterial.
GHGs per net revenue
In 2025, SEB’s GHG intensity ratio was 0.000225 (0.000189), 
­market-based, and 0.000225 (0.000189), location-based. Total GHG 
emissions represent the sum of all emissions reported in Figure 38 
(p. 121), while net revenue comprises interest income, fee and com­
mission income, net financial income and net other income (see the 
Income Statement, p. 220). The 2024 GHG intensity values have been 
recalculated due to the restatement of net interest income and net 
financial income. 
E1-7
GHG removals and 
mitigation projects
SEB manages residual GHG emissions through a combination of emis­
sion reduction actions within its operations and the purchase of veri­
fied carbon removal certificates to offset remaining emissions. 
For 2025, SEB’s approach addressed offsetting residual emissions 
from its own operations, Scope 1, 2 and 3 (category 1–14) including 
energy use, business travel and emissions from purchased goods and 
services. SEB offsets these emissions through the purchase of CO2 
Removal Certificates (CORCs) from Puro.earth, a carbon removal 
marketplace, using carbon credits from outside of the value chain. 
These certificates represent verified CO2 removal credits from bio­
char projects that store carbon for a minimum of 100 years. The pur­
chased certificates were formally retired during 2025, ensuring that 
the associated CO2 removals are uniquely claimed and not subject to 
double counting or resale. 
The projects are certified under the Puro.earth Biochar Methodol­
ogy, which applies lifecycle-based quantification of emissions, includ­
ing upstream and transport emissions, demonstration of long-term 
storage stability, and compliance with defined sustainability criteria. 
Figure 46 outlines SEB’s 2025 GHG credits.
Puro.earth is endorsed by the International Carbon Reduction and 
Offset Alliance (ICROA) Code of Best Practice. ICROA approval is 
obtained annually through an independent third-party compliance 
audit based on the ICROA Code of Best Practice, which sets out 
requirements and guidelines for high integrity and is continuously 
updated to encompass best practices.

EU Taxonomy Regulation
SEB is subject to the reporting requirements under the EU Taxonomy 
Regulation (EU) 2020/852 and its supplementing Delegated Acts. 
The EU Taxonomy is a classification framework that defines which 
economic activities and assets are considered environmentally sus­
tainable. Its purpose is to direct capital towards sustainable activities 
and investments, enhance transparency and comparability, and 
reduce the risk of greenwashing. 
Both financial and non-financial companies that are required to 
publish a sustainability statement under the Corporate Sustainability 
Reporting Directive (CSRD) must disclose the extent to which their 
economic activities are environmentally sustainable in accordance 
with the EU Taxonomy. 
An economic activity qualifies as environmentally sustainable if it: 
•	 Contributes substantially to one or more of EU’s six environmental 
objectives
•	 Does not significantly harm any of the other environmental 
­objectives (DNSH)
•	 	Is carried out in compliance with minimum social safeguards
•	 Complies with technical screening criteria for at least one 
­environmental objective. 
For the 2025 financial year Taxonomy report, SEB has applied the 
reporting requirements of the Disclosure Delegated Act applicable 
until 31 December 2025. The amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 
2026/73, applicable from 1 January 2026, will be implemented by 
SEB for the 2026 financial year report.
The table below summarises the Taxonomy alignment key perfor­
mance indicators (KPIs) relevant for SEB. Complete reporting tables 
and additional qualitative disclosures are available on p. 165–205.
Assets and activities covered by the KPIs 
SEB’s disclosures are based on the Taxonomy classification of the 
underlying economic activities that SEB finances, invests in, and 
­provides financial services to. The 2025 disclosures cover on- and 
off-balance sheet assets. Disclosure of fees and commissions and of 
the trading book has been postponed until 2027, pending a wider 
review of the Taxonomy framework by the European Commission. 
The year 2025 is the first reporting year in which financial compa­
nies disclose the share of assets associated with activities aligned 
with any of the six environmental objectives of the EU Taxonomy, 
namely:
•	 Climate change mitigation
•	 Climate change adaptation
•	 Sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources 
•	 Transition to a circular economy
•	 Pollution prevention and control
•	 Protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems. 
SEB’s main Taxonomy KPI is the Green Asset Ratio (GAR), defined and 
disclosed in accordance with Annex V to the Disclosure Delegated Act 
(EU) 2021/2178. The GAR represents the share of Taxonomy-aligned 
assets relative to the Group’s total GAR-covered assets at gross 
­carrying amount, based on the prudential scope of consolidation 
under the Capital Requirements Regulation (EU) 575/2013 (CRR). 
The KPI for assets under management (AuM) is reported in accord­
ance with Annex III as the share of Taxonomy-aligned AuM relative to 
the total value of in-scope AuM defined in the regulatory require­
ments. This includes assets managed within SEB funds and discretion­
ary mandates across SEB Group, as set out in Directive 2014/65/EU 
(MiFID II) and Regulation (EU) 2019/2088 (SFDR). 
The KPI for insurance investments is defined in accordance with 
Annex IX as the share of Taxonomy-aligned investments relative to 
total direct and indirect investments linked to insurance activities,

for comparability. These weights reflect the proportion of turnover

EU Taxonomy’s role in supporting the transition 
SEB’s greatest impact stems from partnering with customers and 
­supporting their transition efforts. Increasing green lending and green 
income is an important part of SEB’s business strategy, described 
under the Sustainability Activity Index (p. 118). Green lending in SEB 
is defined in accordance with SEB’s Green Bond Framework, which is 
closely aligned with the Taxonomy’s substantial contribution criteria. 
As a result, the SEB green loan portfolio closely mirrors the Taxonomy’s 
technical screening criteria. New product development also draws on 
the Taxonomy where relevant. Internal incentive structures aimed at 
increasing green financing activities therefore indirectly support the 
Taxonomy. However, the GAR itself has not been suitable as a strategic 
steering metric due to its asymmetrical construction in the currently 
applied regulatory framework. SEB welcomes the amending Delegated 
Regulation revising the GAR methodology and will apply the new 
­methodology for the 2026 year-end reporting.
The EU Taxonomy has also informed the development of SEB’s 
­proprietary Customer Sustainability Classification tool (p. 105). The 
tool supports assessments of clients’ transition plans and ambitions, 
where Taxonomy-aligned CapEx and other transition-related CapEx 
are important inputs when evaluating the credibility of such plans.
Through SEB’s participation in the EU Platform on Sustainable 
Finance, SEB has advised customers on the EU Taxonomy over the 
last four years. This advisory work covers topics such as the potential 
role of the Taxonomy in financing and investments and its implications 
for financing structures and access to finance going forward. 
EU Taxonomy reporting development 
The EU Taxonomy is intended to provide transparent, comparable, 
and decision-useful information and KPIs to support sustainable 
investment and transition financing. The first years of reporting 
have highlighted several challenges that affect the usability and 
­practical implementation of the reporting requirements. In February 
2025, the European Commission presented the Omnibus simplifica­
tion package, aimed in part at reducing and simplifying the reporting 
burden for companies in scope of the CSRD, CSDDD, and the 
­Taxonomy Regulation.
In line with the Omnibus initiative, an amending Delegated Act was 
proposed in July 2025, applicable from 1 January 2026. The Act 
amends the Taxonomy Disclosure Delegated Act and the Climate and 
Environmental Delegated Acts and introduces: 
•	 Exclusion of exposures to non-CSRD counter­parties from the 
denominator of the KPIs
•	 	Possibility to include exposures to companies that report 
­Taxonomy KPIs voluntarily, including use-of-proceeds loans 
to such companies
•	 Materiality thresholds at asset and/or KPI-level
•	 Simplified reporting templates (less granularity, fewer data points)
Comparability of KPIs is expected to decrease for the years 2025–
2026 as a result of the three implementation options given in the 
new Act. Financial companies may choose to implement the new 
Act already for 2025, continue reporting under the existing Acts 
for 2025, or pause Taxonomy reporting for both 2025 and 2026. 
­During this period, the Commission will review the reporting require­
ments, technical screening criteria, and DNSH requirements to 
ensure ­simpler, more usable application and alignment with other 
EU ­legislation.
The Fees and Commissions KPI and the Trading book KPI, originally 
scheduled for first-time reporting for 2025, have been postponed 
until 2027 in accordance with the European Commission’s draft 
Fourth Notice and the amending Delegated Act. This reflects their 
perceived limited relevance and decision-usefulness at this stage, 
pending the broader regulatory review.
Some previously identified limitations remain, including:
•	 The economic activities currently covered by the EU Taxonomy, 
combined with the limited number of companies in scope of 
­Taxonomy reporting requirements, result in the GAR covering 
a ­relatively small portion of the credit portfolio. The upcoming 
­Commission review may expand the scope of covered activities 
and update the technical screening criteria in line with scientific 
and technological developments. However, the number of compa­
nies subject to reporting requirements will decrease under the 
Omnibus initiative.
•	 Use of the GAR for purpose-based loans (use-of-proceeds assets) 
remains limited due to challenges in assessing, verifying, and 
­documenting Taxonomy alignment.
•	 The proportion of residential properties with valid energy 
­performance data remains low in Sweden and the Baltic 
­countries compared with other EU Member States, resulting 
in a lower share of Taxonomy-aligned mortgages.
Taxonomy tables and qualitative disclosures forming part of the 
­Sustainability Statement are presented on p. 165–205.

 Strategy
SBM-3 How impacts and risks 
link to strategy
Banking is a people-driven industry in which employee engagement, 
behaviour and performance are key differentiators. For SEB, the 
­ability to attract, develop and retain talent is crucial to delivering on 
the strategy, and creating long-term stakeholder value. Impacts and 
risks (Figure 49) linked to working conditions and equal treatment 
and opportunities are therefore material for SEB and its employees 
and directly influence the bank’ ability to safeguard its business 
model and remain competitive. 
Working conditions
SEB is implementing people policies and procedures to support high 
employee engagement and continuous individual development. 
Annual employee surveys (see SBM-2, p. 133, and S1-2, p. 134–135) 
show strong results on engagement, work-life balance, well-being 
and growth opportunities compared to benchmarks. Other data 
points such as sick leave data, training hours and exit surveys confirm 
SEB’s strong performance. Consequently, SEB concludes that its 
­policies and procedures have positive impacts of working conditions 
for SEB’s workforce. 
SEB mainly operates in northern Europe where labour rights are 
well protected. To ensure compliance with local regulations and 
­market practices, SEB maintains local HR representation in most 
countries of operation. In a limited number of smaller markets, 
HR-services are provided from another country. 84 per cent of 
SEB’s employees are covered by collective bargaining agreements 
regulating adequate wages, working hours, social coverage, and 
workplace health and safety. 
SEB has also identified risks and potential negative impacts related 
to working conditions. Rising levels of financial crime in society may 
increase the risk of threats directed at customer-facing employees 
and at certain high-risk roles, such as those involved in preventing 
money laundering and terrorist financing. While SEB actively works to 
mitigate these risks, they represent a potential negative impact on the 
workforce. Increased financial crime also heightens the risk of internal 
fraud, which exposes SEB to financial and reputational risks.

Ensuring equal treatment and opportunities is essential to unlocking

treatment and opportunities on SEB’s ­workforce.

Our employees are key to SEB’s success, and their views provide

SEB engages regularly with employees to understand their views

Employees can raise concerns through all engagement channels 
described above and can find guidance on where and to whom to 
turn via the intranet. Line managers or employee representatives 
are often an appropriate first point of entry. 
Concern about unethical or unlawful behaviour can be reported 
directly to Group Compliance or Internal Audit. SEB also operates 
a global, anonymous whistleblowing channel (WhistleB), which is 
accessible via the intranet and the external webpage, “Whistle­
blowing at sebgroup.com”. SEB’s Code of Conduct supports whistle­
blowing and emphasises that no action shall be taken against anyone 
who raises a concern.
A measure of our employees’ understanding of this process is the 
completion rate (96 per cent in 2025) of the annual mandatory Code 
of Conduct training, which explains the process. For more information 
about the Whistleblowing process, see G1-1 p. 152.
Regardless of the channel through which an employee raises a 
­concern, the matters are ultimately escalated to HR, which deter­
mines whether further investigation is required. HR operates local 
incident processes in all countries. A staff incident is defined as a 
­violation of internal or external rules of employment, including but 
not limited to policies, instructions, regulations laws and agreements, 
that are not immediately considered to be negligible. As an employer, 
SEB is obliged to investigate the circumstances surrounding any 
­concern raised and remediate where applicable.
In Sweden, investigated incidents by HR are brought for decision 
to a Misconduct & Suitability Committee (senior management; 
anonymised cases to support unbiased decisions), with remedies 
ranging from labour law actions such as verbal/written warnings 
to redeployment or termination with or without notice. Additional 
remedies may apply. SEB has similar processes in other countries 
of operations.

actions
SEB continuously works with a wide range of actions and initiatives to 
enforce positive impacts, prevent and minimise negative impacts and 
manage workforce-related risks. 
How SEB identifies relevant actions
The annual employee survey serves as a key tool for identifying areas 
for improvement, actions, as well as for evaluating the outcomes of 
initiatives implemented in response to previous survey results. Feed­
back and concerns identified through other engagement processes 
(S1-2) and remediation processes (S1-3), also provide important 
input to the prioritisation of actions. HR is represented in all countries 
where SEB operates to ensure the knowledge of local laws, regula­
tions and market conditions needed for action scoping.
Action governance
Depending on the scope, actions are typically handled and owned by 
business area management, or, for group common initiatives, by the 
Group Executive Committee. In addition, SEB established the Group 
Human Resource Committee in 2025 (described in ESRS 2, p. 82), to 
address matters of strategic importance concerning the workforce. 
Decisions with potentially high negative impact on large groups of 
employees require risk management committee approval and union 
agreement. The governing bodies and management strive to ensure 
that SEB as an employer does not cause or contribute to negative 
impacts on our employees.
Leadership for positive working conditions and 
equal treatment and opportunities
SEB’s Transformative Leadership concept is a key component of its 
strategy to build a value-creating, inclusive corporate culture and 
promote good working conditions and equal treatment and opportu­
nities. Aligned with SEB’s core behaviours – Create Value, Act long-
term and Build Positive Relationships, it comprises six business criti­
cal and research-based leadership abilities that are integrated in all 
leadership trainings and is embedded in key people processes such 
as performance management.
As part of the concept, leaders and employees are offered digital 
self-service on SEB Campus, including exercises, videos and practical 
tools to work with feedback in a team, a coaching leadership style 
and psychological safety.
 
Actions on working conditions
•	 Health, wellbeing, and work-life balance: SEB is working with sev­
eral actions to reinforce its positive impact on working conditions. 
To promote work-life balance, SEB’s global remote work instruction 
allows eligible employees remote work up to two days per week. 
Furthermore, a large part of SEB’s staff can leverage flexible work­
ing hours. Most of SEB’s employees work in modern offices with 
on-site canteens and gyms, supporting access to affordable meals 
and promoting physical wellbeing. In addition, SEB provides a 
range of benefits aimed at improving work–life balance, including 
subsidised cleaning services and childcare support. Employees are 
also offered general know-how of healthy living via e.g. lectures 
and SEB Campus. If an employee experiences a physical or mental 
condition or if a team faces challenges such as excessive workload, 
SEB provides a range of support measures. We monitor sick leave 
development closely. In Sweden total number of work hours lost 
to sick leave has fallen from 3 per cent in 2022 to 2.6 per cent 
in 2025.
•	 Competence building: SEB recognises that its highly engaged 
employees value opportunities for continuous learning and devel­
opment. In addition to the actions presented in S1-13, p. 139, SEB 
is focusing on a dynamic internal job market, including both short-
term secondments (job gigs) and longer-term solutions such as 
international assignments, or cross-divisional moves.
•	 Financial crime pressure: SEB continuously monitors the risks and 
potential negative impacts associated with increased financial 
crime pressure. Recent measures implemented in customer-facing 
units in Sweden include centralisation of complex customer 
­handling matters, the discontinuation of drop-in services at branch 
offices, anonymisation of SEB employees in customer agreements 
and a policy to not provide both first and last name in the tele­
phone banking service. To support managers, SEB has adopted the 
“Instruction for Personal Security in the SEB Group” which sets out 
when risk assessments should be performed and how identified 
risks should be mitigated in order to protect SEB’s employees from 
hostile actions within and outside the physical workspace.

Equal treatment and opportunities, including remuneration, is funda­
mental to SEB’s performance and grounded in law and supervision. 
The gender pay gap
Benchmarking by the EBA1) shows a persisting material gender pay 
gap across EU banks, largely driven by workforce composition with 
fewer women in higher-paid roles/functions. In line with this industry 
pattern, SEB’s unadjusted gender pay gap is primarily explained by 
role/functional mix. Given that the adjusted gender pay gap (i.e. pay 
by gender for the same or equivalent jobs) is small in SEB and gender 
representation at leadership level is balanced in SEB (see Figure 57, 
p. 138), this indicates a higher proportion of women in lower-paid 
roles and/or a higher proportion of men in higher-paid roles. 
In SEB, equal pay for equal work is the overall guiding principle in 
all salary decisions and the remuneration structure, processes and 
reviews shall always support equal opportunities and secure non-
bias, fair and transparent remuneration decision-making. To measure 
equal pay, SEB tracks the adjusted pay gap which compares pay 
level per gender for the same jobs or for jobs with the same level of 
­complexity. Work is ongoing to analyse this adjusted gap globally.

Also shown in Figure 59, the total unadjusted gender pay gap for

SEB works actively to address the unbalanced role mix and any 
unjustified pay gaps. The goal is to achieve an even gender distribu­
tion across all roles and managerial levels and closing pay disparities. 
The role/functional mix is tackled through e.g. procedures to ensure 
a broad pool of applicants in recruitment and succession processes. 
Actions to support equal pay include “grandparent” reviews of salary 
proposals, clear and gender-neutral salary setting criteria, a pay 
framework with transparent salary ranges, annual review of the 
adjusted pay gap development, and local equal pay analyses that 
are shared with employees. (See S1-4 p. 136 and S1-5 p. 136).

Information security
 Strategy
SBM-3 How impacts and risks 
link to strategy 
Providing financial products and services involves handling large 
­volumes of personal and confidential customer data. Information 
security is therefore a critical aspect of SEB’s operations, and the 
DMA identified both actual risks and potential negative impacts in 
this area (Figure 60). 
In 2025, the global security threat landscape worsened, with 
cyberattacks becoming more frequent and increasingly sophisti­
cated. Financial institutions and their third-party suppliers were 
­primary targets, ­facing risks such as data theft, ransomware, fraud, 
and growing ­criminal use of AI. Notably, vulnerabilities in outsourcing 
and third-party arrangements contributed to data breaches at 
­several financial institutions. 
The security threat landscape is also closely linked to geopolitics, 
with nation-states increasingly using or supporting cyber activities to 
advance their interests. State-sponsored groups engage in espionage 
and cyberattacks that, as seen in Ukraine, may cause significant oper­
ational and reputational harm to financial institutions. These actions 
are often combined with hybrid tactics and disinformation campaigns, 
potentially undermining stability and trust in the financial system. 
In response, sector-specific and public-private partnerships are 
expanding to strengthen security and resilience.
Cyber threats are expected to remain a material risk for several 
years, with potential negative impacts on SEB’s clients through, for 
example, temporary loss of digital financial services or unwanted 
information being displayed to the public or misused. A potential fail­
ure to manage information securely could give rise to regulatory and 
reputational risks and could negatively affect customer relationships. 
A high level of information security is therefore essential and 
expected by consumers, shareholders, regulators, and society 
at large.
SEB’s approach is to maintain a strong security posture and 
­resilience, founded in a robust information security management 
­system (ISMS) designed to safeguard the organisation, its customers,

business model and strategy. The ISMS incorporates comprehensive 
­policies, instructions, procedures and security measures, providing 
a structured approach to managing threats and risks. 
A strong security culture underpins SEB’s efforts in this area, 
­building a responsive and proactive organisation. Through ongoing 
security awareness initiatives and training, SEB equips employees 
to strengthen the bank’s resilience against attacks, protect sensitive 
information and reduce the risk of human error.
SBM-2 How customer views 
influence strategy
Access to financial services is fundamental in a modern society 
and is part of nations’ critical infrastructure. Without access to 
­reliable financial services the individuals’ security and liberty are 
compromised. The rising number of security threats and security 
­incidents is an increasing concern. 
Consumers and regulators expect financial products and services 
to be secure and reliable. Regular engagement with authorities forms 
part of the ongoing development of SEB’s security capabilities.
Protecting personal and financial information is important for build­
ing trust and confidence. It is also a prerequisite for retaining and 
attracting customers while ensuring compliance with regulations. 
Therefore, SEB’s strategy and business model are under continuous 
adaptation to prevent criminal actions like cybercrime and data 
breaches. Balancing security measures with user-friendly experience 
is crucial and an ongoing process. 
SEB observes that consumers are interested in learning how to 
­protect themselves from security threats and use financial services 
in a secure way. This includes communication regarding security 
measures and incidents that affect them. To meet this demand, SEB 
has continued to work closely with customers and industry peers on 
these matters.
Customers are also showing increased interest in the assurance of 
our security posture and that we enforce security standards with our 
third parties. SEB Kort Bank AB and the SEB AB data centres are ISO 
27001 certified, with further certifications guided by customer and 
market demands.

and guidelines based on leading good and best practices such as:

•	 NIST Cyber Security Framework
•	 Information Security Forum Standard of Good Practice and 
•	 Center for Internet Security (CIS) Critical Security Controls version 8
The ISMS supports continuous improvement, including implementing, 
maintaining, testing and refining security measures within SEB, 
while ensuring that third-party suppliers adhere to rigorous security 
practices. 
The Security Policy for SEB is adopted by the Board of Directors 
and covers information security, cyber and IT security, and physical 
and personnel security. It sets out the importance of information 
security for SEB and its ­customers and establishes objectives,

•	 Protect customers and assets, including people, information, 
­infrastructure, finances and reputation, against potential threats
•	 Associate the SEB brand with robust security
•	 Support SEB’s business goals by enabling trusted, compliant and 
resilient financial solutions globally
All information security policies, instructions and guidelines are 
updated annually through a formal process that takes both external 
and internal factors into account, such as developments in the threat 
landscape, and changing customer requirements and regulations. 
These documents apply across SEB, including third-party suppliers

Through this approach, SEB seeks to ensure robust security

Data privacy
 Strategy
SBM-3 How impacts and risks 
link to strategy
The protection of personal data is a fundamental human right under 
EU law (EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, Article 8) and safe­
guarded by enforceable privacy laws such as the General Data 
­Protection Regulation (GDPR). In delivering its services and fulfilling 
its responsibilities, SEB processes significant volumes of personal 
data and is required to remain compliant with the GDPR. This applies 
to all handling of personal data regardless of whether relating to 
­private individuals or corporate customers and entails a responsibility 
to handle such data appropriately. 
If SEB were to fail to protect personal data or comply with the 
GDPR, this could result in negative impacts on customers, such as the 
use of data for purposes beyond those intended to or the unintended 
exposure of data as a result of criminal breaches. These impacts may 
affect all customer segments. For SEB, such failures could result in 
regulatory sanctions, reputational damage and a loss of trust in its 
ability to act as a responsible custodian of personal data, ultimately 
affecting the bank’s business, strategy and broader role in society. 
SBM-2 How customer views 
influence strategy
In delivering its services, SEB must collect, protect, use, and store 
certain personal data. By upholding the GDPR and monitoring cus­
tomer feedback and complaints through established channels, SEB 
takes stakeholders’ interests, views and rights into account. ­During 
2025, SEB did not receive any material feedback requiring changes 
to its processes or business model.
 Impact, risk and opportunity management
S4-1
Policies related to  
data privacy
As mentioned, the protection of personal data is recognised as a 
­fundamental human right under EU law. SEB’s Social and Human 
Rights Policy outlines SEB’s position and approach to human rights 
and its commitment to both the UN Guiding Principles on Business 
and Human Rights and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enter­
prises. To ensure regulatory compliance, SEB has implemented an 
internal privacy governance framework, supported by instructions 
and guidelines to meet its privacy obligations across all jurisdictions 
in which the bank operates. This includes the internal Instruction on 
Personal Data Protection and Right to Privacy in SEB, adopted by the 
CEO, which applies to all forms of personal data processed by SEB, 
whether from private and corporate customers. These documents 
are reviewed at least annually and updated to address new and 
evolving regulatory requirements.
In 2025, SEB had no significant instances of non-compliance with 
privacy laws and regulations, including human rights issues, for which 
fines, or non-monetary sanctions were incurred.
S4-2
Processes for engaging with customers 
about impacts
SEB publishes an external privacy notice describing how the bank 
adheres to the principles of the GDPR and the rights available to cus­
tomers. These notices explain how, when and why personal data are 
collected and processed, and, where applicable, with whom such 
data may be shared. Privacy notices are reviewed at least annually 
and updated whenever processing activities change or new activities 
are introduced, ensuring transparency in handling of personal data.
SEB also meets data subject (e.g. current, former and potential 
customers, and employees) rights requests, which include the rights 
at any time to:
•	 Request access to their personal data and an extract of these
•	 Correct inaccuracies in their data
•	 Delete their data
•	 Limit how their data is processed
•	 Exercise data portability, allowing the transfer of their data to 
another service provider
 
Several channels are available for people to exercise their data 
­subject rights, including dedicated channels via SEB’s website as 
well as regular customer support channels, such as branch offices 
and the telephone bank (see Information security S4-2, p. 142). 
The process for providing and updating relevant documentation 
(for example, privacy notices) is carried out under the supervision 
of the Head of Privacy or an equivalent role, who is responsible for 
privacy within each respective SEB entity. 
S4-3
Remediation processes and channels  
to raise concern
If an individual is dissatisfied with how SEB has handled their data 
­privacy rights or processed their personal data, or if they have not 
received a satisfactory response, they are entitled to raise the matter 
with the data protection authority. 
To foster trust and awareness in SEB’s processes for handling 
­personal data, the bank has appointed Data Protection Officers 
responsible for monitoring compliance with applicable privacy laws 
and regulations and for ensuring accountability within the organisa­
tion. The Data Protection Officers perform this work independently 
and report to the Board on SEB’s compliance with privacy regulations 
at least once per year. 
Individuals whose personal data are processed by SEB may 
­contact the relevant Data Protection Officer at SEB, who will also 
cooperate with data protection authorities where applicable. Data 
privacy concerns may also be raised through the bank’s various 
­customer interaction and feedback channels.
Customers may be eligible for compensation if damage occurs or 
their rights are violated. Each case is assessed individually in accord­
ance with applicable regulations and agreements as part of SEB’s 
remediation process, see Information security S4-3, p. 142. If a cus­
tomer believes that SEB has failed to act in an ethical or legal manner, 
they can report the concern anonymously through the whistleblowing 
process, detailed in section G1-1, p. 152. 
 Feedback relating to the handling of personal data, as well as cus­
tomer complaints, are documented in internal systems, followed up, 
and reported through the organisation’s risk management processes.
They are also used to improve products and services.
