Access to (quality) information
 Strategy
SBM-3 How impacts and risks 
link to strategy
As part of its strategy, SEB provides private customers with financial 
information and advice on savings, investments, lending and pen­
sions. In 2025, SEB recorded approximately 500 million private cus­
tomer interactions across digital channels, telephone banking and 
branch meetings in Sweden and the Baltic countries. Given the impor­
tance of these services and their potential effects on customers’ 
financial situations, access to (quality) information has been identi­
fied as both a positive impact and a potential negative impact and risk 
for SEB.
High-quality information and professional financial advice are 
essential in enabling customers to make well-informed financial 
­decisions that support their long-term financial well-being. Thereby, 
SEB creates positive impacts for customers while strengthening the 
foundation for long-term relationships and trust in the bank.
Conversely, incorrect, incomplete or missing information and 
advice could lead to poor financial decisions, potentially resulting in 
financial harm to customers and exposing SEB to risks such as com­
pensation claims, reputational damage and increased operational 
costs. In more severe cases, such shortcomings could also result in 
regulatory consequences and loss of customer confidence for SEB.
SEB works continuously through a range of initiatives to ensure 
that customers have access to high-quality information and advice, 
including enhanced digital products and services, analytical tools, 
and employee training to enable well-informed and tailored advi­
sory services.
SBM-2 How customer views 
influence strategy
SEB continuously gathers customer insights through interviews, 
­surveys, user testing, and market analysis. 
Recurring themes raised by customers are the importance of pro­
active engagement, high-quality digital experiences, and feeling seen 
and appreciated. These views guide SEB’s ongoing efforts to enhance 
customer satisfaction.

SEB has undertaken a range of initiatives to provide customers with 
more comprehensive and higher-quality information and advice, 
­informed by customer preferences and their ambition to improve 
their financial situation:
•	 Increased time for advisory: Mortgage application processing has 
been centralised within the division Business and Retail Banking, 
allowing advisors to spend more time on customer interactions 
that involve complex information and advisory services, rather 
than administrative tasks.
•	 Enhanced digital products and services: Activities that provide 
customers with expanded access to information and advice 
through digital channels, available anytime and from anywhere. 
Examples include information distribution through customers’ 
­digital personal mailboxes, improved digital navigation, trading 
on new equity markets, and self-service pension transfers.
In addition to customer feedback, legislation plays a significant role in 
shaping business priorities. Regulatory changes often influence stra­
tegic planning and may pose risks to profitability or create opportuni­
ties for improved financial performance. Such changes often affect 
SEB by, amongst others, requiring investments in updated IT systems. 
Customer insights are regularly reviewed by relevant management 
forums and divisional heads, with quarterly updates provided to the 
Group Executive Committee.
 Impact, risk and opportunity management
S4-1
Policies for access  
to (quality) information
SEB considers access to (quality) information and advice to be essen­
tial for enabling informed financial decisions and preventing negative 
impacts. This is linked to SEB’s human rights commitments through 
the application of the UN Guiding Principles to the bank’s customer 
information and advice (including avoiding misleading claims and pro­
viding remedy when harm occurs) as well as the OECD Guidelines for 
Multinational Enterprises– Consumer Interests (accurate, compara­
ble information, no misleading representations or omissions, and 
accessible complaint channels and remedies). SEB’s Social & Human 
Rights Policy (see S1-1 p. 133) sets these commitments, and the 
Code of Conduct (see G1-1 p. 152) operationalises them by expecting 
employees to provide need-based, understandable advice and infor­
mation, and to handle complaints promptly.
SEB’s Communication Policy defines the principles and procedures 
governing internal and external communication. It aims to ensure that 
all stakeholders receive timely, accurate and reliable information in 
accordance with regulatory requirements. Providing responsible 
advice to customers and delivering correct information at the right 
time are core standards for SEB. Communication shall be character­
ised by speed, proactivity, trustworthiness, transparency and a long-
term perspective, in order to foster confidence and build long-term 
relationships.
SEB’s policies to manage IRO’s related to access to (quality) 
­information are fundamental to ensuring regulatory compliance, 
operational integrity, and the consistent implementation of legal 
requirements. They offer structured, organisation-specific guidance 
that supports accurate and uniform client communication, thereby 
mitigating the risk of misinformation, regulatory breaches, and repu­
tational damage. The policies apply group-wide and are adopted by 
the Board, with annual reviews conducted. 
In addition to these policies, SEB has established practical instruc­
tions and guidelines that translate policy commitments into day-to-
day operations. These include, for example, guidelines and standards 
for written communication presented to customers, such as advisory 
material and product information provided on digital platforms.  
  
S4-2
Processes for engaging with customers  
about impacts
SEB offers financial services through branch offices, digital plat­
forms, telephone, and advisory meetings. These channels provide 
tools and guidance to help customers manage their finances and 
also serve as channels for feedback and requests. Insights that lead 
to service improvements are applied across all channels. SEB is 
­currently reviewing its platform and methodology for collecting 
­customer feedback (excluding complaints) to enhance the process 
and ensure it remains effective. 
Customer insights are continuously gathered through research, 
complaints and external surveys, enabling SEB to identify and 
address recurring issues in a structured, evidence-based manner, 
while also highlighting areas of strength and opportunities for 
improvement. 
Maintaining effective communication with customers in different 
segments is a priority. For example, SEB conducts surveys among sen­
ior customers to assess their awareness of fraud protection measures 
and simultaneously provides information about available security-­
enhancing tools.
SEB’s division heads are responsible for customer engagement 
within their respective product portfolio and customer segment.
S4-3
Processes to remediate negative impacts  
and channels to raise concern
SEB follows the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority’s general 
guidelines on complaints management, and also has a Group instruc­
tion for handling customer complaints.
To facilitate the customer’s ability to submit complaints, a struc­
tured escalation process has been established. Initially, the customer 
is advised to contact the unit where the issue originated. This can 
be done via the designated public website, by telephone to the 
local branch, or through the telephone banking service. The process 
is ­governed by clearly defined procedures and mandates and is 
­followed up and reported through our risk management organisation.
Should the customer remain dissatisfied, the matter may be esca­
lated to an appointed complaints officer, who is committed to provid­
ing a response within 24 hours and is vested with an extended 
­mandate for compensation. If a resolution cannot be reached, the 
­customer has the right to refer the case to the National Board for 
­Consumer Disputes (ARN) or pursue legal action through the courts. 
SEB consistently adheres to the decisions issued by ARN.
Customers can also raise concerns through the whistleblowing 
­process, described in section G1-1, p. 152.

tives described in SBM-2, p. 145, the main activities are outlined

Current actions
Enhanced customer information and tutorials
Examples include offering annual reviews to selected target groups 
and enhancing digital functionality and tools that help customers

educational resources, such as investment tutorials and similar initia­
tives, are provided to increase customer knowledge. These efforts 
not only support customers in making informed decisions but also

engagement, increasing customer satisfaction, and driving growth

Advisory competence
To ensure that employees possess a high level of relevant and up-to-
date competence, SEB offers a broad portfolio of learning opportuni­
ties through SEB Campus. This expertise benefits our clients by 
ensuring that the advice provided is well-substantiated and considers 
a wide range of relevant factors.

foster innovation, and contribute to SEB’s long-term strategic objec­
tives, a recommended annual learning target is in place.
Standardisation and control of advice and offerings
To ensure consistency and quality in the advice and offerings 
­provided, several key measures have been established:

larly in areas such as investment recommendations. To accomplish

ple perspectives. Key aspects, including information security, inter­
nal and external regulatory compliance and best practices, are 
­rigorously evaluated. Relevant risks are identified, classified, and 
addressed through appropriate mitigation measures.
Effectiveness and responsibility for the actions 
Our actions are iterative in nature, with each cycle involving regular 
assessments, thorough evaluations and necessary adjustments. In 
addition to reviewing the actions themselves, we also assess their 
outcomes to ensure they meet expectations and contribute effec­
tively to our objective of providing customers with high-quality 
­information and advice.
As outlined in SBM-2, p. 145, SEB tracks and evaluates customer 
satisfaction connected with its services on an ongoing basis. In addi­
tion, digital customer behaviour is continuously tested to optimise 
usability of our products. Going forward, SEB is also planning to 
amend its customer feedback survey to include specific questions 
on their understanding of the information they received to further 
deepen the understanding of the customer’s needs.

activities within their respective product portfolio and customer 
­segment.

Financial inclusion
 Strategy
SBM-3 How impacts link 
to strategy 
As a universal bank, offering equal access to financial services is part 
of SEB’s strategy. The DMA identified financial inclusion as a material 
positive impact for private customers by broadening access to bank­
ing and supporting financial capability and resilience. SEB recognises 
that customers have diverse needs and circumstances, and that some 
segments, such as customers with disabilities, young people,  senior 
citizens and aspiring entrepreneurs, may benefit from tailored sup­
port, information or solutions. By embed­ding an inclusive approach to 
products, services, operations and partnerships, SEB aims to support 
all customers in managing their finances effectively. The approach 
supports the right to non-discrimination and equal access to services, 
as reflected in SEB’s Social and Human Rights Policy. These efforts 
also reinforce SEB’s relationship-driven model by promoting long-
term customer relationships and trust. 
In practice, SEB works with four focus areas to promote financial 
inclusion: 
•	 Accessible banking 
•	 Inclusion and diversity 
•	 Youth 
•	 	Entrepreneurship  
The areas are further detailed below, in S4-4, p. 148.
SBM-2 How customer views 
influence strategy
SEB collects feedback from private customers through multiple 
­channels, including ongoing customer interactions, dedicated feed­
back and complaints channels, and targeted surveys. In recent years, 
feedback related to financial inclusion has highlighted the usefulness 
of digital services, the demand for more customer-centric advice, 
and young people’s perception of SEB’s ability to meets their needs. 
Against this background, SEB has strengthened its focus on customer 
centricity within its retail operations, undertaken initiatives to 
enhance digital services, including their accessibility, and carried out 
development activities aimed at better serving younger customers. 
Alongside stakeholder views gathered through these broader 
­customer communication channels, SEB also collects feedback in 
connection with the targeted financial inclusion activities described 
below in section S4-4, which is used to inform the continued develop­
ment of these focus areas.
 Impact, risk and opportunity management
S4-1
Policies related  
to financial inclusion
Creating value for customers is a fundamental principle outlined in 
SEB’s Code of Conduct (see G1-1, p. 152), which sets expectations for 
behaviours that aim to promote long-term, trust-based relationships.
In line with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human 
Rights, financial inclusion is related to enabling equitable and non-­
discriminatory access to financial services, thereby supporting human 
rights and preventing adverse impacts on customers. Although SEB 
does not have a group policy dedicated solely to financial inclusion, its 
Social and Human Rights Policy sets out the bank’s positions on busi­
ness and human rights practices in support of SEB’s strategy and role 
as a responsible corporate citizen (see S1-1, p. 133–134). Examples of 
financial inclusion initiatives aligned with this ­policy include measures 
to promote equal access to financial services, as wells as activities 
supporting diversity, inclusion, and social development. 
S4-2
Processes for engaging with customers  
about impacts
SEB has no dedicated process for engaging with consumers and 
end-users regarding financial inclusion. Instead, such engagement 
occurs primarily through regular, day-to-day customer interactions as 
well as through the activities outlined below in S4-4. Customers who 
wish to raise concerns or provide feedback on these activities can do 
so through established channels, detailed in Information security 
S4-2 p. 142.
However, SEB has group-wide processes in place to ensure that 
the inclusion of consumers and end-users is considered when prod­
ucts and services are offered. For example, as SEB continuously 
develops its offering, the mandatory New Product Approval pro­
cess ensures that the impacts of new products and services, includ­
ing impacts on customers, are thoroughly assessed and, where 
appropriate, addressed. 
S4-4
Financial inclusion
 actions 
SEB undertakes various activities to promote financial inclusion, 
structured around the four focus areas: Accessible banking, 
­Inclusion and diversity, Youth, and Entrepreneurship. The bank 
­collects feedback in connection with the activities to track and 
assess their effectiveness.
Accessible banking
SEB provides access to financial services through multiple channels, 
including branch offices, digital banking platforms, telephone 
­services and tailored advisory meetings, enabling customers with 
diverse needs to manage their finances effectively. This includes 
adapted digital tools, personal guidance and product design to 
­support different levels of financial and digital capability.
To ensure that all customers receive the support they need, SEB 
complements its digital offering with personal assistance through 
its branch network and telephone bank. In recent years, SEB has 
strengthened its telephone banking services to better support cus­
tomers, including those who find digital services challenging. The 
aim is to answer calls within three minutes and to resolve the issues 
during the call. With increased staffing and enhanced competencies, 
the telephone bank now assists customers with a broader range of 
matters and provides more comprehensive financial advice. The 
­service is available to all SEB’s private customers, regardless of 
whether they use limited or full banking services.
SEB also works continuously to enhance the accessibility, ­reliability 
and usability of its digital services. Platforms are regularly updated 
and tested, with customer feedback incorporated into development 
and employees trained on accessibility. Most identified accessibility 
issues have been addressed, and accessibility statements for digital 
services have been published. Deficiencies have also been reported 
to the Swedish Post and Telecom Authority in line with applicable 
requirements. Since mid-2025, SEB’s digital banking services have 
been subject to the European Accessibility Act, which sets require­
ments for areas such as digital payments and customer identification.

Entrepreneurship
Sponsorship and community engagement are key components of 
SEB’s efforts to support financial inclusion. By supporting and

SEB Entrepreneur Ladder (Entreprenörstrappan): Through 
­collaborations with leading organisations, SEB works to strengthen 
Sweden’s business climate and promote sustainable, inclusive 
­entrepreneurship. The entrepreneur ladder is a conceptual model 
illustrating the stages of an entrepreneur’s journey, from idea to inter­
national expansion, bringing together SEB’s initiatives and partner­
ships to provide access to advice, capital and networks. The ladder is 
available across Sweden and includes targeted initiatives supporting, 
for example, female, young and immigrant entrepreneurs. 
SEB Klubben: A network and platform where women in business 
come together to exchange ideas, gain inspiration, address 
­challenges, explore opportunities, and foster growth. The platform 
serves as a forum where successful women, leaders and entrepre­
neurs across all ages have an opportunity to share experiences and 
gain new insights that can support continued progress and success.
SEB Growth program for small and medium enterprises: A busi­
ness accelerator for ambitious entrepreneurs in the Baltics to design 
new business ideas, build partnerships, and boost their innovation 
capacity.

Corporate culture
 Strategy
SBM-3
How impacts and risks
 link to strategy
SEB’s business model depends on consistent ethical behaviour 
in ­customer interactions and internal processes. SEB’s corporate 
­culture plays a key role and has been identified as a positive 
impact by supporting prudent risk-­taking and maintaining stake­
holder ­confidence. Conversely, a breach of trust, for example 
through ­misconduct, poses a material risk to the bank’s reputation, 
­regulatory standing and execution of its strategy. 
SEB’s approach to business conduct is guided by the Board and 
anchored in policies (see G1-1 p. 152). Management embeds the 
­corporate culture in day-to-day operations through leadership 
­practices and HR processes (see S1-2–S1-4, p. 133–136).
 Governance
GOV-1
Governance related  
to corporate culture
SEB maintains high standards of business ethics and continually 
strengthens its governance, processes and procedures. The 
bank’s approach to business conduct is anchored in regulatory 
requirements, global initiatives, and international standards and 
­operationalised through group-wide policies and instructions. 
Policies and instructions that define the division of duties within 
the Group are tools for the Board and the CEO in their governing and 
controlling roles. The Board has overarching responsibility for SEB, 
including its business conduct, while the CEO is responsible for 
­execution and day-to-day management of related activities. The 
Board annually reviews and adopts SEB’s policy framework for 
­business conduct, including the Code of Conduct (see G1-1 p. 152). 
According to SEB’s governance model, each business division and 
group function is responsible to implement SEB’s ethical and sustain­
ability endeavours in their business activities, and to report the 
­progress to the Board and the CEO.

Further details on the roles of the Board and the CEO in business 
­conduct, as well as the expertise of board members and CEO com­
mittee members are found in the Corporate Governance report, 
p. 59 and 64. 
 Impact, risk and opportunity management
IRO-1
Processes to identify and assessment  
corporate culture impacts and risks
SEB’s double materiality assessment (detailed in ESRS 2, p. 98–99) 
is both informed by and informs other risk materiality assessment 
and due diligence processes. SEB has a comprehensive framework 
for risk management to ensure regulatory compliance and safeguard 
the Group’s financial position. The framework is continuously devel­
oped to reflect current market trends, new regulations, as well as to 
detect emerging risks. 
Managing risk is an integral part of banking, and risk awareness 
is deeply embedded in SEB’s corporate culture. SEB’s governance 
structure and operating model include three lines of defence to 
ensure effective risk management and preserve high standards 
of business conduct. This is further described in the Corporate 
­Governance report, p. 61.
To assess corporate culture impacts, relevant drivers are 
­monitored, including Insight survey results on inclusion and 
­leadership, staff turnover, and misconduct incidents. 
G1-1
Policies related to  
corporate culture
Policy overview
SEB’s primary policy related to corporate culture is its Code of Conduct 
(the Code), supported by instructions and procedures. The Code sets 
SEB’s approach to ethical matters, defines expected, so-called core 
behaviours and guides employees on the bank’s ways of working and 
adhering to standards of business conduct. It applies to all employees, 
is reviewed annually, approved by the CEO, and adopted by the Board. 
A sound corporate culture is central to SEB’s ability to build long-
term relationships with customers and stakeholders and meet their 
expectations. SEB’s Code underpins this by articulating the bank’s 
purpose and core behaviours, grounded in compliance with all appli­
cable laws and regulations in the countries where SEB operates, as 
well as in maintaining high ethical standards.
The core behaviours are to create value, act long-term, and build 
positive relationships.
The Code guides specifically on several topics including:
•	 Customer relationships
•	 Financial crime
•	 How we handle information and secrecy
•	 How we communicate
•	 How we manage conflicts of interest
•	 Our relationships with suppliers, other business partners and 
­competitors 
•	 	SEB as a workplace
Implementation
Mandatory training: All employees are required to complete Code of 
Conduct training at onboarding and then every three years (for con­
sultants in the Baltics, this training is optional). Completion rates for 
mandatory trainings are shown in Figure 65 and 66 (p. 153).
Leadership training: SEB embeds culture through its concept 
­Transformative Leadership, aligned with the core behaviours and 
integrated into all leadership programmes. A self-service toolkit on 
SEB Campus (available to all employees) offers practical exercises, 
videos and tools (for example regarding giving/receiving feedback, 
coaching leadership, and building psychological safety).
Employee processes: The core behaviours are integrated in several 
employee processes, e.g., measured in the Insight survey and 
reflected in performance dialogues and performance development. 
(see also S1-2, p. 134–135 and S1-4, p. 135–136).
Advice channels: Employees can seek guidance from line 
­managers, HR or Group Compliance on how to apply the Code 
in ­specific ­situations.
Reporting breaches 
SEB is committed to maintaining a transparent business environment 
and upholding high standards of business ethics. Ethical behaviour 
and proactive measures to prevent irregularities are important parts 
of the bank’s culture. The Code explains how employees can raise 
concerns about unethical behaviour or potential or actual breaches of 
the Code, or other regulatory or internal requirements. As described 
in S1-3, p. 135, employees may contact their line manager, HR, Group 
Compliance or report through SEB’s whistleblowing process. Whistle­
blowing can be carried out anonymously via the external digital 
­service WhistleB or directly to Head of Group Compliance or Head of 
Group Internal Audit. 
SEB falls within the scope of the EU Whistleblower Protection 
Directive (Directive (EU) 2019/1937), as transposed into the relevant 
local regulations, and is committed to protecting whistleblowers. As 
stated in the Code, SEB encourages whistleblowing and ensures no 
measures are taken against anyone who has filed a whistleblowing 
report, either at the time of reporting or thereafter. 
The Code, with its training, includes a detailed description of the 
whistleblowing process. This information is also accessible on SEB’s 
internal and external websites, such as “Whistleblowing at SEB”, 
which provides a direct link to WhistleB. This process can be used 
both by SEB employees and external stakeholders. 
Report handling and enforcement
Whistleblowing reports are received by two independent control 
functions: Group Compliance and Group Internal Audit. The Head of 
Group Compliance, the Head of Group Internal Audit, or designated 
staff within these departments review the reports and take 
­appropriate action. 
The number of whistleblowing cases is detailed in Figure 67, p. 153.
Violations of the Code, other internal rules, or laws and regulations 
lead to appropriate action. The Code stresses that potential incidents 
related to corruption and other illegal activities are naturally subject 
to immediate actions. The process to handle staff incidents is 
described in S1-3, p. 135.

G1-2
Management of relationships  
with suppliers
SEB believes that working with suppliers that demonstrate strong per­
formance in regard to environmental, social and ethical aspects creates 
value for both the bank and for its suppliers. These expectations are 
set out in SEB’s Code of Conduct for Suppliers. 
SEB has established procedures to evaluate and select suppliers 
and contractors, based on financial, environmental, social and gov­
ernance aspects. To identify sustainability risks among our suppliers, 
SEB performs, when applicable, an initial assessment using a risk 
model tool that takes country, industry sector and business criticality 
into account. 
Suppliers that are identified in the initial assessment as having a 
potential elevated risk and negative impact are subject to an 
enhanced screening. Risk factors include climate and environment, 
labour practices and human rights, fair business practices and sus­
tainable procurement. These are to be considered in procurement 
decisions along with other risk factors and commercial aspects. 
SEB continuously monitors suppliers’ processes and performance 
based on relevant aspects in similar manners where appropriate. 
SEB strives to treat its suppliers with fairness, transparency, and 
ethical conduct. By including several suppliers in the sourcing pro­
cess, fair competition is encouraged. Supplier relationships are gov­
erned by adherence to our internal framework with clear policies to 
prevent conflicts of interest, bribery, and misuse of sensitive informa­
tion. SEB is continuously improving the way of working with suppliers 
to facilitate and standardise the sourcing process, particulary in light 
of increasing regulatory and data requirements. The overall approach 
aims to build long-term, economically sustainable relationships.
Timely payments to suppliers are ensured via invoice processing 
systems, strict internal policies and process controls that prioritise pay­
ment discipline. These measures are supported by automated payment 
scheduling, approval workflows, governance and escalation proce­
dures to prevent delays and maintain SEB’s reputation.

Financial crime
 Strategy
SBM-3
How impacts and risks
 link to strategy
Financial crime prevention is essential to SEB’s strategy and business 
model. Across the world, societies face economic and social chal­
lenges from criminal activities such as human trafficking, terrorism, 
corruption, drug smuggling, and tax evasion. A critical step in combat­
ing these crimes is to identify and disrupt the financial flows that sus­
tain them, and financial institutions, in their role as a financial inter­
mediary, are uniquely positioned to contribute to this effort. SEB is, 
similar to all other major actors on the financial markets, exposed to 
the risk of being used for financial crime purposes, including money 
laundering, terrorist financing, sanctions avoidance, fraud, and mar­
ket abuse. As the financial sector represents a vital part of society’s 
infrastructure and economy, financial crime poses a serious threat 
to the financial system and, by extension, to society at large. For SEB, 
financial crime prevention, including preventing corruption and 
­bribery within our own operations, is essential for maintaining trust, 
mitigating reputational risks and ensuring regulatory compliance.
To combat financial crime, SEB has implemented a comprehensive 
set of measures designed to detect and deter illicit activity, ensuring 
that its services remain secure and trustworthy for customers. These 
measures include ongoing training for our staff, advanced monitoring 
systems, close collaboration with supervisory authorities and law 
enforcement agencies, and effective response to emerging threats.
 Governance
GOV-1
Governance related  
to financial crime
Financial crime
Financial crime governance is an integral part of SEB’s enterprise 
risk management framework and is structured according to the three 
lines of defence model. This model ensures a clear segregation of 
duties, independent oversight, and consistent application of the 
Group’s governing documents across all levels of the organisation.
The first line of defence consists of the business areas and the 
independent Financial Crime Prevention function, which together 
manage financial crime risks in daily operations and are responsible 
for implementing effective controls. The second line of defence com­
prises independent oversight functions that monitor the adequacy 
and effectiveness of these controls and regulatory compliance, 
while challenging and guiding the first line. The third line of defence, 
Group Internal Audit, provides independent assurance on the overall 
effectiveness of the framework and reports directly to the Board 
and the CEO.
Ultimate accountability for financial crime prevention rests with 
the Board and senior management. Roles, responsibilities, and 
accountability are defined across all three lines of defence, includ­
ing the appointment of designated Anti-Money Laundering (AML), 
Counter-­Financing of Terrorism (CFT), and Sanctions Regulated 
­Persons, in full compliance with applicable European Union, European 
Banking Authority (EBA), and national legal requirements. The Board 
and senior management are provided with quarterly reports to sup­
port follow-up and strategic oversight. 
Corruption and bribery
Like other business conduct matters, the Board has overarching 
responsibility for anti-corruption and bribery in SEB and is informed 
through relevant reporting on a regular basis. The CEO is responsible 
for execution and day-to-day management of related activities. The 
anti-corruption policy is reviewed annually and adopted by the Board.
 Impact, risk and opportunity management
IRO-1
Processes to identify and assessment  
financial crime impacts and risks
SEB is committed to safeguarding the financial system from misuse 
and criminal abuse, operating with integrity, transparency, and 
accountability. To combat financial crime, mitigate its impact on 
­society, and reduce the risk of SEB’s products and services being 
used to commit financial crimes, SEB has implemented a risk-based 
approach across all areas of its business. SEB conducts an annual, 
Group-wide risk assessment of financial crime risks, evaluating how 
products, services, geographies, and customer segments could 
potentially be exploited. 
The results of this assessment directly inform the design and 
implementation of internal rules, controls, and monitoring proce­
dures, ensuring that preventive measures are proportionate, tar­
geted, and aligned with actual risk exposure.
SEB does not have formally assigned functions-at-risk, instead 
SEB’s annual risk analyses include which corruption risks SEB faces 
and to what extent business areas are exposed. Conclusions from 
these analyses form the basis for actions and controls during 
the year. 
MDR-P
Policies related to  
financial crime
The bank’s financial crime prevention measures are guided by a 
­risk-based methodology, aligned with the Swedish Anti-Money 
­Laundering Act, EU directives, and European Banking Authority (EBA) 
Guidelines, and are implemented through comprehensive group-wide 
policies for financial crime, e.g., Policy on Anti-Money Laundering and 
Combating Financing of Terrorism for the SEB Group and Sanctions 
Policy for the SEB Group. The Board approves these policies, which 
set clear principles and requirements based on SEB’s risk appetite 
framework, to ensure regulatory compliance and effectively mitigate 
money laundering, terrorist financing, and sanctions risks.
In addition, SEB has an established Anti-Corruption Policy, reflect­
ing relevant applicable regulations and the “Code to Prevent Corrup­
tion in Business” by the Swedish Anti-Corruption Institute. The policy 
is reviewed annually and adopted by the Board.

measures at SEB. It establishes principles for analysing corruption 
risks and implementing preventive measures based on the outcomes 
of such analyses. Additionally, the policy provides guidance for

Prevention and detection of financial crime ­
Financial crime
A core element of SEB’s approach to prevent and detect financial 
crime is Know Your Customer (KYC). The bank collects sufficient 
information to verify each customer’s identity, ownership structures, 
purpose of the relationship, and expected transactional behaviour. 
Customers are assigned risk profiles based on assessments and 
ongoing updates about their activity. 
Higher-risk relationships are subject to enhanced due diligence, 
stricter controls, and continuous monitoring. Transaction anomalies 
are investigated using behavioural indicators and advanced data 
­analytics, and when necessary, Suspicious Activity Reports, 
­Suspicious Transaction Reports, or Terror Financing Reports are 
­submitted to the competent authorities. Customer relationships 
may be restricted or terminated to prevent misuse.
To manage the high volume of transactions and evolving threats, 
SEB uses advanced automated monitoring and screening systems. 
These systems employ scenario-based logic to detect potentially 
­suspicious activity in real time or post-event, with alerts escalated 
for detailed review and investigations. 
Algorithm-based systems are treated as formal models subject 
to rigorous validation, including testing of assumptions, accuracy 
­verification, and ongoing model risk management. This ensures that 
monitoring systems remain effective, transparent, and aligned with 
regulatory standards.
SEB also ensures full compliance with international sanctions 
regimes, screening customers, transactions, and counterparties 
against up-to-date lists, while actively preventing external fraud, 
including cyber-enabled fraud, identity theft, and payment fraud. 
Fraud controls integrate authentication, behavioural analytics, and 
real-time monitoring, and are continuously updated to respond to 
new patterns and threats.
Through this integrated, risk-based, and governance-driven 
­framework, SEB actively manages financial crime risks with rigour 
and accountability. These actions protect the bank, its customers, 
and society, strengthen the integrity of the financial system, and 
­reinforce SEB’s position as a responsible, resilient, and transparent 
financial partner. 
SEB has a structured incident handling framework to manage situa­
tions where preventive measures may not fully avert financial crime 
risks. All incidents are promptly identified, escalated, and investi­
gated, with clear accountability and governance. Lessons learned are 
systematically used to strengthen controls and enhance the overall 
Financial Crime Prevention framework, ensuring continuous improve­
ment, transparency, and resilience in protecting customers and the 
financial system.
Training and awareness are central to preventing, detecting, and 
responding to financial crime. Knowledge, awareness, and a strong 
risk culture are embedded across SEB, from the Board to all employ­
ees. Mandatory programs on anti-money laundering, combating 
financing of terrorism, sanctions, fraud awareness, and the Code of 
Conduct combined with targeted role-based training strengthen the 
capabilities of employees exposed to financial crime risks and those 
who work in dedicated roles to prevent financial crime. 
SEB is part of the public-private partnership Swedish Anti-Money 
Laundering Intelligence Task Force (SAMLIT), a collaboration 
between Sweden’s major banks and the Swedish Police, supported 
by the Swedish Bankers’ Association and the National Operations 
Department (NOA). 
SEB has also seconded staff to the Finansiellt Underrättelse­
centrum (FINUC). FINUC builds on the foundation laid by SAMLIT 
and is aligned with Article 75 of the forthcoming EU AML Regulation 
(AMLR), which will enter into force in 2027. FINUC is structured as ­
a central hub that brings together key stakeholders for intelli­
gence-sharing and collaboration. 
Corruption and bribery
SEB actively works to prevent the risk of being used for corruption 
in line with applicable laws and regulations, internal rules, and high 
ethical standards. 
To ensure that all employees and relevant contractors maintain a 
general understanding of anti-corruption and bribery measures and 
the associated risks, SEB requires completion of the mandatory Code 
of Conduct training every third year. The training includes modules on 
anti-corruption and bribery. In addition, staff is reminded by senior 
management of the rules around gift and business entertainment on 
an annual basis. The Code is also part of the training for the Board.
Processes to investigate business conduct incidents, including 
­corruption and bribery, are elaborated on in S1-3, see p. 135. 
­Incidents handled by the committees described in S1-3 are processed 
anonymously to ensure impartial decisions.
No SEB employee has been convicted of any violations of 
­anti-­corruption or anti-bribery laws during 2025. ­Consequently, 
no fines have been imposed.

Financial crime prevention is a vital part of SEB’s business, and we 
have zero tolerance towards such crimes. SEB has well-established

compliance, outlined in Figure 68.
To support this work, SEB uses a structured set of Key Risk 
­Indicators (KRIs), and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) to continu­
ously and periodically monitor progress against defined targets. 
These metrics provide transparency on risk exposure, control effec­
tiveness, and operational performance, enabling proactive manage­
ment and ongoing enhancement of SEB’s financial crime prevention 
framework. These metrics are not publicly disclosed, as they are 
­classified as sensitive information.
In addition, SEB measures and monitors employee training and 
awareness, through the completion rate of the mandatory financial 
crime trainings for all employees. See Figure 69. On average for 
these three trainings, the completion rate was 95 per cent in 2025. 
Corruption and bribery
SEB does not tolerate unlawful or unethical business practices, 
including any involvement in or association with corruption under any 
circumstances. No SEB employee, board member, independent con­
tractor, consultant, or other party representing or associated with 
SEB may, directly or indirectly, offer, promise, give, solicit, or accept 
a bribe. 
SEB monitors the completion rate for the mandatory Code of 
­Conduct training to ensure a high level of employee awareness of 
the bank’s stance on corruption and bribery, prevention measures 
and risks. See Figure 70.

06. Other information

EU Taxonomy disclosures
SEB is subject to the EU Taxonomy reporting requirements and 
prepares a consolidated Sustainability Statement covering the 
Taxonomy disclosures of the parent bank and the subsidiaries 
within the SEB Group. For the 2025 reporting SEB has applied 
the disclosure requirements set out in the Delegated Acts 
applicable until 31 December 2025. The amending Delegated 
Regulation (EU) 2026/73, applicable from 1 January 2026, 
will be implemented by SEB for the 2026 year-end report.
As a credit institution, the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) is SEB’s 
primary EU Taxonomy KPI (see tables 1-5). The GAR is calcu­
lated based on the prudential scope of consolidation in accord­
ance with the Capital Requirements Regulation (EU) 575/2013 
(CRR), under which SEB’s insurance entities are included using 
the equity method. As a financial conglomerate, SEB also 
­discloses business segment KPIs and consolidated KPIs (see 
tables 8-10) in line with the European Commission’s Third 
Notice (EC) 2024/6691. Business segment KPIs covering 
banking, asset management, and insurance activities are 
reported at Group level. The Group-consolidated KPIs 
­represent weighted averages of the segment KPIs, using the 
2024 proportion of revenue derived from each respective 
activity relative to total revenue as weighting factors. 
The activities and business model of the Group, as well as 
those of individual entities within the Group, are assessed to 
be coherent in all significant respects, meaning that no mate­
rial differences in risks or impacts have been identified. 
Accordingly, the disclosed segment level and consolidated 
KPIs are considered to provide a relevant and representative 
view of the Group’s activities. For information about subsidi­
aries exempt from publishing their own non-financial infor­
mation pursuant to Article 19a(9) and Article 29a(9) of the 
Accounting Directive, see BP-1, Basis for Preparation of the 
Sustainability Statement, p. 80.
Evaluation of assets and investments 
for alignment with the EU Taxonomy
The reported Taxonomy KPIs are based on the classification 
of the underlying economic activities that SEB finances, 
invests in, and provides financial services to. The 2025 dis­
closures cover assets only, while the reporting of revenues 
(fees and commissions) and transactions (trading book) 
has been postponed until 2027, in accordance with the 
­European Commission’s Fourth Notice and the amending 
Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/73.
Credit institutions calculate and disclose KPIs based 
on turnover and CapEx, respectively. The classification of 
general purpose exposures and investments (with unknown 
use of proceeds) is based on the Taxonomy KPIs reported 
by each counterparty or investee subject to the Taxonomy 
reporting requirements. Classification of purpose-based 
loans (with known use of proceeds) shall be based on 
­information that enables an individual assessment.
 
Data sources and limitations
To fulfil the Taxonomy reporting requirements, financial 
­institutions rely on the underlying Taxonomy KPIs reported 
by both financial and non-financial counterparties and inves­
tees, as well as on energy performance and geolocation data 
for residential real estate collateral related to mortgages. 
Access to data, its coverage, timeliness, and quality is key. 
SEB sources Taxonomy data from external data provid­
ers. Deficiencies in data quality have been observed, 
­stemming from inaccuracies in both reported data and in 
third-party data collection. SEB has taken steps to exclude 
erroneous corporate data. Where data failed internal 
­validity checks, logical consistency tests, or comparisons, 
the relevant data were set to zero (0) at the counterparty 
or investee level. Adjustments include:
•	 Where disaggregated aligned values for environmental 
objectives exceeded the corresponding eligible values, 
the aligned values were set to zero.
•	 Where the sum of eligible or aligned values for the 
­environmental objectives exceeded the total eligible or 
aligned values, the disaggregated values were set to zero.
Based on analysis of the data, the reported total eligible and 
total aligned ratios were assessed as more reliable and there­
fore were not set to zero. As a result, the sum of KPIs ­broken 
down by environmental objective may appear lower than the 
total figures. 
For parent companies reporting consolidated Taxonomy 
KPIs, the parent company’s KPIs are applied to exposures 
to subsidiaries within the reporting group. 
Loans with a known use of proceeds must be evaluated 
for compliance with the alignment criteria on the basis of 
adequate documentary evidence provided by the counter­
party. Due to challenges related to collecting, validating, 
documenting, and assessing the fulfilment of alignment 
­criteria for each individual loan and counterparty, SEB has 
not yet disclosed any purpose-based loans other than 
­mortgage loans. 
SEB’s household mortgage loans in Sweden and the 
­Baltic countries have been assessed as aligned based on 
the technical screening criteria set out in Section 7.7/7.1 
of Annex I to the Climate Delegated Act, including:
•	 Buildings constructed before 2021 with an Energy 
­Performance Certificate (EPC) class A
•	 Buildings constructed after August 2020 (in Sweden, 
BBR29) but before 2021 (new construction), falling 
within the top 15 per cent of the national building stock 
in terms of operational Primary Energy Demand (PED)
•	 Buildings constructed in 2021 or later with a PED at least 
10 per cent below the threshold set for nearly zero 
energy building (NZEB) requirements, under the applic­
able national standards (in Sweden BBR29). 
The top 15 per cent of buildings have been identified based 
on the PED thresholds established in each country. The Do No 
Significant Harm (DNSH) criterion has been evaluated for 
each property with respect to physical climate risks, specifi­
cally flooding, using available geolocation data and flood risk 
maps. The DNSH requirement is considered met only where 
the risk of flooding is assessed as excluded.

Nuclear energy and fossil gas-related activities reported in accordance 
with the EU Commission Delegated Regulation 2022/1214
For the financial year 2025, SEB Group continues to report on 
exposures to economic activities in nuclear energy and fossil 
gas in accordance with the European Commission’s Delega­
ted Regulations (EU) 2021/2139 and 2022/1214. From 2026 
onward, we will report on environmentally sustainable activi­
ties in line with the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 
2026/73, which entered into force on 28 January 2026. The 
revised regulation is intended to simplify the content and pre­
sentation of sustainability-related information. With the entry 
into force of the regulation, reporting on nuclear energy and 
fossil gas activities will be subject to materiality, and at pre­
sent there is no indication that the activities are material for 
any of the reported SEB Group’s business segments. 
Nevertheless, SEB will assess their materiality and relevance 
for future reporting.
As in the prior year, we disclose key performance indica­
tors for four areas identified as relevant for nuclear energy 
and fossil gas activities referred to in Sections 4.26-4.31 of 
Annexes I and II to Delegated Regulation 2021/2139: credit 
portfolio, financial guarantees, asset management and insur­
ance. Additionally, we provide consolidated KPIs for SEB 
Group, which are presented as weighted averages of the cor­
responding KPIs for these four segments. Weightings reflect 
each segment’s share of SEB Group’s consolidated revenue. 
The scope of assets included in these KPIs is consistent with 
the scope of assets covered by the KPIs disclosed in accord­
ance with Annexes IV, VI, and X to the Commission Delegated 
Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 in this report. 
We calculate the KPIs using financial exposures as of 31 
December 2025 and the most recent available data from 
counterparties and investees on the proportion of their busi­
ness activities linked to nuclear energy and fossil gas. Data is 
sourced from third‑party providers that collect reported infor­
mation from companies’ own disclosures. The KPIs are pre­
sented relative to both the denominator (total covered 
assets) and the numerator (the value of assets associated 
with Taxonomy‑aligned activities). Turnover‑based KPIs for 
the climate change adaptation (CCA) objective are not 
­applicable, as the relevant nuclear and fossil gas activities 
are not classified as enabling activities under the Climate 
­Delegated Act.
While CapEx related to making an activity climate-resilient 
is relevant for reporting, no significant exposures to nuclear 
energy or fossil gas activities associated with the CCA objec­
tive have been identified. Flow-related KPIs for nuclear and 
fossil gas activities are not disclosed separately, as no signifi­
cant new investments have been linked to these activities 
across the four areas based on the currently available data. 
While SEB Group has borrowers and investees in the nuclear 
and fossil gas sectors, the new exposures to these activities 
appear to be minimal. This could be due to continued limita­
tions in the availability and quality of data on nuclear energy 
and fossil gas activities, with inherent data deficiencies 
­persisting even in the third year of reporting.
Due to the lack of complete and consistent data, meaning­
ful conclusions and comparisons remain difficult. With the 
entry into force of the Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/73, 
SEB will reassess the materiality and reporting relevance 
of these activities for future disclosures. As this set of KPIs 
becomes integrated into the core Taxonomy reporting 
­templates from 2026, we expect more accurate application 
of denominators and greater methodological consistency 
from reporting entities, reducing the need for our own data 
quality adjustments in future reporting cycles. However, as 
the revised regulation will apply to a smaller population of 
companies, the overall coverage of reported data is expected 
to decrease. While the narrower scope may help reduce 
­certain qualitative gaps through more consistent reporting, 
it may simultaneously widen quantitative gaps, as the under­
lying data will represent a smaller share of our financial 
­exposures.

Although the mandatory reporting requirements for non­
financial undertakings commenced in 2022, and for financial 
undertakings in 2023, the reported data is still characterised 
by the significant qualitative and quantitative gaps. Although 
our aim is to rely on company‑reported data wherever possi­

reduce inaccuracies in our KPIs. Some companies reported 
proportions of nuclear and fossil gas activities relative to the 
value of those activities rather than to their total revenue or 
total CapEx, as required for Tables 2, 4 and 5. To avoid distor­
tions in our KPI calculations, we excluded datapoint values 
that were clearly erroneous and would otherwise materially 
distort our results.
SEB Group’s exposure to nuclear and 
fossil gas activities in 2025 
Activities referred to in Sections 4.26-4.31 of Annexes I and II 
to Delegated Regulation 2021/2139 represent a very small 
proportion of SEB Group’s business. Turnover‑ and CapEx‑­
based KPIs indicate that the proportion of Taxonomy‑­aligned 
nuclear and fossil gas activities relative to the gross carrying 
amount or total covered assets (denominator) remains low, 
ranging from 0.00 to 0.05 per cent across ­business segments.
For turnover-based KPIs, the collective contribution of the 
nuclear and fossil gas activities to the total value of SEB’s 
assets associated with Taxonomy-aligned activities 
(­numerator) is as follows: 
• Credit portfolio: 0.45 per cent
• Asset management: 2.49 per cent
• Insurance: 1.76 per cent
• Financial guarantees: 0.
For CapEx-based KPIs, the contribution of these activities in 
the numerator is respectively: 
• Credit portfolio: 0.22 per cent
• Asset management: 1.77 per cent
• Insurance: 1.03 per cent
• Financial guarantees: 0.
Overall trends are broadly consistent with the prior year, 
based on the currently available data. At Group-consolidated 
level, the largest share of Taxonomy‑aligned nuclear and 
­fossil gas activities is attributable to construction and safe 
operation of new nuclear power plants (activity referred to in 
Section 4.27), and electricity generation from nuclear energy 
in existing installations (activity referred to in Section 4.28). 
This is reflected in both turnover- and CapEx-based KPIs for 
all segments except financial guarantees. No significant 
exposure has been observed within financial guarantees. 
Electricity generation from fossil gaseous fuels (activity 
referred to in Section 4.29) and high-efficiency co-generation 
of heat/cool and power from fossil gaseous fuels (activity 
referred to in Section 4.30) comprise the majority of 
Taxonomy‑­eligible but not aligned activities. This pattern 
is predominantly evident in turnover-based KPIs, while 
its influence on CapEx-based KPIs appears to be less 
­substantial.

Accounting policies
Significant accounting policies 
for the group
Statement of compliance
The group’s consolidated accounts have been prepared in 
accordance with the International Financial Reporting 
Standards (IFRS) and interpretations of these standards as 
adopted by the EU. The accounting also follows the Annual 
Accounts Act for Credit Institutions and Securities Compa­
nies (1995:1559) and the regulation and general guidelines 
issued by the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority, 
Annual Reports in Credit Institutions and Securities Compa­
nies (FFFS 2008:25). In addition to this the Supplementary 
Accounting Rules for Groups RFR 1 and the additional UFR 
statements issued by the Swedish Corporate Reporting 
Board have been applied.
Basis of preparation
The consolidated accounts are based on amortised cost, 
except for the fair value measurement of financial assets at 
fair value through other comprehensive income, financial 
assets and liabilities measured at fair value through profit or 
loss including derivatives and investment properties meas­
ured at fair value. The carrying amount of financial assets 
and liabilities subject to hedge accounting at fair value has 
been adjusted for changes in fair value attributable to the 
hedged risk. The financial statements are presented in mil­
lion Swedish kronor (SEKm), unless indicated otherwise.
Significant accounting judgements, 
­estimates and assumptions
In preparing the group’s consolidated financial statements, 
management has made judgements, estimates and assump­
tions, that affect the reported amounts of revenues, 
expenses, assets and liabilities, and the accompanying dis­
closures. Uncertainty about these assumptions and esti­
mates could result in outcomes that require a material 
adjustment to the carrying amount of assets or liabilities 
affected in future periods. The estimates are based on 
expert judgements and assumptions that management 
believes are true and fair. The management continuously 
evaluates these judgements and estimates. The significant 
accounting judgements, estimates and assumptions which 
management has assessed to have the most significant 
effects are described in relevant sections below.
Consolidation
Subsidiaries
The consolidated accounts combine the financial statements 
of the parent company and its subsidiaries. Subsidiaries are 
companies, over which the group has control. The group 
­controls an entity when it has power over an investee, is 
exposed to, or has rights to, variable returns from its involve­
ment and has the ability to use its power to affect the 
amount of the returns. Control is deemed to exist when the 
parent company holds, directly or indirectly, more than 
50 per cent of the voting rights, unless there is evidence that 
another investor has the practical ability to unilaterally 
direct the relevant activities of the entity. Companies in 
which the parent company or its subsidiaries hold more than 
50 per cent of the votes but are unable to exercise control 
due to contractual or legal reasons, are not included in the 
consolidated accounts. The group also assesses if control 
exists when it holds less than 50 per cent of the voting rights. 
The financial statements of the parent company and the 
consolidated subsidiaries refer to the same period and have 
been drawn up according to the accounting policies applica­
ble to the group. A subsidiary is included in the consolidated 
accounts from the time of acquisition, being the date when 
the parent company gains control over the subsidiary. The 
subsidiary is included in the consolidated accounts until the 
date when control over the company ceases to exist.
Business combinations are accounted for using the acqui­
sition method. The acquisition value is measured as the fair 
value of the assets given, equity instruments issued and lia­
bilities incurred or assumed. The identifiable assets 
acquired, the liabilities and contingent liabilities assumed in 
a business combination are measured initially at their fair 
values on acquisition date, irrespective of any non-control­
ling interest. The excess of the consideration transferred for 
the acquisition over the fair value of the group’s share of the 
identifiable acquired net assets is recorded as goodwill. If 
the consideration transferred is less than the fair value of the 
net assets of the acquired subsidiary, the difference is recog­
nised directly against profit or loss.

Intra-group transactions, balance sheet items and unreal­
ised gains and losses on transactions between group compa­

Significant accounting judgements, estimates 
and assumptions – Consolidation of mutual life 
­insurance companies and funds 
Within the life insurance operations of the SEB Group, Gamla 
Livförsäkringsaktiebolaget SEB Trygg Liv operates as a 
mutual life insurance company. The entity is not consoli­
dated, as the judgement of the group is that it does not have 
control of the entity. Control is seen to imply the power to 
govern the financial and operating policies of an entity in 
order to affect the amount of its returns from the entity. Life 
insurance entities operated as mutual life insurance compa­
nies cannot pay dividends which is why the group deems 
that it cannot obtain benefits. In Gamla Livförsäkringsaktie­
bolaget SEB Trygg Liv there are specific policies specifying 
the composition of the board, which implies that the SEB 
Group is not able to govern the financial and operating poli­
cies of the entity.
In the assessment whether to consolidate funds, an 
assessment is made whether the group is considered to be 
an agent or a principal. The group is considered a principal, 
and hence controls the fund, when it is the fund manager, 
cannot be removed without cause, has significant right to 
returns from the fund by holding units and earning fee 
income and has the practical ability to influence its return by 
using its power. Funds managed by the group in which enti­
ties within the group owns more than 20 per cent are ana­
lysed further for consolidation. 
The policyholders in SEB’s unit-linked company choose to 
invest in a variety of funds. The insurance company provid­
ing unit-linked products invests in the funds chosen by the 
customers. By doing so SEB might, in some cases, hold more 
than 50 per cent of the funds, which it holds on behalf of the 
customers for whom it acts as investment manager. Due to 
the legislation regarding fund operations, SEB considers that 
it does not have the power to govern the financial and oper­
ating policies of such investment funds to obtain benefits. 
This applies irrespective of whether the funds held on behalf 
of customers are greater or less than 50 per cent of a fund. It 
is the policyholders who carry the investment risk, not SEB. 
Consequently, the policyholders are entitled to all of the 
returns generated by the funds. SEB only charges fees, on 
market conditions, for managing the funds. SEB has come to 
the conclusion that these funds which it manages should not 
be consolidated. However, the shares that the group holds in 
such funds on behalf of its customers are recognised in the 
balance sheet.
Associated companies and joint ventures
The consolidated accounts also include associated compa­
nies and joint ventures that are companies in which the 
group has significant influence or joint control, but not sole 
control. Significant influence means that the group can par­
ticipate in the financial and operating policy decisions of the 
company, whilst not determining or controlling such financial 
and operating policies. A significant influence is generally 
deemed to exist if the group, directly or indirectly, holds 
between 20 and 50 per cent of the voting rights of an entity. 
A joint venture is an arrangement in which the group has joint 
control, whereby the group has rights to the net assets of the 
arrangement rather than rights to its assets and obligations 
for its liabilities.
According to the main principle, associated companies 
and joint ventures are consolidated in accordance with the 
equity method. This means that the holding is initially 
reported at its acquisition cost. Associated companies and 
joint ventures are subsequently carried at a value that corre­
sponds to the group’s share of the net assets. However, the 
group has chosen to designate investments in associates 
held by the group’s venture capital organisation at fair value 
through profit or loss on the basis that these are managed 
and evaluated based on fair value. 
Segment reporting
An operating segment is identified on the basis of internal 
reports about components of the group that are regularly 
reviewed by the chief operating decision maker in order to 
allocate resources to the segments and to assess their per­
formance. The business divisions are identified as separate 
operating segments, considering size and regulatory envi­
ronment. Group functions consists of Group & Business Ser­
vices, Technology, Treasury, staff units, SEBx, SEB Embed­
ded and German run-off operations. In the context of 
defining the segments the President and Chief Executive 
Officer (CEO) is the group’s chief operating decision maker.
Foreign currency translation 
Foreign currency transactions are translated into the appro­
priate functional currency using the exchange rates prevail­
ing at the dates of the transactions. On subsequent balance 
sheet dates monetary items in foreign currency are trans­
lated using the closing rate. Non-monetary items, which are 
measured in terms of historical cost in foreign currency, are 
translated using the exchange rate on the date of the trans­
action. Non-monetary items, which are measured at fair 
value in a foreign currency, are translated applying the 
exchange rate on the date on which the fair value is deter­
mined.
Gains and losses arising as a result of exchange rate dif­
ferences on settlement or translation of monetary items are 
recognised in profit or loss. Translation differences on non-
monetary items, classified as financial assets or financial lia­
bilities at fair value through profit or loss, are included in the 
change in fair value of those items. Translation differences 
from non-monetary items, e.g. financial assets at fair value 
through other comprehensive income, are recognised in 
other comprehensive income. Exchange rate differences 
referring to monetary items comprising part of a net invest­
ment in a foreign operation are reported in other comprehen­
sive income.
The income statements and balance sheets of group enti­
ties, with a functional currency other than the group’s pres­
entation currency, are translated to SEK in the consolidated 
accounts. Assets and liabilities in foreign group entities are 
translated at the closing rate and income and expenses in 
the income statement are translated at the average 
exchange rate for the year. The exchange rate differences 
are recognised as a separate component of other compre­
hensive income.
Goodwill arising in conjunction with acquisitions of for­
eign group entities, as well as adjustments to the fair value 
of assets and liabilities made in conjunction with acquisitions 
are included in the assets and liabilities of the foreign entity 
in question and are translated at the closing rate.
Financial assets and liabilities
Financial assets are recognised on the balance sheet when 
the group becomes a party to the contractual provisions of 
the instrument and are measured at fair value on initial rec­
ognition. Transaction costs are included in the fair value on 
initial recognition except for financial assets at fair value 
through profit or loss where transaction costs are expensed 
in profit or loss. Financial assets are derecognised when the 
rights to receive cash flows have expired, the group has 
transferred substantially all risks and rewards and upon sub­
stantial modification. Transfers of financial assets with 
retention of all or substantially all risks and rewards include 
for example repurchase transactions and securities lending 
transactions. Financial assets at fair value are recognised on 
the balance sheet on trade date, with exception of loans and 
reversed repos which are recognised on settlement date. 
Financial assets measured at amortised cost are recognised 
on settlement date. 
Financial liabilities are measured at fair value on initial 
recognition. In the case of financial liabilities measured at 
fair value through profit or loss, transaction costs directly 
attributable to the acquisition or the issuance of the financial 
liability are recognised in profit or loss. For other financial lia­
bilities direct transaction cost are recognised as a deduction 
from the fair value. Financial liabilities are derecognised 
when extinguished, that is, when the obligation is dis­
charged, cancelled or expired.
Classification of financial assets and liabilities 
The group classifies and subsequently measures its financial 
assets in the following categories: financial instruments at 
fair value through profit or loss; fair value through other 
comprehensive income and amortised cost. The classifica­
tion will depend on if the financial asset is a debt instrument, 
an equity instrument or a derivative.

Note G1 continued Accounting policies
Debt instruments (Loans and debt securities)
The classification is based on a combination of assessing the 
business model for managing the financial assets and 
whether the contractual cash flow characteristics consist of 
solely payments of principal and interest (‘SPPI’). The busi­
ness model assessment is performed for homogenous port­
folios identified based on how the business is managed in the 
divisions of the group. The assessment is based on reasona­
ble scenarios taking into consideration how the portfolio is 
evaluated and reported to management; the risks affecting 
the performance of the portfolio and how these risks are 
managed; how managers are compensated; and the fre­
quency, value and timing of sales including the reasons for 
the sales. In determining if the cash flows consist solely of 
principal and interest, the principal is defined as the fair 
value of the debt instrument at initial recognition, which can 
change over the life if there are repayments or capitalisation 
of interest. Interest cash flows are consistent with compo­
nents with a basic lending arrangement including considera­
tion for time value of money, credit risk, liquidity risk as well 
as administrative costs and profit margin. If there are con­
tractual features introducing an exposure to other risks or 
volatility, it is not considered to consist of solely payments of 
principal and interest. Debt instruments are presented in the 
balance sheet items; Cash and cash balances at central 
banks, Loans to credit institutions, Loans to the public and 
Debt securities, and include instruments in the following 
measurement categories. 
Fair value through profit or loss: Debt instruments are clas­
sified in this category if not meeting the criteria for amor­
tised cost or fair value through other comprehensive income. 
This is the case if the business model is held for trading; 
where financial assets are considered held for trading if they 
are held with the intention to be sold in the short-term and 
for the purpose of generating profits. Debt instruments are 
mandatorily measured at fair value through profit or loss if 
the assets are managed and evaluated on a fair value basis 
or the assets are held with an intention to sell alternatively if 
the cash flows do not consist of solely payments of principal 
and interest. Debt instruments that would otherwise be clas­
sified as fair value through other comprehensive income or 
amortised cost are also included in this category if, upon ini­
tial recognition, designated at fair value through profit or 
loss (fair value option). The fair value option can be applied 
only in situations where such designation reduces measure­
ment inconsistencies. 
Amortised cost: Debt instruments are classified in this cat­
egory if both of the following criteria are met (a) the busi­
ness model objective is to hold assets to collect contractual 
cash flows and (b) the contractual cash flow characteristics 
consist of solely payments of principal and interest. The 
gross carrying amount of these assets is measured using the 
effective interest method and adjusted for expected credit 
losses.
Equity instruments
Equity instruments are classified as financial assets at fair 
value through profit or loss. 
Derivatives
Derivatives are classified as fair value through profit or loss 
(held for trading) unless designated as hedging instruments. 
If designated as hedging instruments, the principles for 
hedge accounting are applied. 
Financial liabilities
Financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss: Financial 
liabilities at fair value through profit or loss are either classi­
fied as held for trading or designated as fair value through 
profit or loss on initial recognition (fair value option). 
Changes in fair value are recognised in profit or loss within 
Net financial income, with the exception of changes in fair 
value due to changes in the group’s own credit risk. Such 
changes are presented in other comprehensive income, with 
no subsequent reclassification to the income statement. The 
fair value option can be applied for classification of financial 
liabilities if meeting either of the following criteria: the con­
tracts include one or more embedded derivatives, the instru­
ments are managed and evaluated on a fair value basis or in 
situations where such designation reduces measurement 
inconsistencies. Liabilities to policyholders and some debt 
securities are included in this category. Financial liabilities 
held for trading are primarily short positions in interest-bear­
ing securities, equity instruments and derivatives not desig­
nated as hedging instruments. 
Other financial liabilities: The category other financial lia­
bilities primarily include the group’s short-term and long-
term borrowings. After initial recognition other financial lia­
bilities are measured at amortised cost, using the effective 
interest method. The balance sheet items Deposits from 
central banks and credit institutions, Deposits and borrow­
ings from the public and Debt securities issued are included 
in this category.
Embedded derivatives
Some combined contracts contain both a derivative and a 
non-derivative component. In such cases, the derivative 
component is termed an embedded derivative. If the host 
contract is a financial asset in scope of IFRS 9 Financial 
Instruments, the contract is assessed for classification in its 
entirety and the embedded derivative is not separated. For 
other hybrid instruments (i.e. the host contract is not a finan­
cial asset in scope of IFRS 9) where the economic character­
istics and risks of the embedded derivatives are not closely 
related to those of the host contract, the embedded deriva­
tive is bifurcated and reported at fair value with gains and 
losses being recognised in the income statement. This does 
not apply if the host contract is carried at fair value through 
profit or loss.
Certain combined instruments are classified as financial 
liabilities at fair value through profit or loss according to the 
fair value option. The designation implies that the entire 
combined instrument is measured at fair value through profit 
and loss. 
Offsetting financial transactions
Financial assets and liabilities are offset and the net amount 
reported in the balance sheet when there is a legal right to 
offset transactions and an intention to settle net or realise 
the asset and settle the liability simultaneously.
Repurchase agreements
Securities may be lent or sold subject to a commitment to 
repurchase them (a ‘repo’) at a fixed price and at a predeter­
mined date. Such securities are retained on the balance 
sheet and in addition included separately as collateral 
pledged for own liabilities when cash consideration is 
received. Depending on the counterparty, payment received 
is recognised under Deposits by credit institutions or as 
Deposits and borrowing from the public. 
Similarly, where the group borrows or purchases securi­
ties subject to a commitment to resell them (a ‘reverse 
repo’), the securities are not included in the balance sheet. 
Payments made are recognised as Loans to credit institu­
tions or as Loans to the public.
The difference between sale and repurchase price is 
accrued over the life of the agreements using the effective 
interest method.
Securities borrowing and lending
Securities borrowing and lending transactions are entered 
into on a collateralised basis. Fair values of securities 
received or delivered are monitored on a daily basis to 
require or provide additional collateral. Cash collateral deliv­
ered is derecognised from the balance sheet and a corre­
sponding receivable is recognised. Cash collateral received 
is recognised in the balance sheet and a corresponding obli­
gation to return it, is recognised. Securities lent remain on 
the balance sheet and are in addition reported as pledged 
assets. Borrowed securities are not recognised as assets. 
When borrowed securities are sold (short position), an 
amount corresponding to the fair value of the securities is 
booked as a liability. Securities received in a borrowing or 
lending transaction are disclosed as obligations.
Modification 
The group may renegotiate loans and modify contractual 
terms. If the new terms are substantially different from the 
original terms, the group derecognises the original financial 
asset and recognises a new asset. The group also assesses 
whether the new financial asset is credit-impaired at initial 
recognition. If the terms are not substantially different, the 
modification does not result in derecognition and the group 
recalculates the gross carrying amount based on the new 
cash flows using the original effective interest rate of the 
financial asset and recognises a modification gain or loss.
Fair value measurement
Fair value is defined as the price that would be received to 
sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly mar­
ket between market participants at the measurement date.
